en: The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra of the Mahāyāna, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, by Imperial Command.
Chapter One: The Request of King Rāvaṇa Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Malaya by the shore of the great ocean, within the city of Laṅkā, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas.

All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had already thoroughly mastered the five dharmas, the three natures, and the selflessness of all consciousnesses; they were well-versed in the meaning that objective realms are manifestations of one's own mind. They sported in immeasurable sovereign samādhis, supernatural powers, and various strengths, manifesting diverse forms according to the minds of sentient beings to subdue them through skillful means. All Buddhas had poured water upon their crowns, and they had all come to this assembly from various Buddha-lands, with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati as their leader.

At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma in the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara. After seven days had passed, he emerged from the great ocean, whereupon immeasurable billions of Brahmās, Śakras, World-Protectors, devas, nāgas, and others came forth to welcome the Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata raised his eyes and beheld the great city of Laṅkā on Mount Malaya; he then smiled and spoke these words:

"In the past, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have, within this very city, expounded the Dharma realized through their own noble wisdom—a realm that is not the object of the speculative false views of the non-Buddhists nor the sphere of practice for the followers of the Two Vehicles. I, too, shall now reveal this Dharma for King Rāvaṇa."

At that time, Rāvaṇa, the Yakṣa King, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, heard the sound of the Buddha’s voice. He learned from afar that the Tathāgata had emerged from the Dragon Palace, surrounded by Brahmā, Śakra, the World-Protectors, devas, and nāgas. Seeing the waves of the ocean, he observed that within the great ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*—the realm of the assembly—the winds of objective conditions were stirring the waves of the *pravṛttivijñānas*. Filled with joy, he raised his voice loudly within the city, proclaiming:
"I shall go to the Buddha and request him to enter this city, so that I and all the devas, humans, and worldlings may obtain great benefit throughout the long night."
Having spoken these words, he immediately ascended a flower-palace with his retinue and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
Upon arrival, he descended from the palace, circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, and performed various musical offerings to the Tathāgata.

The musical instruments they held were all made of great blue *indranīla* jewels, interspersed with *vaidūrya* and other precious gems, and wrapped in priceless upper garments. Their sounds were exquisite and their rhythms harmonized as they spoke verses in praise of the Buddha:
"The Dharma-treasury of the mind’s own nature, Selfless and free from the stains of views;
That which is known by realized wisdom— We pray that the Buddha will proclaim it for us."
The body is a collection of wholesome dharmas; realized wisdom is ever-abiding bliss.
O Master of Sovereign Transformations, we pray that you enter the city of Laṅkā.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past have all dwelt within this city.
"May this assembly of yakṣas, with one mind, wish to hear the Dharma.
At that time, Rāvaṇa, the King of Laṅkā, having praised the Buddha with the *dundubhaka* melody, further spoke these verses in song:
"The World-Honored One, for seven days, dwelt within the waters of the ocean of Magadha;"
Thereafter, he departed from the dragon palace and calmly ascended this shore.
I, along with my various court ladies, as well as the yakṣa retinue and Śuka-sarāna—
the most wise among the assembly— [accompanied him].
By means of their supernatural powers, they all proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata was;
each descended from their flower-palaces and paid homage to the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they addressed the Buddha and announced their own names:
"I am the Rākṣasa King, the ten-headed Rāvaṇa;
now I have come to the presence of the Buddha.
I pray that the Buddha will accept me, as well as all sentient beings within the city of Laṅkā."
The immeasurable Buddhas of the past, All ascended to the summit of the Jewel Mountain;
Dwelling within the city of Laṅkā, They expounded the Dharma realized by themselves.
The World-Honored One should likewise do so, Dwelling upon that mountain adorned with jewels.
Surrounded by the assembly of bodhisattvas, he expounds the pure Dharma.
We, on this very day, together with the multitude dwelling in Laṅkā,
desire with one mind to hear the Dharma that is beyond words and realized within oneself.
I recall all the immeasurable Buddhas of the past and future,
Surrounded by Bodhisattvas, as they expound the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
This scripture of the Laṅkāvatāra was praised by the Buddhas of old;
We pray that the Honored One will go together with us, and likewise expound [the Dharma] for the sake of the assembly.
We beseech the Buddha out of compassion for the immeasurable hosts of yakṣas to enter that city adorned with jewels and preach this wondrous Dharma gate.
This wondrous city of Laṅkā is adorned with various jewels;
its walls are not of earth or stone, and its nets are entirely of precious gems.
These hosts of yakṣas have, in the past, made offerings to the Buddhas.
Practicing to remain free from all faults, they realize and know with constant clarity.
The yakṣas, both male and female, thirst for and yearn for the Mahāyāna;
having gained confidence in the Mahāyāna themselves, they also delight in establishing others therein.
I pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One, for the sake of the assembly of rākṣasas and their retinue,
such as Kumbhakarṇa and others, will proceed to Laṅkāpurī.
Throughout the past, future, and present, I have diligently made offerings to all Buddhas.
I pray to hear the Dharma of self-realization, the ultimate path of the Mahāyāna.
May the Buddha, out of compassion for me and the host of yakṣas,
together with all the sons of the Buddhas, enter this city of Laṅkā.
My palace and its maidens, as well as all my necklaces and ornaments;
and the lovely Aśoka grove— I pray that the Buddha will compassionately accept them.
Regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there is nothing I would not relinquish.
"Even to the point of serving you with my own body, I only pray that you will compassionately accept me.
When the World-Honored One heard these words, he immediately addressed him, saying:
"Yakṣa King!"

In past ages, all the Great Teachers, out of compassion for you, accepted your invitation and went to the Jewel Mountain to preach the Dharma of their own realization; the Buddhas of the future shall do likewise.

"This is the dwelling place of those who practice profound contemplation and experience the happiness of the present life; out of compassion for you, I and the other bodhisattvas accept your request."
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
Then King Rāvaṇa immediately offered the exquisite Flower-Palace (Puṣpaka-vimāna) upon which he traveled to the Buddha;
the Buddha sat within it, while the king and the various bodhisattvas escorted him from front and rear. Immeasurable court ladies sang praises and offered worship as they proceeded toward that city.
Having arrived at that city, King Rāvaṇa and his retinue again presented various kinds of sublime offerings;
among the yakṣas, the boys and girls offered jeweled nets to the Buddha, and King Rāvaṇa bestowed precious necklaces upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to hang around their necks.
At that time, after the World-Honored One and the various bodhisattvas had accepted the offerings, each briefly expounded for them the profound Dharma of their own realized realm.
Then King Rāvaṇa, together with his retinue, again made offerings to Mahāmati Bodhisattva and entreated him, saying:
"I now request the Great Being to inquire on my behalf of the World-Honored One."
All Tathāgatas, the realm of their own realized wisdom—
I, together with the hosts of yakṣas And these bodhisattvas,
wish with one mind to hear it; Therefore, we all entreat you.
You are a practitioner, supreme among those who discourse;
therefore, out of respect, I urge you to inquire about the Dharma.
Having personally realized the pure Dharma, you have ultimately entered the stage of a Buddha.
"Free from the paths of externalists and those of the two vehicles, and devoid of all faults.

At that time, by means of his supernatural powers, the World-Honored One further manifested immeasurable jewel-mountains within those mountains, all adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite celestial jewels.
Upon each mountain, the body of a Buddha appeared; before each Buddha, there was King Rāvaṇa together with his assembly.
All lands throughout the ten directions appear therein;
in each and every land there is a Tathāgata;
and before each Buddha there is King Rāvaṇa together with his retinue.

In the Aśoka Garden of the great city of Laṅkā, the splendors were adorned in exactly this way, without any difference; in each instance, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati posed questions, and the Buddha revealed for him the realm of self-realized gnosis. Having spoken this sutra with hundreds of thousands of wondrous voices, the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas vanished from the air and became invisible.
King Rāvaṇa saw only himself remaining within his own palace and thought to himself:
"Who was that? Who heard what was said?"
What is it that is seen?
Who is it that is able to see?
Where now are such things as the Buddha, the city, the various jewels, the mountains, and the forests?
Is it created by a dream?
Is it produced by an illusion?
Or is it like a city of the Gandharvas?
Is it seen because of cataracts?
Is it deluded by a mirage?
Or is it like a stone woman giving birth to a child in a dream?
"Is it like smoke, a flame, or a whirling firebrand? He further reflected: "The nature of all dharmas is thus;

they are merely the objects of one's own mind’s discrimination. Ordinary people are deluded and cannot understand this. There is nothing that can see, nor anything that is seen; there is nothing that can speak, nor anything that is spoken. Seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma are both forms of discrimination. Just as what was seen before, one cannot see the Buddha; by not giving rise to discrimination, one is then able to see."
At that time, King Laṅkā immediately attained awakening; free from all defilements, he realized that [all things] are but his own mind and dwelt in non-conceptuality.
By the power of the roots of goodness planted in the past, he attained the vision of all phenomena as they truly are, no longer relying on the awakening of others.

Being able to skillfully observe with one’s own wisdom, they are forever free from all speculative and erroneous understandings. Abiding in great cultivation as a teacher of practice, they manifest various bodies and are adept in skillful means; they skillfully know the signs of progress through the stages (*bhūmi*). They constantly delight in distancing themselves from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); they sever the views of the three continuities, abandon the attachments of non-Buddhists, and through internal self-awakening, enter the *tathāgatagarbha* and proceed toward the stage of Buddhahood.
From within the void and inside the palace, voices were heard saying: "Excellent,
Great King!"
As you have studied, all practitioners should train in this way and see in this way; all Tathāgatas see in this way, for to view any of all dharmas otherwise is the view of annihilationism.

You should forever distance yourself from mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); you should diligently investigate all dharmas, cultivate internal practice, and not cling to external views. Do not fall into the two vehicles or among the non-Buddhists, nor become attached to the phrases and meanings of your cultivation, the realms you perceive, or the various *samādhi* dharmas you are to attain.

You should not delight in frivolous debate or idle chatter; you should not give rise to the various views of the Vedas, nor should you be attached to royal power or sovereignty, nor should you dwell within the six meditative concentrations and the like.

If one can act in this way, it is the practice of one who practices according to reality; such a person can refute the arguments of others and destroy evil views, can relinquish all attachment to the view of self, can transform the foundational consciousness through sublime wisdom, can cultivate the Mahāyāna path of the Bodhisattva, and can enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

You should thus diligently practice and study so that the dharmas you have attained become ever more pure. Skillfully cultivate samādhi and samāpatti, and do not cling to the realms of the two vehicles or external paths as supreme bliss, as ordinary practitioners falsely discriminate. Do not, like those of external paths who grasp at the view of self and perceive the marks of a self, or who give rise to attachment based on real *guṇas*, harbor such views. Nor should you, like those of the two vehicles who perceive ignorance as the condition for formations, engage in distracted conceptualization regarding the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
O King of Laṅkā!
This Dharma is supreme; it is the Mahāyāna path that enables the accomplishment of the noble wisdom of self-realization and leads to the attainment of sublime births within all realms of existence.
Lokagarbharāja!
This practice of the Mahāyāna shatters the cataracts of ignorance, extinguishes the waves of consciousness, and does not fall into the various erroneous practices of the non-Buddhists.
Lokagarbharāja!

The practitioners of external paths cling to a self and produce various heterodox arguments; they are unable to expound upon the two meanings of being free from clinging views and the nature of consciousness.
Excellent, O King of Laṅkā!
"You previously saw the Buddha while contemplating this meaning; to contemplate in such a way is indeed to see the Buddha. At that time, King Rāvaṇa again had this thought:
"May I once more be granted the privilege of seeing the Tathāgata.

The World-Honored Tathāgata, regarding Avalokiteśvara, has transcended the teachings of the non-Buddhists and is able to expound the realm of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). He surpasses all matters of manifested emanations and dwells in the concentration of the Tathāgata, entering the bliss of samādhi. For this reason, he is called the Great Master of Contemplative Practice and is also named the Great Compassionate One. He is able to burn away the fuel of afflictions and conceptual discrimination until it is exhausted; he is surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons, universally enters the hearts of all sentient beings, pervades all places, possesses all-knowledge, and is forever free from all conceptualized phenomena and signs."
I now pray that I may once again behold the Tathāgata’s great supernormal powers;

by virtue of beholding them, may I attain what I have not yet attained and not regress from what I have already attained, leaving behind all conceptual discrimination to dwell in the bliss of samādhi, and increasing and fulfilling the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that King Laṅkā was about to realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), manifested his body out of compassion so that the transformed scene returned to its original state.

At that time, King Daśaśīrṣa beheld what he had never seen before: immeasurable mountain cities, all adorned with jewels, and within each city was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
He saw his own body appearing before all the Buddhas, each surrounded by great wisdom-yakṣas who were expounding the Dharma practiced through the wisdom of personal realization;
he also saw the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, and that all such matters were without any distinction.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire assembly with his wisdom-eye rather than his physical eye; like a lion king, he turned his gaze with vigorous majesty and laughed heartily.

From the syllable *De* located between his eyebrows, upon his thighs, flanks, waist, neck, and shoulders and arms, immeasurable rays of wondrous-colored light were emitted from every single pore; they trailed like rainbows, radiated like the sun, and blazed like the fierce flames of the kalpa-ending fire.

At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the four heavenly kings, seeing from afar the Tathāgata sitting atop Mount Laṅkā, which was like Sumeru, laughing joyfully, all the bodhisattvas and the assembly of devas had this thought:
"The World-Honored Tathāgata possesses mastery over the Dharma; for what cause and condition does he laugh so joyfully?"

His body radiated light as he remained silent and motionless, dwelling in the realm of self-realization and entering the bliss of samādhi; like a lion king surveying his surroundings, he gazed upon Rāvaṇa while contemplating the Dharma as it truly is.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati had previously accepted the invitation of King Rāvaṇa; furthermore, he understood the thoughts of the assembly of bodhisattvas and observed all future sentient beings, who were all delighting in and attached to words and letters, grasping at meaning according to the words and thereby giving rise to delusion, and adhering to the practices of the two vehicles and non-Buddhists.
Some may think:
"The World-Honored One has already transcended the sphere of all consciousness; for what cause and condition does he smile with such great joy?
To sever that doubt, they question the Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, Mahamati! Excellent, Mahamati!"

Observe how you look upon the world with compassion for all sentient beings, who are entangled by evil views throughout the three periods of time; you have questioned me out of a desire to bring them to awakening.
Only those of wisdom, seeking the benefit of both themselves and others, are capable of asking such questions.
"Mahāmati!

This King of Laṅkā has previously inquired about the two kinds of meaning from all the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he now wishes to inquire about them as well, and so shall he in the future."
"The characteristics that differentiate these two kinds of meanings cannot be fathomed by any of the followers of the Two Vehicles or by any of the non-Buddhists.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that King Laṅkā was about to inquire about this meaning, addressed him, saying: "King Laṅkā!"

If you wish to question me, you should do so quickly; I shall analyze and explain it for you, fulfilling your aspirations and bringing you joy. By means of wisdom, you should contemplate and investigate, remaining free from all conceptual discrimination. You shall come to know well the stages (*bhūmi*) and their respective remedies, realize the true meaning, enter the bliss of samādhi, be sustained by all Tathāgatas, abide in the bliss of śamatha, remain far removed from the faults of the samādhis of the two vehicles, and dwell upon the Bodhisattva grounds of Immovable Wisdom and the Cloud of Dharma.
One who can know all phenomena as being without self as they truly are shall have the water of samādhi poured upon their crown within the Great Jewel Lotus Palace.

Furthermore, immeasurable lotuses will manifest surrounding them, with countless bodhisattvas dwelling therein; these beings and the entire assembly gaze at one another, and such a realm is inconceivable.
“Lokagarbharāja!

You should give rise to one skillful means to abide in the stage of cultivation, and further give rise to immeasurable skillful means; you will certainly attain the inconceivable matters described above, dwelling in the rank of a Tathāgata and responding to beings according to their forms.”
"What you shall attain has never before been seen by any of the followers of the two vehicles, nor by any of the non-Buddhists, Brahmā, Śakra, or the gods.

At that time, King Laṅkā, having received the Buddha’s permission, rose from his seat upon the summit of the mountain of pure radiant jewels—which was like a great lotus—and, surrounded by a host of celestial maidens, manifested countless varieties of flowers in diverse colors, as well as various fragrant powders, unguents, banners, streamers, canopies, crowns, pendants, necklaces, and other such exquisite and wondrous ornaments never before seen or heard of in the world;
furthermore, he manifested all manner of infinite musical instruments belonging to the desire realm, surpassing everything possessed by the gods, nāgas, gandharvas, and all other beings in the world.
Furthermore, he further manifested all kinds of musical instruments that he had previously seen in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
he further manifested great jeweled nets that completely covered all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
and he further displayed various kinds of exquisite garments, erecting banners and pennants as offerings.

Having performed these deeds, he immediately ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees. From mid-air, he rained down various clouds of offerings and played all kinds of music. Descending from the sky, he sat upon the summit of the second mountain of radiant jewels—which was like a great lotus—and with joy and reverence, spoke these words:

"I now wish to ask the Tathāgata about two matters. Regarding these two matters, I have previously asked past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and those Buddha-Bhagavāns already explained them to me."
I now also wish to inquire about this matter; I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain it for me.
World-Honored One!
It is the Nirmāṇa-Tathāgata who speaks of these two meanings, not the Fundamental Buddha.
The Fundamental Buddha speaks of the realm of the bliss of samādhi; he does not speak of that which is practiced through false discrimination.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
"Having attained mastery over all phenomena, I pray that you will compassionately explain these two meanings, for all the sons of the Buddha long to hear them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the king, saying:
"You should ask, and I shall explain it for you."
Then the Yakṣa King further donned various jeweled crowns and necklaces, adorning his body with all manner of ornaments, and spoke these words:
"The Tathāgata has always said:
'Even phenomena should be relinquished, how much more so that which is non-phenomenal.'"
"How can these two kinds of dharmas be abandoned?
What is dharma? What is non-dharma?"
If dharmas were to be abandoned, how could there be duality?
To have duality is to fall into the realm of conceptualized characteristics (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*).

Whether it be existence or non-existence, reality or unreality—all such things are merely conceptualizations and cannot lead to the realization of the undifferentiated characteristic of the *ālayavijñāna*.
"Just as the appearance of floating hairs does not exist within the domain of pure cognition, such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); how could it be abandoned?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the King of Laṅkā, saying: "King of Laṅkā!"
Do you not see that jars and other such things are impermanent phenomena subject to decay and destruction, yet ordinary people give rise to false conceptualizations regarding them?
Why do you now fail to understand in this way the distinguishing characteristics between what is dharma and what is non-dharma?
This is the conceptual construction of ordinary beings, not the vision of realized wisdom;
ordinary beings fall into various marks, whereas those who have realized do not.
O King of Laṅkā!

It is like seeing various flames when a palace or garden is burning; although the nature of fire is one, the light and flames produced differ in length, size, and magnitude according to the power of the fuel.
Why do you now not understand in this way the distinguishing characteristics between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma?
O King of Laṅkā!
Just as a single seed gives rise to an immeasurable variety of sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, so it is with external phenomena; internal phenomena are likewise.

This means that with ignorance as a condition, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—all phenomena—arise; within the three realms, one undergoes birth in various destinies, wherein there are the respective distinctions of suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness, speech and silence, and movement and stillness. Furthermore, although the characteristics of the various consciousnesses are one, they exhibit diverse distinctions such as superior, middling, and inferior, or defiled, pure, wholesome, and unwholesome, according to their objects.
O King of Laṅkā!

Not only do the aforementioned dharmas possess distinctions, but when practitioners cultivate meditative practices, they likewise perceive marks of distinction within the domain of their own wisdom; how much more so, then, could there not be various distinctions and discriminations between dharma and non-dharma?
"O King of Laṅkā!
You should know that the distinguishing characteristics of phenomena and non-phenomena are entirely due to the discrimination of marks.
O King of Laṅkā!"
What is this "dharma"?

It refers to the two vehicles and various non-Buddhists who, through false discrimination, assert that such things as "existence" and "reality" are the causes of all dharmas. Such dharmas as these should be abandoned and left behind; one should not engage in conceptual discrimination or grasp at their signs within them.

When one perceives the *dharmatā* of one's own mind, there is no attachment; for objects such as vases, which are grasped by the ignorant, have no inherent essence from the beginning. When practitioners of meditation observe them as they truly are through *vipaśyanā*, this is called "renouncing all phenomena."
"O King of Laṅkā!
What is that which is non-dharma?

It refers to all dharmas being without intrinsic nature and without marks, eternally free from conceptual discrimination. For one who sees according to reality, such objects as 'existence' or 'non-existence' do not arise at all; this is called the relinquishing of non-dharma."

Furthermore, there are non-dharmas, namely such things as the horns of a rabbit or the son of a barren woman; these all lack intrinsic nature and characteristics and cannot be differentiated. They exist only as names spoken in accordance with worldly convention, and unlike jars and the like, they are not objects to be grasped. Since they are not what consciousness can apprehend, such conceptualizations should also be abandoned; this is called abandoning both dharma and non-dharma.
"O King of Laṅkā!
What you previously asked has now been fully explained by me.
O King of Laṅkā!"
"You said:
'I have already asked about this matter before the Tathāgatas of the past, and those Tathāgatas have already explained it to me.
O King of Laṅkā!"
You say that the past is merely conceptual construction and the future is likewise;
I am the same as you in this regard. O King of Laṅkā!

Those dharmas of the Buddhas are all free from conceptual construction and have already transcended all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). They are not like the characteristics of form, which can only be realized through wisdom. Rather, they teach the Dharma for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain peace and happiness; it is by means of signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) that they are called Tathāgatas.

Therefore, the Tathāgata takes wisdom as his essence; because he has wisdom as his body, he cannot be differentiated, nor can he be differentiated by means of objects of differentiation, nor can he be differentiated by means of the marks of self, person, or sentient being.
Why is it unable to discriminate?

Because the mental consciousness arises dependent on objects, grasping at the forms and characteristics of matter; therefore, it is devoid of both the subject that discriminates and the object that is discriminated.
"O King of Laṅkā!

Just as sentient beings depicted in colorful paintings on a wall have no perception or awareness, so too are all worldly beings: they possess neither karma nor retribution. All phenomena are likewise: there is neither hearing nor speaking."
"O King of Laṅkā!
Sentient beings in the world are like magical transformations, which ordinary people and non-Buddhists are unable to comprehend.
O King of Laṅkā!"
To be able to see in this way is called right view; if one sees otherwise, it is called discriminative view, for due to discrimination, one grasps at duality.
"O King of Laṅkā!

It is, for example, like a person who sees their own reflection in water or a mirror, their own shadow in a lamp or the moon, or hears their own echo in a mountain valley, and then gives rise to discrimination and attachment; this case is also like that.
Dharma and non-Dharma are merely conceptual constructions; because of these constructions, one cannot relinquish them, but rather further increases all that is false and fails to attain quiescence.
Quiescence refers to the single object; this single object is the most excellent samādhi, from which the noble wisdom of self-realization arises, taking the tathāgatagarbha as its objective sphere.

**Chapter Two: On the Collection of All Dharmas (1–3)** *The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra on Entering the Mahāyāna, Chapter Two, Part One: On the Collection of All Dharmas* At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, together with the Bodhisattva Māti, who had both traveled through all the lands of the Buddhas, rose from their seats by the Buddha’s spiritual power. With his right shoulder bared and his right knee touching the ground, he joined his palms toward the Buddha, bowed in reverence, and spoke in verse:
“The world is free from arising and ceasing, Like flowers in the sky;
Since wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, One gives rise to the heart of great compassion.”
All phenomena are like illusions, transcending mind and consciousness;
wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet gives rise to great compassion.
The world is ever like a dream, transcending the extremes of annihilation and permanence.
Wisdom does not apprehend existence or non-existence, yet it gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Knowing that persons and phenomena lack selfhood, and that afflictions as well as the objects of cognition are eternally pure and signless,
it gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
The Buddha does not abide in nirvāṇa, nor does nirvāṇa abide in the Buddha;
far removed from awakening and non-awakening, from existence and non-existence.
The Dharma-body is like an illusion or a dream—how can it be praised?
Knowing that there is no intrinsic nature and no arising, one is then said to praise the Buddha.
Since the Buddha has no characteristics of sense-faculties or objects, not seeing is called seeing the Buddha;
how, then, could there be praise or blame for the Muni?
"If one sees the Muni, who is tranquil and detached from birth;
that person, in this and future lives, will be free from attachment and have nothing to perceive.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having praised the Buddha with these verses, spoke his own name:

"What is the arrangement of the trees?

These and other meanings—you now ask me about them all.
As previously taught by the Buddhas, there are one hundred and eight phrases;

"What are these one hundred and eight statements?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
That is to say: the phrase of arising and the phrase of non-arising; the phrase of permanence and the phrase of impermanence; the phrase of characteristics and the phrase of non-characteristics;

"Mahāmati!

These one hundred and eight phrases are all those spoken by the Buddhas of the past; they are missing two phrases from the superior correct enumeration [I previously gave], and you should seek them out.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses?
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which cannot be known by those who rely on mere speculation. These are:
the continuous arising and the arising of characteristics; the continuous abiding and the abiding of characteristics; and the continuous cessation and the cessation of characteristics.”
All consciousnesses have three characteristics, namely: the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of activity, and the characteristic of reality. Mahāmati!
Consciousness is extensively explained as being eightfold, but briefly it consists of only two: the manifesting consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates objects.
Mahāmati!
Just as various forms and images appear in a bright mirror, so too does the manifesting consciousness (nirbhāsivijñāna). Mahāmati!

The manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*)—these two consciousnesses are not different and serve as mutual causes for one another.
Mahāmati! The manifesting consciousness takes inconceivable perfuming and transformation as its cause.

The consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) takes as its causes the discrimination of objects and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless conceptual proliferation. Mahāmati!

When the various habitual tendencies of false discrimination within the *ālaya-vijñāna* are extinguished, all the sense-consciousnesses are extinguished; this is called the extinction of characteristics (*nimitta-nirodha*).

Mahāmati! As for the cessation of the continuity [of existence], it refers to the cessation of the causal basis and the cessation of the objective referent; this is what constitutes the cessation of continuity.
The causal basis refers to the beginningless habitual tendencies of false conceptual proliferation.
As for the object of perception (*ālambana*), it refers to the objects of differentiation perceived by one's own mind.
Mahāmati, it is like a lump of clay and its subtle particles, which are neither different nor not different; gold and its ornaments are also like this.
Mahāmati! If the lump of clay were different from its atoms, it would not be composed of them; yet, in reality, it is so composed. Therefore, they are not different.
If they were not different, there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its atoms.
Mahāmati! If the evolving consciousnesses were different from the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause.
If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease.
However, its true nature does not perish. Mahāmati!
It is the characteristic of consciousness that does not perish; it is only the characteristic of karma that perishes. If the true nature were to perish, the ālayavijñāna would have to perish.
If the storehouse consciousness were to cease, it would not differ from the nihilistic doctrine of the non-Buddhists.
"Mahāmati! Those non-Buddhists speak in this way:"
"When the consciousness that grasps the characteristics of objects ceases, the beginningless, continuous consciousness ceases. Mahāmati!

Those heterodox teachers claim that the continuous consciousness arises from a creator; they do not say that visual consciousness arises based on the conjunction of form and light, for they assert that the creator alone is the cause of its arising.
Who is the creator?
They reckon that primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Person (*puruṣa*), the Lord (*īśvara*), time (*kāla*), and atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the creators.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
There are seven kinds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), namely:

the intrinsic nature of accumulation, the intrinsic nature of essence, the intrinsic nature of characteristics, the intrinsic nature of the great elements, the intrinsic nature of cause, the intrinsic nature of conditions, and the intrinsic nature of accomplishment.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), namely:

that which is the range of the mind (*citta-gocara*); that which is the range of wisdom (*jñāna-gocara*); that which is the range of the two views; that which transcends the range of the two views; that which transcends the range of the stages of the sons [of the Buddha]; that which is the range of the Tathāgata; and that which is the range of the Tathāgata’s personally realized noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*).
Mahāmati! This is the ultimate reality-mind (*paramārtha-citta*) of the intrinsic nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present;

by means of this mind, the Tathāgatas accomplish the supreme mundane and supramundane dharmas. With the eye of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñācakṣus*), they enter into the various established conventions of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); these establishments do not share anything in common with the evil views of the outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Mahāmati! What are the evil views of the non-Buddhists? They are as follows:
not knowing that objects appear through one's own discrimination, they give rise to verbal expressions regarding the primary truth of self-nature by perceiving it as either existent or nonexistent.
Mahāmati!

I shall now explain: if one realizes that objects are like illusions and are manifestations of one's own mind, then the suffering of the three realms of existence arising from false conceptualization, as well as the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma, will be extinguished.

“Mahāmati! There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who falsely speculate that there are things both non-existent and existent, which manifest as external objects apart from cause and effect and abide according to time;
or they speculate that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) arise and abide based on conditions, and having existed, they immediately perish.”
Mahāmati!

Whether it be regarding continuity, activity, arising, cessation, the various realms of existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, its fruit, or the truths—this is the doctrine of nihilistic annihilationism.
Why is this? Because the present dharma cannot be attained and its root cannot be seen, Mahāmati!
For example, just as a broken jar cannot perform the function of a jar, or as a scorched seed cannot produce a sprout;

so it is with this: if the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases have already perished or are about to perish, one should know that there is no further continuity of birth, because there is no cause. It is merely what is falsely perceived by one’s own mind.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

If consciousness were originally non-existent and yet produced through the conjunction of three conditions, then tortoises would grow hair and sand would yield oil; your own tenet would be destroyed, it would contradict established principles, and all activities would be empty and useless."
“Mahāmati!

The three [factors] coming together as conditions constitute the nature of cause and effect, which can be said to exist. That the past, present, and future arise from non-existence to existence is a statement made by those who abide on the stage of conceptualization, based upon their own philosophical systems, teachings, and the residual impressions of their own evil views.”
"Mahāmati!
Foolish ordinary beings, bitten by evil views and intoxicated by false perspectives, being devoid of wisdom, falsely claim that [these teachings] were spoken by the Omniscient One. Mahāmati!"

Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who contemplate all phenomena as being devoid of intrinsic nature, like clouds in the sky, like a whirling firebrand, like a city of the gandharvas, like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water, and like what is seen in a dream—all of which do not depart from one's own mind;
yet, due to false perceptions since beginningless time, they grasp them as being external.

Having performed this contemplation, one cuts off the conditions for conceptual discrimination and detaches from the names and meanings grasped by the deluded mind. One knows that the body, objects, and the dwelling place are all entirely the sphere of the *ālayavijñāna*, devoid of subject and object of grasping, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing. Contemplating in this manner, one dwells therein constantly and without relinquishing it.
“Mahāmati!

Before long, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva shall attain the twofold equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Through the skillful means of great compassion and effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), he contemplates sentient beings as being like illusions and shadows arising from conditions. Knowing that all objective realms are devoid of mind and cannot be apprehended, he practices the path of signlessness (*animitta-mārga*) and gradually ascends through the stages (*bhūmi*), dwelling in the state of samādhi. Realizing that the triple world is solely one’s own mind, he attains the illusion-like concentration (*māyopama-samādhi*) which transcends all mental images, achieves wisdom, and realizes the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma*).

Entering the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), he shall attain the Buddha-body, abide eternally in suchness (*tathatā*), and manifest various transformations with mastery over powers and supernormal faculties.”
Mahāmati!

Adorned with skillful means, one wanders through the various Buddha-lands, remains free from all external paths as well as mind, thought, and consciousness, and by transforming through successive stages, accomplishes the body of a Tathāgata.
Mahāmati!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to attain the Buddha-body should remain far removed from the conceptual proliferation and discrimination regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as the phenomena produced by causes and conditions that arise, abide, and perish. Rather, they should dwell within mind-only (*cittamātra*) and observe the three realms of existence as arising from the false habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time. Contemplating the stage of Buddhahood—which is signless, unborn, and the self-realized noble dharma—they shall attain mastery over the mind and effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*). Like a wish-fulfilling gem, they manifest bodies according to the needs of beings, leading them to realize that all is mind-only and gradually entering the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, Mahāmati,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully train in his own established tenet (svasiddhānta).
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra of the Mahāyāna, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Zhou Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
The Second Part of the Second Chapter, "The Collection of All Dharmas. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I pray that you will explain for me the wondrous Dharma-gates of mind, thought, mentation, the five dharmas, and the self-natures and characteristics. These are the means by which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas enter their own mental objects and depart from the characteristics of objective practice; they are called the true meaning and the heart of the teachings of all Buddhas."

We only pray that the Tathāgata, following the example of the Buddhas of the past, will expound for this assembly of bodhisattvas in the mountains the realm of the dharmakāya, which is like the ocean waves of the ālayavijñāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"There are four kinds of causes and conditions by which visual consciousness arises. What are these four?"
That is to say:

because of grasping at what is merely the manifestation of one's own mind without realizing it; because of the false habitual tendencies of attachment to form since beginningless time; because such is the intrinsic nature of consciousness; and because of the delight in seeing various kinds of formal appearances.
Mahāmati! By these four conditions, the ālayavijñāna—like a torrential stream—gives rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
As it is with the visual consciousness, so it is with the others as well.
Within all the sense organs, atoms, pores, eyes, and so forth, the evolving consciousnesses may arise simultaneously, like a bright mirror manifesting various forms and images;
or they may arise sequentially, like a violent wind blowing upon the waters of the great ocean.
The ocean of the mind is likewise: stirred by the winds of objective realms, the waves of the various consciousnesses arise in an uninterrupted succession. Mahāmati!

Because the characteristics of causes and effects are neither identical nor different, the characteristics of karma and birth are bound together in deep fetters; unable to comprehend the self-nature of form and so forth, the five bodies of consciousness evolve.
Mahāmati!

Accompanying the five consciousnesses, or due to the discernment of various differentiated objective appearances, the mental consciousness arises; yet those various consciousnesses do not form the thought:
"We exist simultaneously, acting as mutual causes for one another."

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, within the objects manifested by one's own mind, conceptualization and attachment arise simultaneously; though they lack distinct characteristics, each perceives its own respective object."
When practitioners enter samādhi, because the power of their practice arises subtly, they do not perceive it; they merely think:
"I have extinguished all consciousnesses and entered samādhi."

In truth, he does not extinguish consciousness to enter samādhi; because the seeds of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) have not been extinguished therein, it is merely that he does not grasp at objects, which is termed the "extinction of consciousness."

“Mahāmati! Thus, the mode of activity of the ālayavijñāna is subtle; except for the Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who dwell on the stages, all others—whether followers of the two vehicles or non-Buddhists—cannot know it by the power of their concentration or wisdom.”

Only those who practice according to reality, through the power of wisdom, can comprehend the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*) and skillfully master their meanings; having extensively gathered roots of goodness under infinite Buddhas, they do not falsely discriminate what is seen by their own minds, and thus are able to know it.
“Mahāmati!

Those practitioners who dwell in seclusion within mountain forests and cultivate the practice in its superior, middling, and inferior degrees, are able to perceive the flowing stream of their own mind’s discrimination. They attain the sovereign power and supernormal penetrations of the various samādhis, are surrounded by Bodhisattvas who have received the Buddhas’ consecration, and understand the spheres of activity of the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness. Thus they transcend the great ocean of birth and death, which consists of craving, karma, and ignorance. For this reason, you all should draw near to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and practice according to reality under the guidance of true spiritual friends.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Just as the vast waves of the great ocean, Arise from the forceful winds,
As massive billows surge through the deep abyss, Without a moment's interruption."
The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) abides eternally, stirred by the winds of objective realms;
the various waves of consciousness surge and arise in succession.
Blue, red, and other such colors, as well as salt, conch, milk, stone, and honey—
The sun, moon, flowers, and fruits are neither different nor not different [from their reflections].
One should know that the seven kinds of consciousness, such as the mental consciousness, are likewise;
like the ocean together with its waves, they arise in conjunction with the mind.
Just as the waters of the ocean move, with various waves surging;
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), from which various cognitions arise.
Mind (manas), intellect (citta), and mental consciousness (manovijñāna) are taught for the sake of [distinguishing] various characteristics.
The eight consciousnesses have no distinct characteristics; there is neither the grasper nor the grasped.
Just as with the waves of the ocean, they are without differentiation;
so it is with the various consciousnesses and the mind—no difference can be found.
"The mind (*citta*) can accumulate karma; the intellect (*manas*) can extensively accumulate it.
Because it discerns, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); the five are spoken of in relation to present objects.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati asked in verse:
“The various forms and colors, blue and red, Are manifested by the consciousness of sentient beings;
Like waves, so too are the manifold phenomena— How may I pray that the Buddha explain this?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
Blue, red, and all such forms and images cannot be found within the waves;
yet the mind is said to give rise to manifold appearances in order to awaken ordinary beings.
In truth, they never arise at all, for they are free from what the self-mind grasps.
The grasper and the grasped are like those waves;
The body, resources, and dwelling place are manifestations of the consciousness of sentient beings.
Therefore, seeing these arise is no different from seeing waves.
At that time, Mahāmati spoke again in verse:
"The nature of the waves of the great ocean Can be discerned as they surge and leap;
The Ālayavijñāna arises in this same way— Why is it not perceived?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“The ālayavijñāna is like the ocean, And the evolving consciousnesses are like its waves;
For the sake of ordinary beings who lack wisdom, I have extensively expounded this through parables.”
At that time, Mahāmati spoke again in verse:
"Just as when the sun rises, It illuminates all things above and below;
So too is the lamp of the world: One should speak the truth for the sake of the ignorant."
“Since you have already been able to reveal the Dharma, why do you not manifest the ultimate reality?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“If one speaks of ultimate reality, that mind itself lacks ultimate reality.”
Just as the waves of the ocean, The images in a mirror, and dreams— They manifest simultaneously; So too are the objects of the mind.
Because objects are not fully present, They arise and evolve in succession.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is so called because it can cognize; the mental faculty (*manas*) likewise functions in this way.
The five consciousnesses cognize present objects, and there is no fixed order [to their arising];
they are like a master painter and the master’s disciple.
Applying colors to depict various images, my teaching is also like this.
Within the colors there is no pattern; it is neither the brush nor the canvas.
For the sake of delighting sentient beings, these brilliant hues form various images.
Verbal expression is subject to change, while reality is beyond words.
The true Dharma in which I abide, I teach for the sake of all practitioners;
it is the state of self-realization where both subject and object are transcended.
This is taught for the sons of the Buddha; for the foolish, it is explained separately.
All varieties are like illusions; that which is seen cannot be apprehended.
Such various teachings vary according to the circumstances.
What is spoken that is not appropriate for them is not taught to them.
Just as a skilled physician prescribes medicine according to each patient's condition,
so the Tathāgata teaches sentient beings according to their inclinations and capacities.
The refuge of the world is the sphere of activity for those who have realized wisdom;
it is not the domain of non-Buddhists, nor is it that of the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to thoroughly understand that the objects of discrimination—the grasper and the grasped—are all manifestations of one's own mind, they should distance themselves from clamor, mental stagnation, and sleep; they should diligently practice throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night;

and they should remain far removed from the heterodox doctrines previously heard from non-Buddhists as well as the teachings of the Two Vehicles, thereby penetrating the characteristics of the discriminations of their own minds.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established themselves in the characteristics of the state wherein the mind of wisdom abides, they should diligently cultivate and train in the three marks of the higher noble wisdom."
What are these three?

They are: the characteristic of being without images, the characteristic of being sustained by the vows of all Buddhas, and the characteristic of the destination of the noble wisdom of self-realization.

Once practitioners have attained these signs, they immediately abandon the mental characteristics of the lame donkey-like wisdom and enter the eighth stage of the bodhisattva, wherein they practice these three signs without relinquishing them.
Mahāmati! That which is characterized by the absence of images arises due to the habitual tendencies toward the signs of all the vehicles of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists.
That which is characterized by the sustaining power of the vows of all Buddhas arises due to the empowerment of the Buddhas' own original vow-power.

Regarding the characteristics of the state toward which self-realized noble wisdom proceeds: it arises by virtue of not grasping at the characteristics of any phenomena, thereby accomplishing the bodies of various samādhis that are like illusions, and proceeding toward the wisdom of the Buddha-ground.
Mahāmati! These are called the three characteristics of the supreme noble wisdom.
If one attains these characteristics, one reaches the sphere traversed by the noble wisdom of self-realization; you and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice and study them.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of all the bodhisattvas and sustained by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that you will expound for us the Dharma-gate of the self-nature of phenomena based on the distinctions of the hundred and eight phrases—the noble wisdom that serves as the basis for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, to explain for the sake of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have fallen into [the views of] specific and general characteristics, this door of meaning concerning the distinctions of the nature of false conceptualization."

Having understood this meaning, one is then able to purify and cultivate the objects of the two-fold contemplation of selflessness, illuminating all the stages (*bhūmi*). One transcends the bliss of the samādhis of all followers of the Two Vehicles and non-Buddhists, beholds the inconceivable spheres of activity of all Tathāgatas, and ultimately abandons the five dharmas and the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Adorned by the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddha-dharmas, one enters into all lands as if they were like illusions, and within the Tuṣita Palace and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, one accomplishes the body of a Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!

There is a class of non-Buddhists who, seeing that all phenomena perish in accordance with their causes, give rise to conceptual understanding. They conceive of the notion that a rabbit has no horns and thereby give rise to the view of non-existence, thinking: 'Just as a rabbit's horn does not exist, so too are all phenomena. "

Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who, having observed the various differences in shape, dimension, and position among entities such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*), qualities (*guṇa*), and atoms (*paramāṇu*), cling to the notion that while a rabbit has no horns, a cow possesses them.
Mahāmati!
Those who fall into these two views fail to understand that there is nothing but mind; they merely increase their own mental discrimination. Mahāmati!
The body, the means of subsistence, the receptacle world, and so forth—all these are manifested solely through discrimination.
Mahāmati, you should know that just as a rabbit’s horn is beyond existence and non-existence, so it is with all phenomena; do not give rise to discrimination.
How is it that a rabbit's horn is free from existence and non-existence?

Because they are mutually dependent, if one analyzes the horns of an ox down to their subtlest particles, its essential nature and characteristics can never be found. That which is the domain of noble wisdom is far removed from such views; therefore, one should not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding this.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Does he not, by means of false views arising from signs, through inference and relative observation, falsely conceptualize 'non-existence'?"
The Buddha said:
"One does not give rise to the notion of 'non-existence' by relying on the conceptualization of mutual dependence. Why is this?"

Since that [hare's horn] has conceptual construction as its cause of arising, it takes the conceptualization of a horn as its basis; and since this basis serves as its cause in a manner that is neither different nor non-different, the non-existence of the hare's horn is not manifested through mutual dependence.
Mahāmati! If this conceptualization were different from the rabbit’s horns, it would not be the cause of the horns;
if it were not different, it would arise dependent upon them.
Mahāmati! If one analyzes the horns of an ox down to their ultimate atoms (paramāṇu), they cannot be found;
yet to say that there are no horns because they differ from those that do exist—such a conceptual distinction is certainly irrational.
Since neither of the two exists, what could depend on what?
If dependence is not established, then to say that "the rabbit's horns do not exist" because they depend on something existent is an improper distinction, as it is based on an invalid reason.
Those who hold to the views of existence or non-existence cling to either existence or non-existence, yet neither position is established. "Mahāmati!

Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who, seeing the boundaries of space within the forms and shapes of matter, give rise to attachment and claim that matter is distinct from space, thereby engendering conceptual discrimination."
Mahāmati! Space is that which enters into form according to the categories of form. Mahāmati!
Form is empty space, because it possesses the nature of establishing both the container and the contained; the limits of form and emptiness should be understood in this way.
Mahāmati! When the great elements arise, their specific characteristics are distinct and they do not abide within empty space, yet it is not that they lack empty space.
Mahāmati! It is the same with the horns of a rabbit; in dependence upon the horns of an ox, one says that those horns do not exist. Mahāmati!
If one analyzes a cow’s horn down to its subtle particles, and further analyzes those particles until their characteristics no longer appear,
what is it that they depend upon for which one could say they are "non-existent"?
If they depend on other things, those [other things] would likewise be the same.
Mahāmati!

You should remain far removed from all conceptual discriminations regarding rabbit horns, cow horns, space, and form. You and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should constantly observe the marks of conceptual discrimination as they appear within your own minds, and for the sake of all the sons of the Buddha in every land, you should teach the method of practice that consists in observing one's own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"What is seen by the mind does not exist; it arises solely in dependence upon the mind.
The reflections of the body, its requisites, and its dwelling place are manifested within the *ālayavijñāna* of sentient beings."
Mind, mentation, and consciousness, along with the five factors of self-nature—
these are the two purities of selflessness as expounded by the Teachers.
Length and shortness exist in mutual dependence, arising from one another in succession.
Because of existence, non-existence is established; because of non-existence, existence is established.
When things are analyzed down to their subtle atoms, the conceptualization of form does not arise;
this is merely established by the mind, yet those with evil views do not believe it.
"It is not the sphere of practice for outsiders, nor is it so for the śrāvakas;
it is the realm of self-realization taught by the Savior of the World.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, in order to purify the manifestation of the stream of mind, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How are the streams of the self-mind’s manifestations purified in all sentient beings?
Is it by gradual purification?”
"Is it purified instantaneously?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
Purification is gradual, not sudden.

Just as the mango fruit ripens gradually and not all at once, so too do the Tathāgatas purify the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of sentient beings; it is likewise gradual and not sudden.

Just as a potter fashions vessels gradually and not all at once, so too do the Tathāgatas purify the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of sentient beings; it is likewise gradual and not sudden.

Just as the great earth produces all grasses and trees gradually rather than instantaneously, so too do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, purify the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of sentient beings; this occurs gradually and not instantaneously.
Mahāmati!

Just as when a person learns music, writing, painting, and various arts and crafts, they are accomplished gradually and not instantaneously; so too it is with the Tathāgatas, who purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of sentient beings—this occurs gradually and not instantaneously.

For example, just as a bright mirror suddenly manifests all images without discrimination, so too do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, purify the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of sentient beings; they suddenly manifest all signless realms without discrimination.

Just as the orbs of the sun and moon simultaneously illuminate all forms and images, so too do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, purify the habitual tendencies within the minds of sentient beings; they likewise suddenly manifest the inconceivable realm of wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

For example, just as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) suddenly manifests the body, the objects of sustenance, and the entire realm of the land, so too does the Reward Buddha (vipākabuddha), in the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha), suddenly bring all sentient beings to maturity, causing them to cultivate all spiritual practices.

Just as the Dharma-buddha suddenly manifests the Reward-buddha and the Transformation-buddhas, whose radiance shines forth, so too is the self-realized holy realm: it suddenly manifests the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) to shine forth, causing one to leave behind all evil views of existence and non-existence.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Flowing from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Buddha has taught that the self-characteristics and common characteristics of all dharmas are the causal marks of the habitual tendencies manifested by one's own mind, and the causal marks grasped through false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). These are mutually interconnected; like various illusory phenomena, they all lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Yet, sentient beings cling to them in various ways, taking them to be real, though none of these can be found."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The attachment to the nature of false imagination arises from the nature of dependent origination.
Mahāmati!"

For example, it is like a magician who, by the power of his illusory arts, uses grass, wood, tiles, and stones to conjure various forms of sentient beings, causing those who see them to engage in manifold conceptual discriminations—all of which lack any reality.
Mahāmati! It is the same in this case:

due to the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from clinging to objects, various characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) appear within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); this is called the arising of the imagined nature.
"Mahāmati!
This is called the appearance of the Dharma taught by the Buddha as it flows from the nature of reality (dharmatā). Mahāmati!"
The Dharma-nature Buddha establishes that which is the domain of self-realized wisdom, free from the intrinsic characteristics of the mind.

Mahāmati! The Transformation Buddha teaches generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; as well as the various liberations and the modes of activity of the consciousnesses. He establishes these distinctions to transcend the views of the non-Buddhists and to surpass the practices of the formless realm.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Buddha of Dharma-nature (dharmatā-buddha) is not an object of apprehension. It is entirely free from all characteristics of objects of cognition, all characteristics of activity, and all characteristics of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). It is not a realm grasped by ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or various non-Buddhists who are attached to the characteristic of a self (ātman).
Therefore, Mahāmati!
You should diligently cultivate and study the supreme realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, and you should swiftly abandon the perceptions of discrimination manifested within your own mind.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are two kinds of distinguishing characteristics of the Śrāvaka vehicle, namely:
the characteristic of the excellence of the noble wisdom of personal realization, and the characteristic of the conceptual attachment to intrinsic nature."
What is the characteristic of the excellence of the noble wisdom of personal realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*)?

It refers to clearly seeing the realms of the truths—suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self—and because of detachment, quiescence, and cessation, one understands, as it truly is, the unbreakable characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, whether individual or collective, in relation to the external world. Thus, the mind abides in a single object; having so abided, one attains the fruits of the path through dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, and achieves deliverance. One dwells in the bliss of the realm of the noble wisdom of personal realization, yet has not yet abandoned habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the inconceivable death of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*). This is called the characteristic of the realm of the noble wisdom of personal realization in the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also attain this realm of noble wisdom, because they have compassion for sentient beings and are sustained by their original vows, they do not realize the gate of cessation or the bliss of samādhi; therefore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not practice for the sake of the bliss of this self-realized noble wisdom alone.
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the attachment to the nature of differentiation?
It is as follows:

To know that such phenomena as solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, blue, yellow, red, and white are not produced by a creator, yet—relying on teachings and reasoning—to perceive their specific and general characteristics and engage in conceptualization and attachment, is called the characteristic of conceptual attachment in the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Within this Dharma, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand and relinquish [these views], departing from the view of the selflessness of persons and entering into the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena, gradually abiding in the various stages (*bhūmi*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha,

saying: “World-Honored One, regarding the realm of the ultimate truth— the eternal, inconceivable, self-realized noble wisdom— spoken of by the Tathāgata, could it not be the same as the eternal, inconceivable creator spoken of by the various non-Buddhists?”
The Buddha said,
"Mahāmati! It is not through the agency of externalists that the eternal and inconceivable is attained."
Why is this so? Because the eternal and inconceivable causes posited by the various non-Buddhists do not establish their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Since their causes do not establish their own characteristics, by what means could they demonstrate that these causes are eternal and inconceivable?
Mahāmati! Regarding the eternal and inconceivable taught by the non-Buddhists: if it were established through its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), then it would indeed be eternal;
however, because they take a creator as the causal characteristic, their eternal and inconceivable is not established.

"Mahāmati! My ultimate truth (paramārtha) is eternal and inconceivable. It is established through the characteristics of the cause of ultimate truth; it is free from existence and non-existence, yet possesses characteristics because it is the sphere of activity of the self-realized noble wisdom (pratyātma-āryajñāna).

Because the wisdom of ultimate truth serves as its cause, it possesses a cause; because it is free from existence and non-existence, it is not a creator. Like space, nirvāṇa, and the dharma of cessation, it is eternal and inconceivable."
Therefore, I speak of the eternal and the inconceivable, which is not like the contentious arguments held by the non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati! This eternity and inconceivability is the truth realized through the noble wisdom of self-attestation by all Tathāgatas; therefore, Bodhisattvas should diligently practice and study it.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, the eternal and inconceivable of the non-Buddhists is eternal because it is caused by the dissimilar characteristic of impermanence; it is not eternal by virtue of the power of its own intrinsic characteristic."
“Mahāmati!

The heterodox teachers regard that which is eternal and inconceivable as such because they see that created phenomena exist and then cease to exist; having perceived this impermanence, they infer that there must be something permanent.
I, too, see that created phenomena exist and then cease to exist, yet I do not, on this basis of impermanence, declare them to be eternal.”
Mahāmati!

The non-Buddhists establish their notions of permanence and inconceivability based on such causal characteristics; however, these causal characteristics do not exist, as they are like the horns of a rabbit. Thus, permanence and inconceivability are merely conceptual constructions and exist only as verbal designations.
Why is that cause the same as a rabbit's horn?
Because it lacks the characteristics of its own cause, Mahāmati!
I always regard the inconceivable as having self-realization as its causal characteristic; I do not take the impermanence of external phenomena—existing and then ceasing—as its cause.

The non-Buddhists are the opposite of this; they have never been able to know the characteristic of the self-cause that is eternal and inconceivable, and thus they constantly remain outside the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom of self-realization. This [view of theirs] should not be spoken of.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are śrāvakas who, fearing the suffering of the conceptualization of birth and death, seek nirvāṇa; yet they do not understand the distinction between the characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Since all things exist only through false discrimination and are ultimately non-existent, they falsely reckon the cessation of future sense-faculties and objects to be nirvāṇa. They do not know that the realization of the realm of one's own wisdom—through the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is the basis of existence—is Great Nirvāṇa. Those deluded people speak of three vehicles, but do not speak of Mind-only and the non-existence of external objects."
Mahāmati!

Those people do not understand that the realms of their own minds are what have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; instead, they grasp at external objects and thus perpetually revolve in the cycle of birth and death without end.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present all teach that all phenomena are unarisen. Why is this?

Because that which is seen by one's own mind is not of an existent nature, and because it is free from arising as either existence or non-existence—just as the horns of rabbits or horses are falsely grasped by the ignorant—it is the domain traversed solely by the noble wisdom of self-realization, and is not the object of the dualistic discrimination of ordinary people.
Mahāmati!
The body, the objects of livelihood, and the receptacle world—all these are but reflections of the ālayavijñāna, appearing as the two aspects of the grasped and the grasper.
Because those foolish people fall into the two views of arising and ceasing, they falsely give rise to the discrimination of existence and non-existence within them.
"Mahāmati! You should diligently cultivate and study this meaning.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
There are five kinds of spiritual lineages (*gotra*). What are the five?
They are as follows:
The śrāvaka-vehicle lineage, the pratyekabuddha-vehicle lineage, the tathāgata-vehicle lineage, the indeterminate lineage, and the absence of lineage.
Mahāmati!
How is one to know that this is the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle?

It is when, upon hearing an exposition of the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, one understands or realizes them such that the hairs on one’s entire body stand on end and the mind delights in cultivation; yet, one does not delight in examining the characteristics of dependent origination. One should know that this is the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Having realized what is to be seen within their own vehicle, they sever the fetters of affliction at the fifth or sixth stage, but do not sever the habitual tendencies of affliction, abiding in inconceivable death.
He makes a true lion’s roar, saying:
"Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence.
By cultivating the selflessness of persons, he eventually gives rise to the realization of attaining nirvana.
Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who seek to realize nirvāṇa, claiming that the ability to perceive a self, a person, a sentient being, a nourisher, and a grasper is itself nirvāṇa;
others say that seeing all phenomena as existing because of an agent is nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati! They possess no liberation because they have not yet perceived the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

This is the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle and of the non-Buddhists; while not having emerged [from saṃsāra], they conceive the notion of emergence. You should diligently cultivate the practice of abandoning this evil view.
“Mahāmati! How is one to know the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna?

It is when, upon hearing the teaching of the Pratyekabuddhayāna, their hair stands on end and they weep with flowing tears, remaining free from attachment and avoiding the conditions of worldly clamor.”

If at times they hear it said that various bodies are manifested, whether gathering or dispersing through supernormal transformations, and they accept this with faith without any contradiction, you should know that this is the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna;
for them, one should preach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
“Mahāmati! There are three kinds of dharmas realized by those of the lineage of the Tathāgata-yāna:
namely, the dharma of self-nature and lack of self-nature, the dharma of the noble wisdom personally realized within one’s own body, and the dharma of the vastness of the external Buddha-fields.”
Mahāmati!

If there are those who, upon hearing this exposition of each of these dharmas and the inconceivable realm of the ālayavijñāna established through the manifestations of one’s own mind as body and wealth, are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that they possess the nature of the Tathāgata-yāna.

“Mahāmati! Those of indeterminate lineage are those who, upon hearing the teaching of those three kinds of dharmas, give rise to faith and understanding accordingly and practice them in accordance with that understanding. Mahāmati!”

For the sake of those who are beginners on the stages of practice, the lineage (*gotra*) is taught, with the aim of causing them to enter the stage of imagelessness; it is for this purpose that this establishment is made. Mahāmati!

Those Śrāvakas who abide in the bliss of samādhi, if they can realize the consciousness upon which their own [minds] depend, perceive the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and purify the habitual tendencies of afflictions, will ultimately attain the body of a Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Those who have attained the fruits of Stream-enterer and Once-returner, As well as Non-returners and Arhats—
Even these noble ones Have their minds entirely deluded.”
The three vehicles I establish, as well as the single vehicle and the non-vehicle,
were taught by the sages for the sake of the foolish with little wisdom and those who delight in tranquility.
This gateway to the Dharma of the ultimate truth is far removed from the two types of grasping.
Abiding in the realm of no-object, how could one establish the three vehicles?
The various dhyānas and immeasurables, the formless attainments and samādhis,
even up to the cessation of sensation and perception— these are all but mind, and cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
For what reason does this icchantika not give rise to the desire for liberation?
Mahāmati!"
