Because they have abandoned all roots of goodness, and because they have generated vows for the sake of sentient beings who have no beginning.
How do they abandon all roots of goodness?
It means slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, saying:
"This is not a teaching that accords with the sūtras, the discipline, or liberation.
When he spoke these words, his roots of goodness were completely severed and he did not enter nirvāṇa.
How, then, can one give rise to vows for the sake of sentient beings who have no beginning?

This means that by means of their original vows and skillful means, bodhisattvas vow that all sentient beings shall enter nirvana; if even a single sentient being has not entered nirvana, they themselves will ultimately not enter.
"These also abide in the realm of icchantikas; this is the characteristic of the lineage that lacks the nature for nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
"Among these, which ones will ultimately not enter nirvana?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
That bodhisattva icchantika knows that all dharmas are originally in nirvana and ultimately does not enter [samsara]; yet this is not because he has abandoned his roots of goodness. Why is this?
Even those icchantikas who have severed their roots of goodness may, through the power of the Buddha, at times give rise to roots of goodness. Why is this?
Because there is no time when the Buddha abandons any sentient being.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva-icchantika does not enter nirvana.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully understand the characteristics of the three natures (trisvabhāva).
What are these three?
They are: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Mahāmati!
The imagined nature arises from signs.
How does it arise from signs?
This is because they give rise to attachment based on the manifestation of the various categories of phenomena arising from dependent origination.
Mahāmati, that attachment to the characteristics of phenomena arises from two kinds of imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), as taught by all the Tathāgatas; namely:
The characteristic of attachment to names and signs, and the characteristic of attachment to the characteristics of things. Mahāmati,
as for the characteristic of attachment to things, it refers to attachment to internal and external dharmas.
"Attachment to the characteristics of conceptualization" means that within those very internal and external phenomena, one is attached to their specific and general characteristics;
this is called the two kinds of characteristics of the falsely imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Mahāmati!
Arising from the basis and the object of cognition is the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
What is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?
It is suchness (*tathatā*), the domain of the personally realized noble wisdom, which is free from all conceptual constructions regarding names, signs, and the characteristics of things.
"Mahāmati!
This is the perfected nature, the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The conceptualization of names and marks is the characteristic of the two natures;
correct wisdom and suchness are the perfected nature. Mahāmati!"

This is called the Dharma-gate of observing the characteristics of the five dharmas and their own-nature; it is the sphere of activity of the personally realized noble wisdom, which you and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should diligently cultivate and study.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully observe the two characteristics of selflessness. What are these two?
That is to say:
the mark of selflessness in persons and the mark of selflessness in phenomena. Mahāmati!
What is the characteristic of the selflessness of persons?

It refers to the fact that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are devoid of a self or what belongs to a self; yet, through the arising of ignorance, craving, and karma, the eye-consciousness and other cognitions are produced, which then grasp at forms and other objects, giving rise to conceptual attachment.

Furthermore, the body and the vessel-world perceived by one's own mind are both manifestations of the *ālaya-vijñāna*. They arise in a continuous succession of moments, undergoing transformation and decay without ceasing—like a flowing river, like a seed, like a lamp flame, like a swift wind, or like drifting clouds. They are restless and unstable like a monkey; they delight in impure places like a fly; and they know no satiety like a raging fire. With the beginningless habitual tendencies of falsehood as their cause, they flow incessantly through the various realms of existence like a waterwheel. Their various physical forms, postures, and movements are like a corpse moving through the power of a spell, or like a wooden puppet moved by a mechanical device. If one can thoroughly understand these characteristics, this is called the wisdom of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya-jñāna*).
“Mahāmati! What is the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*)?

It refers to knowing that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are of an imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*). Just as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are devoid of a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), they are merely a common accumulation bound by the ropes of craving and karma, arising through mutual conditionality (*pratītyasamutpāda*) without any agent. The aggregates and so forth are likewise devoid of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); various appearances manifest through false discrimination (*vikalpa*), which is the conceptualization of fools and not that of the noble ones (*ārya*). Observing all phenomena in this way—being free from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the five dharmas, and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena.”

Having attained this wisdom, one realizes that there is no objective realm; having clearly understood the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), one enters the first stage with a heart of joy. Proceeding gradually through the stages up to the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*) and the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), all that was to be accomplished has been fully completed.

Having dwelt in this stage, there appears a great king of jewel lotuses adorned with various treasures; upon that flower is a jeweled palace shaped like a lotus, which has been accomplished through the Bodhisattva’s prior cultivation of the dharma-gate of the illusory nature. Seated upon it, surrounded by fellow sons of the Buddha, all the Tathāgatas of every buddha-field extend their hands and consecrate his crown according to the rite of the coronation of a wheel-turning monarch's son. Thus he transcends the stages of the sons of the Buddha, attains the Dharma of self-realization, and accomplishes the sovereign Dharma-body of a Tathāgata.
“Mahāmati!
This is called seeing the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena; you and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice and study it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will explain the characteristics of establishing [existence] and slandering [non-existence], so that I and all other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may leave behind these evil views and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and having attained bodhi, we shall destroy the views of eternalism through establishment and nihilism through slander, ensuring that they do not give rise to disparagement toward the True Dharma.”
The Buddha accepted his request and immediately spoke in verse:
"The body, material wealth, and the dwelling place— All are but images of the mind alone.
Ordinary fools fail to understand this, Giving rise to both affirmation and denial."
"What arises is merely mind; apart from mind, nothing can be found.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, addressed Mahāmati, saying:
"There are four kinds of established views regarding non-existence."
What are these four? They are: establishing characteristics where there are no characteristics;
establishing views where there are no views; establishing causes where there are no causes; and establishing natures where there are no natures. These are the four.
Mahāmati!

As for "denigration," it refers to seeking something among the phenomena established by various evil views and failing to find it; through a lack of skillful investigation, one consequently gives rise to denigration. This is the characteristic of establishment and denigration.
Mahāmati! What is the establishment of characteristics where no characteristics exist?

It refers to the arising of attachment toward the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—which are fundamentally non-existent—thinking, "It is thus," or "It is not otherwise. This discrimination arises from various evil habits since beginningless time; this is called the establishment of characteristics where no characteristics exist.
What is the view that establishes a view where none exists?

It refers to establishing views such as a self, a person, or a sentient being with respect to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; this is called the view that establishes a view where none exists.
What is the establishment of causes where no cause exists?

It refers to the fact that prior to the initial consciousness, there is no cause and thus it does not arise; that initial consciousness is fundamentally non-existent, yet subsequently arises like an illusion through causes such as the eye, forms, light, and attention. Once arisen, it exists, and having existed, it ceases. This is called the establishment of causes where no cause exists.
What is the establishment of a nature where no nature exists?
It refers to the attachment and conceptual construction regarding the unconditioned nature of space, nirvāṇa, and analytical cessation. Mahāmati!

This is the departure from both existence and non-existence; all phenomena are free from being and non-being, like the appearance of hair-tufts or the horns of rabbits and horses. This is called the establishment of the nature of non-existence.

Mahāmati! The establishment of [views] and the commission of denigration both arise from the discrimination of the ignorant and foolish who do not understand that all is mind-only; they do not belong to the noble ones. Therefore, you should diligently investigate and remain far removed from such views.
“Mahāmati! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have thoroughly understood the mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures,

and the two characteristics of selflessness, they manifest various bodies for the sake of sentient beings, arising in dependence upon conditions, just as [a reflection arises] based on dependent origination.”
The nature of false conceptualization is also like a mani jewel that manifests colors according to the mind;
they universally enter the assemblies of Buddhas to hear the Buddha’s teaching that all dharmas are like illusions, like dreams, like shadows, like images in a mirror,
and like the moon reflected in water— far removed from arising and ceasing, as well as from annihilationism and eternalism— and they do not abide in the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Having heard this, he accomplished immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis.
Having attained these samādhis, he traveled throughout all buddha-fields, made offerings to the Buddhas, was born in the various heavens, proclaimed the Triple Gem,
manifested the body of a Buddha, and for the great assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, expounded upon external objects.
"All realms are solely mind; cause them all to remain far removed from attachments to existence, non-existence, and the like.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Son of the Buddha is able to perceive That the world is nothing but mind."
"Manifesting various bodies, their actions are without obstruction;
with sovereign power of spiritual penetrations, they accomplish everything.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:
“May you explain for me the characteristics of the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
By awakening to these characteristics, I and the other bodhisattvas shall abandon the conceptualization of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati! Emptiness is the referent of the term "imagined nature. Mahāmati!
Because of attachment to the falsely imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of intrinsic nature are taught.
Mahāmati, briefly stated, there are seven kinds of emptiness.
That is to say:

the emptiness of marks, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of non-activity, the emptiness of activity, the emptiness of the ineffability of all dharmas, the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom, and the mutual emptiness of this and that.
What is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?

It means that all phenomena are empty of both their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). This is because they are mutually dependent through successive accumulation; because when analyzed and sought, they are found to be non-existent; and because they are unarisen whether by themselves, from another, or from both. Since there is neither arising nor abiding for either specific or general characteristics, all phenomena are therefore said to be empty of their own characteristics.
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature?
It means that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-arising; this is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
What is the emptiness of the unconditioned?

That which is called the fact that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are primordially in *nirvāṇa* and devoid of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is termed the emptiness of formations (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)?
That which is called the arising of the aggregates through the conjunction of karma and causes, yet being devoid of "I" and "mine," is termed the emptiness of formations.
What is the emptiness of the ineffability of all phenomena?
It refers to the fact that the imagined intrinsic nature of all phenomena is inexpressible; this is called the emptiness of the ineffable.
What is the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom?

It refers to the time when one attains the noble wisdom of self-realization; at that moment, all views and habitual tendencies are completely abandoned. This is called the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom.
What is mutual emptiness (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)?

It means that in this, that is absent; this is called mutual emptiness. For example, if the Squirrel Mother’s Hall (*Mṛgāramātuḥ prāsāda*) is devoid of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth, I say that hall is empty; it is not, however, empty of the community of monks.
Mahāmati!

It is not that the hall lacks the intrinsic nature of a hall; it is not that the bhikṣu lacks the intrinsic nature of a bhikṣu; nor is it that elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep do not exist in other places.
Mahāmati! The specific and general characteristics of all phenomena cannot be found when sought in each respective instance; therefore, it is called "emptiness of this and that.
These are known as the seven kinds of emptiness.
"Mahāmati!
This mutual emptiness (*itaretara-śūnyatā*) is the coarsest among all forms of emptiness;
you should abandon it. Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
"Non-arising" means that while its own essence does not arise, it is not non-arising; with the exception of abiding in samādhi, this is called non-arising.
Mahāmati! "Lack of self-nature" is spoken of with intentional meaning because of non-arising.
Mahāmati!
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature because they do not abide for even a moment and because they are seen to undergo subsequent transformation; this is called the absence of intrinsic nature.
What is meant by the absence of dual characteristics?
Mahāmati! Just as light and shadow, long and short, black and white, are all established in mutual dependence and do not exist independently,
so it is, Mahāmati!
Nirvana does not exist outside of saṃsāra, nor does saṃsāra exist outside of nirvana; there is no characteristic of contradiction between saṃsāra and nirvana.
Just as it is with saṃsāra and nirvana, so it is with all phenomena; this is called the characteristic of non-duality.
"Mahāmati!
You should diligently study the characteristics of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of self-nature.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"I have always taught the Dharma of emptiness, Which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence;
Birth and death are like illusions and dreams, Yet karma is never destroyed.
As with space and nirvāṇa, The cessation of these two pairs is likewise so."
"Ordinary fools engage in false conceptualization; the noble ones are free from existence and non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "Mahāmati!"

This emptiness, non-arising, lack of intrinsic nature, and absence of dual characteristics are all contained within the sūtras spoken by all Buddhas; every scripture taught by the Buddha possesses this meaning.
Mahāmati!

All sūtras are taught in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings, yet true reality does not reside within the words themselves. It is like a mirage that deceives various animals, causing them to perceive it as water when in fact there is no water; the teachings found in the various sūtras are likewise so.

These [teachings] are intended to bring joy to ordinary people according to their own conceptual discriminations; they do not fully reveal the true Dharma that is the sphere of realization of noble wisdom.
Mahāmati, you should conform to the meaning and not be attached to words.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, in the sūtras it is said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is pure by nature, eternal, constant, uninterrupted, and without change; it is endowed with the thirty-two marks and resides within the bodies of all sentient beings. It is wrapped in the soiled garments of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), and is defiled by the stains of false discrimination such as greed, hatred, and delusion—just like a priceless jewel within soiled clothing.”
The non-Buddhists claim that the self is eternal, the creator, free from *guṇas*, sovereign, and indestructible.
Is not the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* taught by the World-Honored One the same as the self of the non-Buddhists?
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! What I call the Tathāgatagarbha is not the same as the 'self' (ātman) spoken of by the non-Buddhists."

Mahāmati! The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by means of such terms as intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nirvāṇa, non-arising, signlessness, and wishlessness, teach the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is done so that foolish people may be freed from the fear of selflessness. They teach the gate of the *tathāgatagarbha* as a state of non-discrimination and imagelessness; future and present bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not cling to this as a self.
Mahāmati! Just as a potter, from a lump of clay, uses human effort, water, a staff, a wheel, and a cord as skillful means to fashion various vessels;

so too does the Tathāgata, within the dharma that is free from all marks of conceptualization and devoid of self, employ various skillful means of wisdom to speak either of the *tathāgatagarbha* or of non-self, using various names each with their own distinctions.
Mahāmati!

I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha in order to gather in those among the various non-Buddhist groups who are attached to a self, so that they may abandon false views, enter the three gates of liberation, and swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, the Buddhas speak of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is not the same as the "self" spoken of by the non-Buddhists.
"If you wish to be free from the views of non-Buddhists, you should understand the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* as being without self.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The person, the continuum, and the aggregates, The various conditions and the atoms..."
"The Victorious One, the Sovereign, the Creator—these are merely the mind's conceptual constructions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, surveying all sentient beings of the future, again requested of the Buddha:
"I pray that you will explain for me the complete method of practice, so that bodhisattvas mahāsattvas may achieve great accomplishment in their cultivation."
The Buddha said,
“Mahāmati! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses four kinds of dharmas achieves great cultivation.”
What are these four? They are:

observing that which is manifested by one's own mind; being free from views regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing; skillfully knowing that external phenomena lack intrinsic nature; and single-mindedly seeking the noble wisdom of self-realization.
If Bodhisattvas accomplish these four dharmas, they are then called great practitioners. Mahāmati,
how does one observe that which is manifested by one's own mind?

This means observing that the three realms are merely one's own mind, devoid of self and what belongs to the self, without action, and without coming or going; they are manifested through the entry of discrimination—which follows after being perfumed by beginningless attachments and habitual tendencies—into the various forms, activities, names, and conventions that bind the body, its resources, and its dwelling place. Thus do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas observe what is manifested from their own minds.
Mahāmati! How does one become free from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing?

It is by observing that all phenomena arise like illusions and dreams, because they do not arise from themselves, from another, or from both; because they appear according to the manifestations of the measure of one's own mind; because one sees that external objects do not exist; because one sees that the various consciousnesses do not arise; and because one understands that the triple world arises through the discrimination of causes and conditions, wherein no accumulation of causal factors exists.

When observing in this manner, if all phenomena, whether internal or external, are found to be unattainable, one knows they lack substantial reality and are far removed from views of arising; realizing their illusory nature, one immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and dwells in the eighth stage. One thoroughly understands the realms of mind, mentation, and consciousness, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two kinds of selflessness, thereby transforming the basis and obtaining the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Mahāmati said:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions is it called the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya)?”
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! As for the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya), it is called the mind-made body because it moves as swiftly and without obstruction as the mind.”
Mahāmati!

It is like the mind and mental consciousness, which, even beyond immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas, recollects various objects previously seen; through the continuous succession of moments, it swiftly reaches them, unimpeded by the physical body or by mountains, rivers, or stone walls.

The mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is likewise so: adorned with the various marks through the power and mastery of the illusory-like samādhi, and because it remembers its original vows to bring sentient beings to fulfillment, it proceeds at will like a thought and is born among all the assemblies of noble ones; this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s attainment of detachment from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Mahāmati! How does one observe that external phenomena lack intrinsic nature?

It means observing all phenomena as being like a mirage, like a dream, or like the appearance of hair-tufts [to those with cataracts]. Because beginningless conceptual proliferation and various attachments, as well as false and evil habitual tendencies, serve as their causes, when one observes all phenomena in this manner, it is precisely the single-minded pursuit of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
“Mahāmati!
These are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes great cultivation; you should thus apply yourself diligently to their study.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:

“Please explain the characteristics of the causal conditions of all phenomena, so that I and all other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may thoroughly comprehend their meaning, abandon views of existence and non-existence, and no longer falsely cling to the notion that phenomena arise either gradually or instantaneously.”
The Buddha said,
"Mahāmati! All dharmas arising from causes and conditions are of two kinds, namely:
There are internal and external [conditions].
As for the external, it refers to the formation of a jar through the combination of conditions such as a lump of clay, water, a staff, a wheel, a cord, and human effort.
Just as with a clay jar, so it is with thread and cloth, grass mats, seeds and sprouts, curd and ghee; all are likewise called external conditions that arise through successive transformation.

The "internal" refers to the arising of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases from ignorance, craving, karma, and so forth; this is internal dependent origination, which is merely a conceptual construction of the foolish.
“Mahāmati! There are six kinds of causes, namely:

the cause of what is to be (bhaviṣyat-hetu), the cause of connection (sambandha-hetu), the cause of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-hetu), the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu), the cause of manifestation (vyañjana-hetu), and the cause of dependence (apekṣā-hetu).”
Mahāmati! As for the "cause as the producer," it refers to internal and external phenomena acting as causes to produce effects.
As for the "cause as the connector," it refers to internal and external phenomena acting as conditions to produce effects such as the aggregates and seeds.
The "mutually dependent cause" (sahabhū-hetu) functions as an uninterrupted condition to produce a continuous effect.
The "efficient cause" (kāraṇa-hetu) refers to that which acts as a predominant influence to bring about a result, such as a universal monarch (cakravartin).
The revealing cause (*abhivyakti-hetu*) refers to that which, arising from discrimination, reveals the characteristics of objects, like a lamp illuminating things.
The dependent cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) refers to the cessation of the continuity at the time of extinction, wherein no further false conceptualization arises.
Mahāmati! This is merely what is discriminated by the ignorant; it is neither produced gradually nor produced instantaneously. Why is this so?
Mahāmati! If [the effect] were to arise instantaneously, there would be no distinction between the agent and the action, because its causal characteristics could not be found.
If it were to arise gradually, its essential nature could likewise not be found; for how can one be called a father before the son has been born?

Those who engage in conceptual speculation claim that things produced through conditions—namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)—are mutually connected and arise in succession; however, such reasoning cannot be established, for all these are merely attachments to signs born of deluded sentiment.

Mahāmati! Neither gradual nor sudden [arising] occurs at all; it is merely because of the manifestation of mind, body, and objects. Since external self-characteristics and common characteristics are all devoid of intrinsic nature, there is nothing but consciousness arising as one's own discriminative views.
“Mahāmati!
Therefore, you should abandon the views of gradual and sudden arising within the characteristics of the conjunction of causes, conditions, and created things.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"All phenomena are without arising, and likewise they are without cessation.
Within those various conditions, one discriminates the marks of arising and ceasing;
it is not that the convergence of conditions is denied, for in this way they cease and then arise again."
It merely halts the delusions of the ignorant, who are attached to their own false sentiments;
as for the existence or non-existence of phenomena within conditions, all these are devoid of arising.
It is through the mind’s revolving confusion caused by habitual tendencies that the three realms of existence manifest.
Originally there is no arising, and likewise there is no cessation.
To contemplate all conditioned phenomena is like viewing flowers in the sky;
they are free from the grasping subject and the grasped object—this is the vision that transcends all delusion.
There is neither that which produces nor that which is produced, nor is there any cause or condition;
it is only in accordance with worldly convention that one speaks of arising and ceasing.
— *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll II.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra of the Mahāyāna, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Dazhou era,
by imperial decree.
The Second Chapter on the Collection of All Dharmas, Part Three. At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the Dharma-gate of the mind characterized by the discrimination of verbal expression."
Because I and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas well understand this, we penetrate both meanings—the speaker and the spoken—and shall swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
furthermore, we cause all sentient beings to attain purity within these two meanings.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! There are four kinds of characteristics of conceptualization regarding verbal expression."
That is to say:
discourse on signs, discourse on dreams, discourse on the attachment to faults and evils, and discourse on beginningless false conceptualization. Mahāmati!
Discourse based on signs refers to the arising of attachment to the forms produced by one's own conceptualization.
Discourse based on dreams refers to the recollection, after waking, of objects previously experienced in a dream; it arises based on unreal objects.
Attachment to erroneous speech arises from recollecting the past actions committed by enemies.
Beginningless speech of false conceptualization arises from the habitual tendencies of beginningless frivolous proliferation and false clinging.
"These are the four.
Mahāmati spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
I pray that you will further explain the characteristics of the sphere of activity consisting of the discrimination of speech:
where does it occur, and by what cause?
"How do they arise?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
"It arises through the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, nose, lips, palate, teeth, and tongue.
Mahāmati spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"Are linguistic discrimination and [the object] different or not different?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
It is neither different nor not different.

Why is this? Because language arises with conceptualization as its cause; if it were different, conceptualization would not be the cause, and if it were not different, language would not manifest meaning. Therefore, it is neither different nor not different.
Mahāmati spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
is speech the ultimate truth?"
"Is that which is spoken the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Neither is it the speech, nor is it that which is spoken."
Why is this? The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the sphere of the noble ones' bliss; one enters it by means of words, yet it is not the words themselves.
The ultimate truth is the object internally realized by the noble wisdom; it is not the object of the wisdom of verbal conceptualization, for verbal conceptualization cannot manifest it.
Mahāmati!
Language arises through origination and cessation, fluctuation, and the reciprocal conditions of causes; if it arises from reciprocal conditions, it cannot manifest the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is devoid of the characteristics of self and other; it cannot be manifested by language, for language possesses characteristics.
The ultimate truth is merely one's own mind; all various external perceptions are entirely non-existent, and it cannot be manifested by linguistic discrimination.
"Therefore, Mahāmati,
you should remain far removed from verbal discrimination.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"All phenomena lack intrinsic nature, And likewise are beyond verbal expression;
Failing to perceive the meaning of emptiness within emptiness, The foolish therefore wander in saṃsāra.
All dharmas are without nature, Transcending language and conceptual discrimination."
All existences are like dreams and transformations; they are neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
Just as a king or a householder, in order to delight his children, first shows them objects that resemble the real ones, and later bestows the actual ones.
"I am now likewise so: first I teach the semblance-dharma;
afterwards, for their sake, I expound the dharma of the personally realized reality-limit.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! May you, for my sake,
explain that realm which transcends being one or different, both or neither, existent or non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent, permanent or impermanent, and so forth—
a realm that cannot be traversed by any of the externalists, but is the domain of the personally realized noble wisdom.”
The realm (*dhātu*) is far removed from the false conceptualization of specific and general characteristics; it enters the true state of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
By gradually purifying the stages (*bhūmi*), one enters the rank of the Tathāgata.
Through the power of effortless original vows, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), one universally manifests all boundless realms; all phenomena are nothing other than one's own mind.
May I and all other bodhisattvas, by discerning these distinctions, become free from the views of the imagined nature regarding the specific and general characteristics of such dharmas,
swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*),
and cause all sentient beings everywhere to be fully endowed with all merits.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, Mahāmati!”
Excellent!
Out of compassion for the world, you have requested this meaning from me; it will bring great benefit and great peace and happiness. Mahāmati!

Ordinary beings lack wisdom and do not understand the measure of the mind; taking deluded habituation as their cause, they cling to external objects and discriminate among all self-natures—such as unity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, neither existent nor non-existent, permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Mahāmati! It is like a herd of animals, driven by thirst, perceiving a mirage in the heat of the sun as water; deluded, they rush toward it, unaware that it is not water.

So too it is with foolish ordinary beings: perfumed by beginningless conceptual proliferation and discrimination, their minds scorched by the three poisons, they delight in the realm of forms, perceive arising, abiding, and ceasing, and grasp at internal and external dharmas, falling into attachments such as oneness and difference.
Mahāmati!

It is like a city of the gandharvas, which is neither a city nor not a city. Due to the habitual perfuming of false tendencies regarding the seeds of a city, people lacking wisdom have, since beginningless time, conceived the notion of a city.

The non-Buddhists are likewise; because they have been perfumed by false habitual tendencies since beginningless time, they are unable to comprehend that which is manifested by their own minds, and thus they cling to various verbal expressions such as "identity" and "difference."
Mahāmati!

It is like a person who, in a dream, sees men and women, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, as well as cities, towns, gardens, and groves, all magnificently adorned; upon waking, they still recollect those unreal things.
"Mahāmati!
What do you think? Is such a person wise?"
He replied, "No, Great Maitreya.
"Great Maitreya! [the Buddha continued].
The non-Buddhists are likewise; bitten by evil views and failing to realize that all is but mind, they cling to views such as oneness and difference, existence and non-existence. Mahāmati!
It is like a painted image which has neither height nor depth, yet the foolish, through false perception, conceive the notion of height and depth.

In the future, non-Buddhists will likewise be thus: their deluded minds, perfumed by evil views, will increase, and by clinging to notions such as identity and difference, they will ruin themselves and others. Regarding the discourse on the absence of birth that transcends existence and non-existence, they will even claim it to be non-existent. Such slander of cause and effect uproots the foundation of all virtue; one should know that these people, through their discrimination between existence and non-existence, give rise to views of self and other, and shall surely fall into hell. Those who seek the supreme Dharma should quickly distance themselves from them.
Mahāmati!
It is like those with cataracts seeing a net of hair; they say to one another, "This is marvelous!
Yet this net of hair neither exists nor does not exist, because it is seen by some and not seen by others.

The non-Buddhists are likewise; through their evil views and conceptual discriminations, they cling to notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, thereby slandering the true Dharma and causing themselves as well as others to fall into ruin.
Mahāmati!
For example, a fire-wheel is not actually a wheel, yet the foolish grasp at it as such, while the wise do not.
It is the same with the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); through their evil views and desires, they cling to notions of oneness, difference, both, or neither regarding the arising of all phenomena.
Mahāmati! It is like a bubble on water that resembles a crystal bead;
the foolish grasp it as real and run after it to seize it. Yet that bubble is neither a bead nor not a bead, because of the nature of grasping and non-grasping.
The non-Buddhists are likewise; perfumed by the habitual tendencies of false views and conceptual discrimination, they claim that what is non-existent arises and destroy the existence of conditions.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Having established the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one gives rise to the conceptualization of existence regarding phenomena that are internally realized by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and are free from the two natures (*svabhāva*). Mahāmati!

Those practitioners who have transformed the mind, mentation, and consciousness (*cittamanovijñāna*), who are free from the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhaka*), and who abide in the stage of the Tathāgata—the self-realized noble dharma—do not give rise to the notion of either existence or non-existence.
"Mahāmati!
If practitioners give rise to attachments to existence and non-existence regarding objective realms, they will become attached to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Mahāmati!"
The self-characteristics and common characteristics of all dharmas are taught by the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (emanation Buddha), not by the *dharma-buddha* (Dharma Buddha).

Mahāmati! The teachings of the *nirmāṇa-buddha* merely accord with the views arising from the minds of foolish worldlings; they do not reveal the realm of the blissful samādhi of the personally realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
Mahāmati!
It is like the reflection of a tree appearing in water; it is neither a reflection nor not a reflection, neither the form of a tree nor not the form of a tree.

So it is with the heterodox teachers: permeated by various views and failing to understand that all is their own mind, they give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding identity, difference, and so forth.
Mahāmati!

It is like a bright mirror that is devoid of discrimination; it manifests various forms and images in accordance with conditions. Those images are neither images nor non-images, yet one perceives what is neither image nor non-image as an image; the deluded person discriminates and forms the conceptualization of an image.
The non-Buddhists are likewise; regarding the various forms manifested within their own minds, they cling to the characteristics of oneness, difference, both, or neither.
Mahāmati! It is like an echo, which arises from the conjunction of wind, water, people, and sound; it is neither existent nor non-existent, because what is heard is neither sound nor non-sound.

The same is true for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of their own mental discrimination, they give rise to views of identity, difference, both, or neither.

Mahāmati! It is like a place on the great earth where there is no grass or trees; when the sunlight strikes it, the shimmering water-waves appear. These are neither existent nor non-existent, because they arise from inverted perception rather than true perception.

Ignorant ordinary beings are likewise so: perfumed by the evil habits of beginningless conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they perceive within the gateway of the dharma-nature realized through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-svasaṃvedya*) such qualities as arising, abiding, and ceasing; identity and difference; existence and non-existence; or both and neither.
Mahāmati!
It is like a wooden puppet or a reanimated corpse that moves, turns, and acts without ceasing through the power of a piśāca or a mechanical device; those lacking wisdom take these to be real.
Ignorant worldlings are likewise thus: they follow after non-Buddhists and give rise to various evil views, clinging to false discourses such as oneness and difference.
Therefore, Mahāmati!

"One should remain free from all conceptual constructions—such as arising, abiding, and ceasing; oneness and difference; existence and non-existence; and bothness and neitherness—within the dharmas realized by noble wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The five aggregates of consciousness Are like the reflections of trees in water."
What is perceived is like a phantom or a dream; one should not engage in false conceptualization.
The three realms of existence are like a mirage, a phantom, a dream, or the optical illusion of falling hairs;
if one can contemplate them in this way, one will ultimately attain liberation.
Just as a mirage in the heat causes the mind to waver and become deluded,
so that thirsty beasts take it for water while in reality there is no substance of water;
likewise, the seeds of consciousness waver and perceive objective realms.
Just as that which is seen by one with cataracts, the foolish give rise to attachment.
Within beginningless birth and death, they are shrouded by attachment to objects of perception;
by relinquishing them, they bring about liberation, like using a wedge to extract a wedge.
Created by illusion, spells, or machinery, Like floating clouds, dreams, or flashes of lightning;
One should view the world as always thus, Forever severing the continuity of the three marks.
Within this, nothing exists, Like a mirage in the sky.
To know all phenomena in this way is to have no knowledge at all.
The aggregates are like the appearance of falling hairs; within them, one falsely discriminates.
They are merely conventional designations; when sought for their characteristics, they cannot be found.
Like painted hanging hair, an illusion, a dream, or a city of Gandharvas;
like a fire-wheel or a mirage in the heat—though non-existent in reality, they appear as if they exist.
So too are permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, bothness and neitherness.
Due to bonds from beginningless time, the deluded ordinary person engages in false conceptualization.
Within a bright mirror, clear water, a pure eye, or a wondrous mani jewel, forms and images appear; yet in reality, they do not exist at all.
The mind-consciousness is also like this, universally manifesting all forms and appearances;
it is like a dream, a mirage in the sky, and also like the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The Buddhas teach the Dharma free from the four positions;
that is, they are free from the conceptual constructions and denials of identity, difference, both, neither, existence, non-existence, and so forth. Mahāmati!

The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma takes the truths, dependent origination, cessation, the path, and liberation as its primary focus; it does not accord with such [theories] as the Primal Nature (pradhāna), the Lord (īśvara), past actions (pūrvakṛta), spontaneity (svabhāva), time (kāla), or atoms (paramāṇu).
Mahāmati!

The Buddhas teach the Dharma in order to purify the two obstacles of afflictions and knowledge; they lead beings step by step to abide within the one hundred and eight phrases of the signless Dharma, while skillfully distinguishing the characteristics of the various vehicles and stages, just as a caravan leader skillfully guides a multitude of people.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four?
They are: the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna of observing meanings, the dhyāna of taking true suchness as its object, and the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati!

What is the dhyāna practiced by fools? It refers to practitioners among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who realize the selflessness of persons and perceive the bones of their own and others' bodies as linked together in a chain, all of which they regard as having the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and impurity.

Observing in this manner with firm attachment and without relinquishing it, one gradually progresses toward excellence until reaching the meditative absorption of cessation of perception; this is called the dhyāna practiced by fools.
What is the dhyāna that observes the meaning?

This refers to having understood the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as well as the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), and then, having also abandoned the non-Buddhist views of creation by self, other, or both, one observes in accordance with the meaning of the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*) regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*); this is called the dhyāna of observing meaning.
What is the dhyāna that takes true suchness as its object?

It refers to the fact that if one discriminates that there are two regarding selflessness, that is false conceptualization; if one knows it as it truly is, so that such conceptualization does not arise, this is called the dhyāna that takes true suchness as its object.
What is the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas?

It refers to entering the Buddha-ground and abiding in the three kinds of bliss of self-realized noble wisdom, performing inconceivable deeds for the sake of all sentient beings; this is called the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna of observing the characteristics of meaning,
the dhyāna of taking true suchness as its object, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata."
When a practitioner is in meditative concentration, they may perceive forms such as the sun and moon,
the *pātāla* (the deep abyss), empty space, fire, and paintings;
by perceiving such various signs, they fall into the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
They likewise fall into the realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Abandoning all these, they abide in the objectless;
thus they are able to enter accordingly into the true mark of suchness.
"In all the lands of the ten directions,
All the infinite Buddhas Extend their hands of radiant light And stroke the crown of this person’s head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the nirvāṇa spoken of by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—what dharma is it that is designated as ‘nirvāṇa’?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"When the habitual tendencies of the self-nature of all consciousnesses, as well as those of the ālayavijñāna, manas, and manovijñāna, have been transformed, I and the Buddhas call this 'nirvāṇa'; it is the realm of the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas."
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Nirvāṇa is the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, as well as existence and non-existence.
Why is it not permanent?
This means that it is free from all conceptual constructions regarding specific and general characteristics.
Why is it not annihilated?
Because it is the object of the self-realized wisdom of all noble ones of the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, Great Parinirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die.

If it were subject to death, it would have to undergo rebirth; if it were subject to destruction, it would be a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, Nirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die; it is the destination to which all practitioners aspire.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Because there is neither relinquishing nor attaining, because it is neither annihilated nor eternal, and because it is neither identical nor different, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, knowing the specific and general characteristics [of phenomena], abandon worldly clamor; they do not give rise to perversions or conceptual discriminations, and thus they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa therein.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are two kinds of characteristics of self-nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa). What are the two?
That is to say:
clinging to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression, and clinging to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Clinging to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression arises from the habit-energy of clinging to verbal expressions due to beginningless conceptual proliferation.
The attachment to the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena arises because one does not realize that they are manifestations of one's own mind.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the Buddhas possess two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by which they sustain the bodhisattvas, causing them to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and inquire about various meanings.
What are these two? They are:
causing one to enter samādhi, and manifesting their presence before one's body to pour water from their hand upon one's crown.
Mahāmati!

Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the first stage receive the sustaining power of all Buddhas, they enter the Bodhisattva samādhi called "The Radiance of the Great Vehicle. Having entered it, the Buddhas of the ten directions universally manifest before them, bestowing empowerment through their bodies and speech; such is the case for those like Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished such marks of merit.

Mahāmati! Having entered this samādhi through the sustaining power of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having accumulated all roots of goodness over hundreds of thousands of kalpas, gradually enters the various stages (*bhūmi*). Being well-versed in penetrating the characteristics of that which is to be remedied and its remedy, he reaches the stage of Dharma-cloud (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*). There, seated upon a precious throne within a subtle and wondrous palace of great lotuses, surrounded by Bodhisattvas of his own kind, wearing a jeweled crown and with a body like golden *campaka* flowers or the full moon, he emits a great radiance. The Buddhas of the ten directions extend their lotus-hands and perform the empowerment of sprinkling water upon his head while he sits on that throne.
Just as the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch attains sovereign power after receiving the consecration, so too it is with these bodhisattvas; this is called the second.
Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by two kinds of support, they are able to see all buddhas face-to-face; otherwise, they could not.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter samādhi, manifest supernatural powers, and preach the Dharma—all such things arise from the two kinds of sustaining power of the Buddhas.
Mahāmati!
If bodhisattvas were able to teach the Dharma apart from the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, then ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) should also be able to teach it.
Mahāmati!

In mountain forests, grasses, trees, cities, palaces, and all manner of musical instruments, wherever the Tathāgata arrives, they still produce the sound of the Dharma through the power of the Buddha’s sustaining grace; how much more so for sentient beings, who, being freed from suffering, shall be liberated even from deafness, blindness, and muteness.
"Mahāmati!
Such are the vast activities of the Tathāgata’s sustaining power.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata, by means of his sustaining power, cause all bodhisattvas to enter into samādhi and the sublime stages, and pour water upon their heads?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"

In order to cause them to distance themselves from the karmic activities of Māra and all afflictions; in order to prevent them from falling into the stage of the Śrāvaka; in order to cause them to swiftly enter the stage of the Tathāgata; and in order to cause the dharmas they have attained to increase manifold—it is for these reasons that the Buddhas sustain the Bodhisattvas through the power of their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Mahāmati!

If it were not thus, those bodhisattvas would fall into the realms of the externalists, the śrāvakas, and Māra, and would be unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi; therefore, the Tathāgata sustains all bodhisattvas through the power of his empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The World-Honored One’s pure vows possess the power of great empowerment;
From the first stage through the tenth stage, there are samādhis and empowerments.”
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha has taught that dependent origination arises from activity and does not arise from its own intrinsic nature."
The non-Buddhists also claim that all phenomena arise from the Primal Nature (prakṛti), Īśvara, Time, the Self (ātman), or atoms (paramāṇu).
Now, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) using different names; there is no difference in meaning.
“World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists also say that because there is a creator, existence arises from non-existence;

the World-Honored One also says that because of causes and conditions, all dharmas originally do not exist but arise, and having arisen, they return to extinction. According to what the Buddha has taught—that ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, up to old age and death—is this not a teaching of causelessness rather than a teaching of causality?”

The World-Honored One has taught that "because this exists, that exists. If these were established simultaneously rather than being mutually dependent through a sequential process, their meaning would not be established.
Therefore, the doctrine of the non-Buddhists is superior, and not that of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? The non-Buddhists claim that causes give rise to effects without themselves being produced from conditions.

According to what the World-Honored One has taught, the effect depends upon a cause, and the cause in turn depends upon another cause; thus, through such successive dependence, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
Furthermore, if it were the case that "because this exists, that exists," then there would be no cause.
The Buddha said,
"Mahāmati!..."

I have realized that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, devoid of both grasper and grasped; I teach that "because this exists, that exists," which is neither causeless nor subject to the fault of defective causes and conditions.
Mahāmati!

If one does not understand that all phenomena are manifestations of mind-only, but instead calculates the existence of a grasper and a grasped, and clings to external objects as being either existent or non-existent, such a person incurs these faults; this is not what I have taught.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, because there is verbal expression, there must necessarily be dharmas;
if there were no dharmas, upon what would verbal expression depend for its arising?"
The Buddha said: “Mahāmati!

Although all phenomena do not exist, there is still verbal expression. Is it not evident that people in the world give rise to verbal expressions regarding such things as the hair of a tortoise, the horns of a rabbit, and the son of a barren woman?”
Mahāmati! That is neither existent nor non-existent; it is merely a matter of verbal expression. Mahāmati!
As you have said, if it were the case that all phenomena exist because there are verbal expressions, then this treatise would be undermined. Mahāmati!
It is not the case that all Buddha-fields possess verbal expression; verbal expression is merely a conventional designation.

Mahāmati! In some buddha-fields, the Dharma is manifested by gazing fixedly; in others, by manifesting extraordinary signs; or again, by raising the eyebrows, moving the eyes, showing a smile, frowning, clearing the throat, coughing, mindfulness, or gesturing. It is through such means as these that the Dharma is revealed.
Mahāmati!

Just as in the world of Animiṣa, the world of Gandhavatī, and within the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, by merely gazing with unblinking eyes, all bodhisattvas are caused to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and various supreme samādhis.
Mahāmati!
Phenomena do not exist by virtue of verbal expression; for in this world, even insects such as flies and ants accomplish their own purposes despite lacking verbal expression.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Like space, a rabbit’s horns, And the son of a barren woman— To speak of what does not exist;
Such is the nature of falsely conceptualized phenomena.”
"Within the harmony of causes and conditions, the deluded falsely claim there is birth;
unable to understand according to reality, they wander through the three realms of existence.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Based upon what is this spoken sound of ‘permanence’ declared?
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! Based on the teaching of false dharmas, all these false dharmas are manifested even by the noble ones, yet they do not fall into error.
Mahāmati!”

For example, like a mirage, a whirling firebrand, falling hair, a city of Gandharvas, a dream, an illusion, or a reflection in a mirror, those in the world who lack wisdom give rise to perverted understandings, whereas those with wisdom do not; yet, it is not that these things do not appear.
Mahāmati! Although false dharmas manifest in immeasurable varieties, they are not impermanent. Why is this?
Because it is free from existence and non-existence. How is it free from existence and non-existence?

Because all foolish commoners have various understandings, it is like the river Ganges: for those who see it, it exists; for hungry ghosts who do not see it, one cannot say it exists. Yet, because others do see it, one cannot say it does not exist. Thus, the noble ones are free from inverted views regarding illusory phenomena.

Mahāmati! False dharmas are eternal because their characteristics do not differ. It is not that false dharmas possess distinct characteristics; rather, they appear as different only through conceptual discrimination. Therefore, the essence of false dharmas is eternal.
Mahāmati! How does one attain the reality of illusory phenomena?
It means that the noble ones do not give rise to inversion within illusory phenomena, nor do they possess non-inverted cognition.
If there is even the slightest conceptualization regarding false phenomena, it is not noble wisdom;
one should know that such slight conceptualization is merely the frivolous proliferation of fools, not the discourse of the noble ones.
“Mahāmati! If one discriminates whether false dharmas are inverted or non-inverted, one then establishes two kinds of lineage:
namely, the noble lineage and the ordinary lineage.”
Mahāmati! As for the noble lineage, it is further of three kinds, namely:
the distinction between the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha vehicles.
Mahāmati! How do the deluded ordinary people, through their discrimination of false dharmas, give rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle?
It is by means of their attachment to specific and general characteristics.
Mahāmati! What is meant by the further case of a foolish person who discriminates false dharmas and thereby establishes the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna?
It refers to one who, while clinging to self-characteristics and common characteristics, remains detached from worldly clamor.
Mahāmati! What is meant by a wise person discerning false dharmas and thereby achieving the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle?
It is said that they thoroughly understand that all things are merely what is seen through the discrimination of one's own mind, and that no external dharmas exist.
Mahāmati!

There are foolish people who discriminate among various phenomena and manifold objects, asserting with certainty that they are thus and with certainty that they are not otherwise; this constitutes the nature of the vehicle of saṃsāra.
Mahāmati!
Within those false dharmas, the various things and phenomena are neither entities nor non-entities.
Mahāmati!

Regarding those very delusive phenomena, because the noble ones who possess wisdom have undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the nature of the mind, intellect, and consciousness along with all their evil habitual tendencies, this very delusion is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Therefore, Suchness is free from mind and consciousness; I now clearly demonstrate this point: that which is free from conceptualization is entirely free from all forms of conceptualization.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
regarding the false dharmas you have spoken of, do they exist or do they not exist?"
The Buddha said:

"It is like an illusion, because it lacks the characteristic of attachment. If the essence of the characteristic of attachment were existent, it could not be transformed; in that case, all dependent origination would be like the 'creator-produced' asserted by the non-Buddhists."
Mahāmati spoke again:
"If all false dharmas are identical to illusions, then they should serve as the causes for other false things.
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! Illusory phenomena are not the cause of delusion, because illusions do not give rise to various faults and evils, and because illusory phenomena are devoid of discrimination.”

Mahāmati! As for illusory phenomena, they arise from the power of another’s incantations and spells; they do not arise from the force of one's own habitual tendencies of discrimination. Therefore, illusory phenomena do not produce faults or evils.
"Mahāmati!
These dharmas of delusion are merely what the minds of the foolish grasp and cling to; they are not so for the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
The Sage does not perceive delusive dharmas, nor is there anything real in between;
because delusion is itself reality, that which is in between is also truly real.
If, apart from delusive dharmas, there were any arising of marks, [it would be a fallacy].
This, in turn, is itself delusion, like a visual impairment that has not yet been cleared away.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
because one perceives that all phenomena are not illusions and lack any resemblance to them, it is said that "all phenomena are like illusions."
Mahāmati said:
“World-Honored One,
is it because of attachment to various illusory appearances that you say all dharmas are like an illusion?”
Or is it due to a different basis that one clings to these inverted characteristics?
World-Honored One, if it is by relying on the clinging to various illusory appearances that one says all phenomena are like illusions, [then how can they be said to be non-existent?]
It is not the case that all phenomena are entirely like illusions. Why is this?
Because the perception of various forms and characteristics does not occur without a cause.
World-Honored One!
There is no cause whatsoever that causes various forms and appearances to manifest like an illusion.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
"One cannot say that because one relies upon attachment to various illusory appearances, all phenomena are similar to illusions.
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
It is not by relying on or clinging to various illusory appearances that one says all phenomena are like illusions.
Mahāmati! Because all phenomena are unreal and perish as swiftly as lightning, they are said to be like illusions.
Mahāmati!

Just as a flash of lightning is seen and immediately vanishes, so too do all worldly, ignorant people perceive all phenomena; they appear through their own discrimination as individual and common characteristics. Because they are unable to investigate their non-existence, they falsely conceptualize and become attached to various forms and appearances.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Where there is no illusion, there is nothing comparable; Nor do any phenomena truly exist.
Unreal and as swift as lightning, One should know them to be like an illusion."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously taught, all dharmas are entirely without arising;..."
Furthermore, you have said that [all things] are like illusions; is this not a contradiction between what was previously stated and what is now being said?
The Buddha replied, “Mahāmati!
There is no contradiction. Why is this?
Because I realize that birth is itself non-arising, for it is merely what is seen by one's own mind.
Whether existent or non-existent, all external phenomena are seen to be without intrinsic nature because they are fundamentally unarisen. Mahāmati,
it is in order to distance oneself from the non-Buddhist view that things arise from causes that I teach that all dharmas are entirely unarisen.
Mahāmati!

The multitudes of non-Buddhists collectively give rise to evil views, claiming that all phenomena arise from existence and non-existence, rather than from the conditions of one's own self-attached discrimination.
Mahāmati!
I teach that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent in their arising; therefore, they are called "unborn" (anutpāda). Mahāmati!

The teaching of all dharmas is intended to cause disciples to understand that they undergo birth and death through the appropriation of various karmas, thereby preventing them from falling into the view of nihilism. Mahāmati!
The teaching that the characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions is for the purpose of causing one to abandon the notion of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in phenomena.

For the sake of ordinary fools who have fallen into evil views and desires, and who do not understand that all phenomena are manifestations of mind-only, [the Buddha] teaches that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, in order to cause them to distance themselves from attachment to the characteristics of arising through causes and conditions.
Those foolish people, clinging to evil views, deceive both themselves and others; they are unable to clearly perceive the true abiding state of all phenomena as they really are.
Mahāmati!
To see all phenomena in their true state means to be able to thoroughly comprehend that they are manifestations of mind-only.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Because there is no volitional activity, there is no arising; The existence of phenomena encompasses birth and death.
To thoroughly understand them as being like illusions and the like, One does not discriminate among their marks."

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). By skillfully contemplating these characteristics and thoroughly comprehending their meanings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and further be able to awaken all sentient beings."
Mahāmati!
As for the "name-body" (nāmakāya), it refers to establishing names based on phenomena; the name itself is the body, and thus it is called the name-body.
As for the "phrase-body" (padakāya), it refers to that which can manifest the meaning with definitive finality; this is called the phrase-body.
Regarding "syllable-group" (*vyañjana-kāya*): it refers to that by means of which names and phrases are established; this is called the syllable-group.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding "phrase-group" (*pada-kāya*):
it refers to the completion of the meaning of a phrase.
The "name-body" (nāmakāya) refers to the various distinct names formed by individual syllables, such as from the letter *a* up to the letter *ha*.
The "phrase-body" (vyañjanakāya) refers to the distinctions of length, shortness, high pitch, and low pitch.
Furthermore, the "phrase-body" (*padakāya*) is like a footprint, such as the tracks of humans, cattle, or other animals in a street or alleyway.
"Name" (*nāman*) refers to the four formless aggregates (*skandha*), because they are expressed by means of names.
"Phonemes (*vyañjana*) refer to the intrinsic characteristics of names, because they are manifested by phonemes.
These are the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
You should train yourself in these characteristics of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The distinctions between name-bodies, phrase-bodies, and syllable-bodies—
In these the foolish and ignorant are attached, Like an elephant sinking into deep mud.”
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

In future ages there will be those with false wisdom and evil thoughts who, departing from the Dharma of suchness, perceive the characteristics of identity, difference, both, or neither, and question the wise ones."
He replied: "This is not a correct question. Namely:
are form and impermanence different, or are they not different?"

In this way, regarding nirvāṇa and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*): are the characteristic and the characterized, the support and the supported, the primary elements and the derived elements, the seer and the seen, the earth and its atoms, and wisdom and the wise, different or not different?
When such questions regarding indeterminate matters are asked in succession, the World-Honored One declares that they should be set aside as non-answers.
These are not within the capacity of the ignorant and witless to understand; the Buddha does not provide an answer because he wishes to keep them from falling into a state of alarm and fear.
Mahāmati!
The reason for not making a formal declaration is that I wish to cause the non-Buddhists to forever escape from their views regarding an agent.
Mahāmati!
The various groups of non-Buddhists who postulate the existence of a creator make such statements as:
"The life-principle is identical to the body," or "The life-principle is different from the body.
Such assertions as these are called the doctrine of the indeterminate (avyākṛta-vāda).

Mahāmati! It is the deluded heterodox teachers who propound the doctrine of the indeterminate; it is not within my teaching that one should cease [discrimination]. Since [my teaching] involves the departure from the grasped and the grasper and the non-arising of discrimination, how could it be subject to cessation?
Mahāmati! If there are those who cling to the grasper and the grasped, failing to understand that these are merely what is seen of one's own mind, they should be refuted. Mahāmati!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of four kinds of formal responses (*vyākaraṇa*).

Mahāmati! As for the "response by setting aside" (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*), I have taught it as a discourse for another time; it is so called because the teaching is temporarily set aside due to the fact that the faculties [of the listeners] are not yet mature.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
For what reason are all phenomena non-arising?
Because they are devoid of the agent, the action, and the instrument of agency."
Why are all phenomena devoid of intrinsic nature?
Because when observed through realized wisdom, their specific and general characteristics cannot be apprehended.
Why are all phenomena without coming or going?
Because self-characteristics and common characteristics come from nowhere and go nowhere.
Why are all phenomena not extinguished?
It is because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, and are thus unapprehendable.
Why are all phenomena impermanent?
It is because their various characteristics arise with the nature of impermanence.
Why are all phenomena permanent?
"It means that the arising of all characteristics is itself non-arising, because they are non-existent.
The nature of impermanence is permanent; therefore, I say that all dharmas are permanent.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Direct answer, counter-question, analysis, and setting aside;
these four modes of discourse subdue all non-Buddhists.
The Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas claim that existence arises from non-existence."
All such various explanations as these are entirely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
When observed with wisdom, their essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be apprehended;
because they are inexpressible, they are said to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that you will explain to me the distinct characteristics of the various practices of the *srotāpanna* and the fruit of *srotāpatti*. By hearing this meaning, I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas shall all attain skillfulness regarding the expedient characteristics of the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*.”

Thus he expounds the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to realize the two kinds of selflessness and purify the two hindrances; they gradually penetrate the characteristics of the stages and attain the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, like a mani-jewel of manifold colors, universally bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said, "Yes. The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! There are three distinctions among the various types of srotāpannas and the fruit of srotāpatti, namely:
inferior, middling, and superior.”
Mahāmati!

Those of inferior capacity are reborn at most seven times within the various realms of existence; those of middling capacity are reborn three or five times; and those of superior capacity enter nirvāṇa in this very life.
Mahāmati! These three types of persons sever three fetters— namely, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)— and through successive superior progress, they attain the fruit of arhatship.
Mahāmati!

There are two kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi (the view of a self-identity): namely, that which is innate and that which is discriminative, just as the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature) exists based upon the paratantra-svabhāva (dependent origination). Mahāmati!

For example, based upon the nature of dependent origination, various natures of false conceptualization and attachment arise; these phenomena are merely the marks of false discrimination—neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent. Yet, out of ignorance, ordinary people grasp at them perversely, just as a thirsty deer falsely perceives water in a mirage. Because this body-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is associated with a lack of wisdom for a long time, it is abandoned immediately upon seeing the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).

Mahāmati! As for the innate view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one observes universally that among the four formless aggregates—feeling and the others—there is no characteristic of form; that form arises from the great elements (*mahābhūta*); that these great elements are mutually dependent causes; and that form is not a collection [of atoms]. Having observed in this way, one clearly perceives existence and non-existence and immediately abandons them.
Because the view of a self-body is abandoned, craving does not arise. This is called the characteristic of the view of a self-body.

Mahāmati! As for the characteristic of doubt: because one has clearly perceived the characteristics of the Dharma realized, and because the two previous kinds of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have been severed through discrimination, doubt cannot arise regarding any phenomena. Furthermore, one does not conceive of another as a "Great Teacher" in order to determine whether something is pure or impure; this is called the characteristic of doubt.
Mahāmati! For what reason does the srotāpanna not grasp at precepts and observances?
It is because he clearly perceives the characteristics of suffering inherent in the places of rebirth; therefore, he does not grasp at them.

As for "clinging" (*parāmarśa*), it refers to ordinary, deluded beings who, out of attachment to worldly pleasures within the various realms of existence, practice austerities and observe precepts with the wish to be reborn therein.
