A *srotāpanna* does not cling to such signs; rather, they seek only the most supreme, untainted, and non-conceptual Dharma that is to be realized, and thus practice the categories of ethical discipline. This is called the characteristic of clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
“Mahāmati!
Because the srotāpanna has abandoned the three fetters, he is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Mahāmati said:
“There are many kinds of greed; which kind of greed should one abandon?
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!”

Having abandoned the entanglements of craving for female beauty, because one perceives that present pleasure gives rise to suffering in future lives, and because one attains the superior bliss of samādhi, one therefore abandons that craving which is not for nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati! What is the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin?

It refers to one who, failing to understand the characteristics of form, gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding form; having returned once more to this world, they skillfully cultivate the practices of dhyāna, reach the ultimate limit of suffering, and enter parinirvāṇa—this is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Mahāmati! What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmin)?

It means that regarding the marks of form in the past, future, and present, one gives rise to neither the view of existence nor the view of non-existence; one does not give rise to the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of discriminating faults; and having forever abandoned all fetters (saṃyojana), one no longer returns. This is called a non-returner.
Mahāmati!

An arhat is one who has fully accomplished all dhyānas, samādhis, liberations, powers, and superknowledges; because the afflictions, sufferings, and conceptual discriminations have been eternally exhausted, such a person is called an arhat.
Mahāmati said:
"World-Honored One!
There are three kinds of arhats, namely:..."
"One who is solely intent on tranquility, has withdrawn from the vow for enlightenment, and is a transformation of a Buddha—
of whom is this said?
The Buddha replied:
“Mahāmati! This refers to the attainment of tranquility, and not to anything else.
Mahāmati!”
The other two types of persons, Mahāmati,
are those who have already made vows regarding skillful means, and those who manifest birth therein for the purpose of adorning the assemblies of the Buddhas. Mahāmati!

Within the realm of falsehood, various teachings are expounded; that is to say, because both the meditator who realizes the fruit and the meditation itself are by nature detached, and because the appearance of attaining the fruit is merely what is perceived by one's own mind.
Mahāmati! If a srotāpanna should think:
"I am free from all fetters."
"Then there would be two faults, namely:
falling into the view of self and the failure to sever the various fetters.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
If one wishes to transcend the various dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless realms, one should abandon all marks perceived by one’s own mind.
Mahāmati! It is not the case that the samādhi of the cessation of perception and feeling transcends the objects perceived by one’s own mind, for it does not depart from the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The various dhyānas and the immeasurables, The formless attainments and samādhis, As well as the cessation of perception and feeling— All these are but mind; they cannot be found.”
The stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat—all such noble ones exist only through the delusion of the mind.
The practitioner of dhyāna takes the object of meditation as their focus; by severing delusions, they perceive the true reality.
"All these are merely conceptual constructions; to understand them thoroughly is liberation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening-knowledge, namely:
There is the wisdom of observation, as well as the wisdom that establishes conceptualization through grasping at signs and clinging.
Regarding the wisdom of observation: it refers to observing all phenomena as being unapprehendable, transcending the four extremes.
The "four positions" refer to:
identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Since all phenomena are free from these four positions, I say that all phenomena are detached [from them].
Mahāmati! You should practice and study the contemplation of dharmas in this manner.
What is the wisdom that involves grasping at signs, conceptual differentiation, attachment, and establishment?

This refers to the false conceptualization that grasps at signs and clings to the natures of the great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—and falsely establishes them through propositions, reasons, and examples; this is called the wisdom of conceptualizing signs, clinging, and establishment.

These are called the two characteristics of awakened wisdom (*jñāna*). When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands these characteristics of wisdom, they are able to penetrate the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*).

Through the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*), they skillfully observe on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). There, they attain one hundred samādhis; by the power of these superior samādhis, they see one hundred Buddhas and one hundred Bodhisattvas, know the events of one hundred kalpas in both the past and future limits, and their radiance illuminates one hundred Buddha-worlds. They become well-versed in the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*). By the power of superior vows, they manifest transformations with mastery, until reaching the Cloud of Dharma stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) where they receive empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Entering the stage of Buddhahood, they fulfill the ten inexhaustible vows to bring sentient beings to maturity, manifesting in various ways without ceasing, while constantly dwelling in the supreme bliss of the samādhi of the realm of self-realization (*svasaṃvedya-viṣaya-samādhi*).
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully understand the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the matter derived from them (bhautika-rūpa).
How does one understand them?

Mahāmati! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should observe in this way: those great elements are truly unarisen, for the three realms are merely conceptual constructions; they are only manifestations of the mind, and no external objects exist.

When observing in this way, all primary elements and their derivatives are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; transcending the four propositions, they are without self or what belongs to a self, abiding in the state of suchness and achieving the characteristic of non-arising.
Mahāmati! How do those great elements (mahābhūta) construct form? Mahāmati!

That is to say: through false conceptualization, the moistening primary elements form the internal and external water element; the blazing primary elements form the internal and external fire element; the moving primary elements form the internal and external wind element; and the materialized primary elements form the internal and external earth element. Apart from space, due to attachment to false truths, the great elements and derived matter arise as an aggregation of the five aggregates.
Mahāmati!
Because consciousness arises with attachment to the various objects of verbal expression as its cause, it continues to take birth in other realms of existence.
Mahāmati!

The derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) such as earth and so forth has the primary elements (mahābhūta) as its cause; however, the four primary elements themselves do not have the primary elements as their cause. Why is this?
Because if a phenomenon possesses a formal characteristic (saṃsthāna), it is something produced (kṛtaka) and not something without form.
"Mahāmati!
This conceptualization of the primary elements and their derived forms belongs to the non-Buddhists;
it is not my teaching. Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
I shall now explain the essential characteristics of the five aggregates, namely:
form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati!
Form refers to the four great elements and the form derived from them; these each have distinct characteristics.
Sensation and the other [aggregates] are not form, Mahāmati!
The non-material aggregates (*arūpin-skandha*), like space, possess no fourfold numerical designation. Mahāmati!

Just as space transcends all characteristics of number, yet one discriminatively speaks of it, saying "this is space," so too are the non-material aggregates; they are free from all characteristics of number because they are devoid of the four logical positions (*catuṣkoṭi*), such as existence and non-existence.

Characteristics of numerical enumeration are spoken of by the ignorant, not by the noble ones; the noble ones speak only of that which is like a magical creation, a mere conventional designation, neither different nor non-different, like a dream or a reflection, having no separate existence whatsoever.

Because they do not understand the sphere of activity of noble wisdom, they perceive the various aggregates as manifesting through discrimination; this is called the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates. Mahāmati!

You should abandon such discrimination. Having abandoned this, one preaches the dharma of tranquility, severs all the views of externalists throughout the lands, and enters the Far-Going Stage (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*) through the purification of the selflessness of phenomena. One achieves immeasurable sovereign samādhis, attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), and becomes fully endowed with the powers, penetrations, and mastery of the illusory-like samādhi, just as the great earth universally benefits all living beings.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of nirvāṇa. What are the four?
That is to say:

the nirvana of the self-nature of all phenomena being without nature; the nirvana of the various characteristics and natures being without nature; the nirvana of awakening to the self-characteristics and natures being without nature; and the nirvana of severing the continuous flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates.
Mahāmati! These four types of nirvāṇa belong to the doctrines of the non-Buddhists; they are not what I have taught. Mahāmati!
"What I have taught is that the cessation of the consciousness that discriminates objects (*vijñapti*) is called nirvana. Mahamati said,
"World-Honored One!"
"Do you not establish eight kinds of consciousness? The Buddha said, "I do."
Mahāmati said: “If you establish this [teaching], why do you say only that the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) ceases, rather than the cessation of the seven consciousnesses?
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! Because they serve as its cause and its object-condition, the seven consciousnesses arise.
Mahāmati!”

When the manas discriminates objects and gives rise to attachment, various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are produced, which nourish the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Consequently, the manas—which functions in conjunction with it, accompanied by the grasping of "I" and "mine," and characterized by mentation—operates without a distinct ontological identity. Because the storehouse consciousness serves as its cause and its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it clings to objects manifested by its own mind; thus, the collection of mental states arises, each acting as a cause for the next in a continuous succession.
Mahāmati!

It is like the waves of the ocean, which are manifestations of one's own mind; stirred by the wind of objective realms, they arise and cease. Therefore, when the *manovijñāna* (consciousness) ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"I do not [teach] the cessation of the consciousness that discriminates objects By means of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) Or by means of the characteristic of activity (*kriyā-lakṣaṇa*); It is in this way that I speak of nirvāṇa."
Mental consciousness is the cause of the mind, and the mind is the objective sphere of the intellect;
through these causes and their objects, all cognitions arise and dependently manifest.
Just as when a great torrent is exhausted, waves no longer arise.
"In this way, when the mental consciousness ceases, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the distinct characteristics of the nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), so that you and the other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may thoroughly understand this meaning, transcend all deluded imaginings, realize the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), and know the teachings of the non-Buddhists. Thus, you shall remain far removed from the discrimination of grasper and grasped, and no longer cling to the falsely conceptualized characteristics within the various aspects of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the differentiation of the falsely imagined nature?
It is as follows:

The conceptualization of verbal expression, the conceptualization of what is expressed, the conceptualization of marks, the conceptualization of objects, the conceptualization of intrinsic nature, the conceptualization of causes, the conceptualization of views, the conceptualization of principles, the conceptualization of arising, the conceptualization of non-arising, the conceptualization of connection, and the conceptualization of bondage and liberation.
Mahāmati! This is the characteristic of the differentiation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
What, then, is verbal discrimination (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*)?
That is to say, the attachment to various beautiful sounds and words is called the discrimination of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*).
What is the discrimination of the expressed (*abhidheya-vikalpa*)?

It refers to the attachment to the existence of an object that is expressed—the realm realized by noble wisdom—and the arising of speech based upon this; this is called the discrimination of the expressed.
What is the discrimination of characteristics?

It refers to the conceptualization and attachment to all characteristics—such as solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—with respect to those very things already mentioned, like the mental construction of a mirage by a thirsty deer; this is called the discrimination of characteristics.
What is the discrimination of objects?
It refers to the verbal expressions arising from attachment to various treasures such as gold and silver; this is called the discrimination of objects.
What is the discrimination of intrinsic nature?
That is to say, by means of wrong views, one discriminates this intrinsic nature as being definitively nothing other than itself; this is called discrimination of intrinsic nature.
What is discrimination of cause?

This refers to the conceptualization of causes and conditions as either existent or non-existent, because it is through these causal characteristics that [phenomena] are able to arise; this is called the conceptualization of causes.
What is the conceptualization of views?

This refers to the evil views of various non-Buddhists who cling to existence and non-existence, identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, and so forth; this is called the discrimination of views.
What is the discrimination of principles?

That which involves clinging to the characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to self," and thereby giving rise to verbal expression, is called conceptualization through reasoning (*yukti-vikalpa*). What is conceptualization through arising (*utpatti-vikalpa*)?
It refers to the reckoning that all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, arise from conditions; this is called conceptualization through arising.

What is the discrimination of non-arising? It refers to the reckoning that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; that they possess an intrinsic essence prior to the existence of conditions and do not arise from causes. This is called the discrimination of non-arising.
What is the discrimination of mutual connection?
It refers to this and that being mutually linked together, like a needle and thread; this is called the discrimination of mutual connection.
What is the discrimination of bondage and liberation?

This refers to the attachment that the cause is capable of binding and that there is something to be bound; it is like a person who, through the skillful means of a rope, first binds and then releases—this is called the discrimination between bondage and liberation.
Mahāmati! This is the characteristic of the differentiation of the nature of false conceptualization; therein all ordinary, ignorant people cling to existence or non-existence. Mahāmati!

Within dependent origination, one clings to various imagined natures, just as one perceives various objects based on an illusion; yet the ignorant, through their conceptualization, see these as distinct from the illusion itself.
Mahāmati! Illusion and its various manifestations are neither different nor non-different. If they were different, illusion would not be the cause of the various manifestations;
if they were one, there would be no distinction between illusion and its manifestations. Yet, a distinction is perceived. Therefore, they are neither different nor non-different.
“Mahāmati!
You and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should not give rise to attachment regarding the existence or non-existence of illusions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The mind is bound by objects; conceptualization and wisdom follow in turn.
In the most supreme state of signlessness, impartial wisdom arises.
That which is imagined through false discrimination exists, yet within dependent origination it is non-existent."
Deluded conceptualization grasps; dependent origination is free from discrimination.
The various members arise like a magical illusion, lacking inherent existence;
though they manifest in various forms, false discrimination is non-existent.
Those signs are themselves the fault, all arising from the bonds of the mind;
those who engage in false conceptualization do not understand the dharma of dependent origination.
These various natures of false conceptualization are themselves nothing but dependent origination.
There are various false imaginings, which are discriminations within dependent origination.
There are the conventional, the ultimate, and a third, which arises without cause;
false imagination is the conventional, and its cessation is the realm of the noble ones.
Just as for a practitioner of meditation, a single thing appears as manifold;
yet in that [reality] there is no manifoldness—such is the nature of false conceptualization.
Just as one with various eye-impurities sees many colors through deluded thought; so too does the mind perceive the world.
That which is formless is not form; it is thus that one does not understand dependent origination.
Like gold separated from dust and grime, like water free from the turbidity of mud, and like the sky without clouds—thus is the purification of false conceptualization.
There is no nature of false imagination, yet there is dependent origination;
construction and denial arise from the destruction caused by conceptual discrimination.
If there were no nature of false imagination, yet dependent origination existed;
Where there is no dharma, there is dharma; from non-existence, dharma arises.
Depending upon false conceptualization (*parikalpita*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) occurs;
appearance and name constantly follow one another, giving rise to false conceptualization.
Because dependent origination relies on delusion, it is ultimately unestablished;
at that time, what appears as pure is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
There are twelve aspects of false conceptualization (*parikalpita*), and six types of dependent origination (*paratantra*).
The realm of self-realized suchness is without differentiation.
The five dharmas are the reality, and the three natures are likewise;
when practitioners contemplate this, they do not transcend suchness.
Based upon the characteristics of dependent origination, one falsely conceptualizes various names;
those various characteristics of false conceptualization all exist because of dependent origination.
When wisdom observes skillfully, there is neither dependence nor false conceptualization.
In reality there are no things; how, then, could conceptualization arise?
If the perfected nature were existent, it would be free from existence and non-existence.
Since it is already free from existence and non-existence, how could there be two natures?
The two natures are falsely conceptualized; these two natures are established [conventionally].
Various things are seen through discrimination, yet they are the sphere of activity for the pure sages.
One falsely conceptualizes various characteristics, discriminating within dependent origination.
If one discriminates otherwise than this, one falls into the doctrines of the non-Buddhists.
Because of various false views, one falsely conceptualizes upon false conceptualization;
for one who is free from these two types of conceptualization, that is the true Dharma.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the practice of self-realized noble wisdom and the characteristics of the practice of the One Vehicle.”
“I and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having attained this skillful means, shall realize the Buddha-dharma through our own awakening, without depending on others.
The Buddha said:
“Listen attentively!”
"I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said, "Yes,
[I am ready]."
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely on the various holy teachings without conceptual discrimination, dwelling alone in quietude to observe through self-awakening, they do not depend on others for realization and remain free from discriminatory views. Thus ascending higher and higher, they enter the stage of the Tathāgata; such practice is called the characteristic of the practice of self-realized noble wisdom.”
What is called the characteristic of the practice of the One Vehicle?
It refers to attaining the realization and knowledge of the path of the One Vehicle.
What is meant by knowing the path of the One Vehicle?
That is to say, one dwells in accordance with reality, free from the conceptualization of the grasper and the grasped.
Mahāmati, this path of the Single Vehicle can be attained by none other than the Tathāgata; it cannot be attained by outsiders, those of the two vehicles, or even by Brahmā-devas and others.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason do you speak of three vehicles and not of one vehicle?"
The Buddha said: "Mahāmati!
Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack the dharma of self-parinirvāṇa, I teach the One Vehicle."
Because they attain liberation by practicing according to the discipline and renunciation taught by the Tathāgata, rather than through their own independent attainment;

furthermore, because they have not yet eliminated the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the habitual tendencies of karma, have not realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and have not attained what is called the inconceivable transformation-death (*acintyapariṇāmikī cyuti*), I therefore designate them as belonging to the three vehicles.

If they can eliminate all habitual tendencies toward faults and realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), at that time they will be free from the intoxication of samādhi. Having attained awakening within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), they cultivate various merits within the supramundane, supreme, and untainted realm, universally bringing them to fulfillment and attaining the inconceivable, sovereign Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The vehicle of the devas and the vehicle of Brahmā, The vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
And the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas— These are the vehicles taught by me."
As long as there is the arising of mind, the various vehicles have not reached their ultimate end;
once that mind has been transformed and extinguished, there are neither vehicles nor those who ride them.
Since no establishment of vehicles exists, I teach what is called the One Vehicle.
To guide the ignorant, the distinctions between the various vehicles are taught.
There are three kinds of liberation: namely, liberation through the abandonment of all afflictions, liberation through the selflessness of phenomena, and liberation through the wisdom of equality.
Just as wood in the ocean Is constantly tossed by the waves;
So too is the mind of the śrāvaka, Driven and buffeted by the winds of signs.
Though they have extinguished the arising of afflictions, They remain bound by habitual tendencies.
Intoxicated by the wine of samādhi, they dwell in the realm of outflows.
This is not the ultimate destination, yet they do not regress;
having attained the body of samādhi, they remain unawakened for as long as an eon.
Just as a person who is intoxicated awakens only after the wine has worn off;
so it is with the Śrāvakas—they shall attain Buddhahood once they have awakened.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Three.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra of the Mahāyāna, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Zhou Dynasty, by Imperial Command.
Chapter Three: On Impermanence (4–5), Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"I shall now explain for you the various characteristics of the mind-made body."
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
Mahāmati said, "Yes. The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati, there are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three?
That is to say:

the mind-made body produced from the bliss of entering samādhi, the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas, and the mind-made body that arises spontaneously with its kind through effortless practice;
these are realized progressively by practitioners who have entered the first stage.
Mahāmati! What is the body produced by mind that enters the bliss of samādhi?

It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages, wherein one enters samādhi, becomes detached from various mental states, and remains tranquil and unmoving; the ocean of the mind no longer gives rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses, and one realizes that objects are merely manifestations of the mind and are ultimately non-existent. This is called the body produced by mind that enters the bliss of samādhi.
What is the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena? It refers to the realization in the eighth stage that all phenomena are like illusions and are devoid of characteristics;

having transformed the basis of the mind, one dwells in the illusion-like samādhi and other meditative absorptions, able to manifest immeasurable sovereign supernormal powers as swiftly as a flower blooming and according to one's will. Like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, or a reflection, it is not composed of the four great elements yet resembles what is so composed. It is fully adorned with all forms and universally enters Buddha-fields, thoroughly comprehending the nature of all phenomena; this is called the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena.
What is the body made of mind that is spontaneously born of its own kind and characterized by non-conditioned activity?

It refers to the thorough realization of the characteristics of the dharmas realized by all Buddhas for themselves; this is called the body made of mind that is spontaneously born of its own kind and characterized by non-conditioned activity.
"Mahāmati!
You should diligently observe the characteristics of the three bodies.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"My Great Vehicle is no vehicle; it is neither sound nor syllable.
It is not the truths, nor is it liberation, nor is it the ultimate signlessness.
Yet, by means of the Mahāyāna, one attains mastery over samādhi."
"The various mind-made bodies are adorned with the flowers of mastery.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Blessed One has spoken of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), what are these five?
If a person commits them, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said, "Yes.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The five acts of immediate retribution are:
killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a mind of malice and rebellion, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha."
Mahāmati! What is the mother of sentient beings?
It is that which draws forth craving together with greed and delight, nourishing them just as a mother nurtures her child.
What constitutes the father?
It is ignorance, for it causes one to be born within the village of the six sense bases.
To sever these two roots is called killing one's father and mother.
What is meant by "killing an arhat"?
It refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) acting as an enemy like the onset of rat-poison; because one has ultimately severed them, it is called "killing an arhat."
What is the schism of the Saṃgha?
It refers to the ultimate severance of the harmony and accumulation of the various aggregates (skandhas) which possess distinct characteristics; this is called the schism of the Saṃgha.
What is the shedding of the Buddha’s blood with an evil mind?

This refers to the eight consciousnesses giving rise to false thoughts and perceptions, whereby one perceives self-characteristics and common characteristics as existing outside of one's own mind. To use the three liberations and untainted (anāsrava) evil minds to ultimately sever those Buddhas of the eight consciousnesses is called "shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind."
“Mahāmati!
These are the five internal immediate [transgressions]. If there is one who commits them, they immediately attain the realization of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!”
I shall now explain for you the five external acts of immediate retribution, so that you and other bodhisattvas, having heard this teaching, will not give rise to doubt or confusion in future ages.
What are the five external acts of immediate retribution?

This refers to what is taught in other teachings regarding the "immediate" (ānantarya) offenses: if there were a person who committed such an act and was unable to realize the three doors of liberation, with the sole exception of the Tathāgatas, great Bodhisattvas, and great Śrāvakas—who, seeing someone commit an immediate offense, manifest the same act through their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) in order to inspire them to reform—such individuals subsequently repent and eliminate [the karma] to realize liberation; these are all manifested transformations and not actual commissions. If one has actually committed an immediate offense, one will never attain liberation in that present life, except for those who have awakened to the fact that the body, possessions, and dwelling place are manifestations of one's own mind, thereby being free from the conceptualizing and grasping views of "I" and "mine";
or else they will encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in a future birth in another realm, leave behind the faults of conceptualization, and only then realize liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Craving is called the mother, Ignorance is the father;
Consciousness that cognizes objects— This is what is called the Buddha.”
“The latent tendencies are the Arhats; the collection of aggregates is the Saṃgha.
To sever these without remainder or interval—this is called an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain for me the essential nature of all Buddhas.
The Buddha said:

“Mahāmati! To realize the two kinds of selflessness, to eliminate the two kinds of hindrances, to transcend the two kinds of death, and to sever the two kinds of afflictions— this is the essential nature of a Buddha,
Mahāmati!”
“Once Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have realized this Dharma, they too are called Buddhas; it is for this reason that I teach only the One Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, Eliminating the two obstacles and the two afflictions,”
"And inconceivable death—for this reason he is called the Tathāgata.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
With what underlying intention did the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, proclaim these words:
"I am all the Buddhas of the past," and further recount the hundreds of thousands of accounts of his previous births?
"At that time, I was King Mūrdhaja, the Great Elephant, the Parrot, Candraprabha, Sunetra,
and others such as these. The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, based upon the fourfold secret intention of equality, spoke these words in the midst of the great assembly:
"In former times, I was Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha."
"What are the four? They are:
the equality of letters, the equality of speech, the equality of body, and the equality of dharmas."
What is the equality of syllables?
It means that I am called "Buddha," and all Tathāgatas are also called "Buddha"; since the name "Buddha" is without distinction, this is called the equality of syllables.
What is the equality of speech?

It means that I produce sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds in my speech, and all Tathāgatas likewise produce this speech; the nature of the Brahma-sound of the kalaviṅka bird is neither increased nor decreased, and there is no distinction between them—this is called the equality of speech.
What is the equality of the body?

It means that my dharma-body, its physical marks, and its secondary characteristics are no different from those of all Buddhas, except for manifesting bodies according to the various classes of beings in order to subdue them; this is called the equality of the body.
What is the equality of phenomena?
It means that I and all Buddhas have equally realized the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; this is called the equality of phenomena.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, makes such a declaration in the midst of the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and I—
Because of the fourfold equality, I speak for the sake of all sons of the Buddha.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said:”

"From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, not a single word have I spoken in the interval; nor have I spoken, nor shall I speak. What has not been spoken is what the Buddha has spoken."
“World-Honored One, based on what underlying intention did you speak these words?
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!”
It is based on the two secret dharmas that such a statement is made.
What are these two dharmas?
They are as follows:
There are the dharmas realized by oneself (*pratyātma-dharma*) and the dharmas abiding from the beginning (*pūrvasthita-dharma*). What are the dharmas realized by oneself?

It means that what all Buddhas have realized, I too realize in the same way—neither increasing nor decreasing. It is the domain of realized wisdom, free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of conceptual discrimination, and free from the characteristics of names and words.
What is the primordially abiding dharma (*pūrvasthita-dharma*)?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of dharmas, such as gold existing within ore; whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, dharmas abide in their own station, and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are eternally and universally constant.
Mahāmati!
It is like a person traveling through a wilderness who sees an old, level road leading toward an ancient city; he immediately follows it, enters, and there rests and enjoys himself.
Mahāmati, what do you think?
Did he create that path and the various things within the city?
He replied, "No. The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! The *tathatā* realized by myself and all Buddhas, as well as the eternally abiding *dharmatā*, are likewise so.

Therefore it is said that from the moment of attaining Buddhahood until entering *nirvāṇa*, not a single word has been spoken in the interval; nor has anything been spoken in the past, nor shall anything be spoken.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"On the night I attained perfect enlightenment, And on the night I entered parinirvāṇa—
Between these two moments, I have said nothing at all."
"Because I have personally realized the primordially abiding Dharma, I have thus spoken these cryptic words:
'Between myself and all Tathāgatas, there is not the slightest difference.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas,
so that I and all other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may leave behind these characteristics and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said, “Yes,
Blessed One.
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! The sentient beings of the world mostly fall into two views, namely:
the view of existence and the view of non-existence;”
Because they fall into two views, they do not perceive that which has emerged as having emerged.
What is the view of existence?

It is the notion that phenomena arise from causes and conditions that are truly existent and not non-existent; that truly existent phenomena arise from causes and conditions and do not arise from non-existence.
Mahāmati!
One who speaks in this manner is speaking of causelessness.
What is meant by the view of non-existence?
That is to say, having known that greed, hatred, and delusion are within sensation, one falsely calculates and says they do not exist. Mahāmati!

Furthermore, there are those who, while discriminating the marks of existence, do not accept the existence of dharmas; and there are those who know that the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas have no nature of greed, hatred, or delusion, yet calculate them to be non-existent. Among these, who is the destroyer?
Mahāmati said:
"Those who first hold to the existence of the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, and subsequently grasp at their non-existence, are called nihilists.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! You have understood my question.
This person is not merely a destroyer for being devoid of greed, hatred, and delusion; he is also a destroyer of the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas."
Why is this? Because afflictions cannot be apprehended either internally or externally;
their essential nature is neither different nor not different.
Mahāmati!

The nature of greed, hatred, and delusion—whether internal or external—is unfindable, because they lack intrinsic nature and cannot be grasped. Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas are by their very nature liberated, for there is neither that which binds nor any cause of bondage.

Mahāmati! If there were that which binds and a cause for binding, then there would be that which is bound; to speak in such a manner is called a nihilist, and this is the characteristic of non-existence.

It was with this underlying meaning and intention that I spoke: "It would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness while harboring overweening pride.

One who gives rise to such a view is called a destroyer; they fall into the midst of attachment to views—whether personal or shared—and fail to understand that all phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind."

Because of this lack of understanding, they perceive external phenomena as being momentarily impermanent and subject to successive differentiation; they perceive the characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as flowing in a continuous stream, arising and then ceasing; they engage in false discrimination regarding that which is beyond the marks of words, and they conceive of it as both arising and perishing.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Existence and non-existence are two extremes;
even that which is the range of the mind— by purifying those ranges of activity, the mind becomes equanimous and stilled."
One does not grasp at sense objects, nor is there extinction into nothingness;
there exists the wondrous reality of *tathatā*, as practiced by the noble ones.
Originally non-existent yet arising, having arisen, it then ceases.
Existence and non-existence arise through causes and conditions; those do not abide within my Dharma.
They belong neither to outsiders nor to the Buddha, neither to me nor to any other assembly.
Since existence is established through conditions, how could non-existence be attained?
Who could say that what exists by way of conditions is also non-existent?
To speak of "arising" is a false view; through deluded conceptualization, one calculates existence and non-existence.
If one knows that there is nothing produced, there is likewise nothing extinguished.
"Observe that all worlds are entirely empty and quiescent; they are free from both existence and non-existence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I only pray that you will explain the characteristics of its fundamental tenets,
so that I and all other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may thoroughly understand this meaning, not follow any of the various false and deluded interpretations, and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said, “Yes,
Blessed One.
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! All those of the two vehicles and all bodhisattvas have two kinds of doctrinal characteristics. What are these two?
That is to say:
the dharma-characteristic of the ultimate goal (*abhiprāya*) and the dharma-characteristic of verbal expression.

As for the dharma-characteristic of the ultimate goal, it refers to the distinguished characteristic of one's own realization, which is free from the conceptualization of letters and language; it enters the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), accomplishes the practice of its own stage, transcends all improper thoughts and perceptions, subdues Māras and non-Buddhists, and gives rise to the light of wisdom—this is called the dharma-characteristic of the ultimate goal.

Regarding the "characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma," this refers to the exposition of the various teachings of the ninefold canon, which are free from characteristics such as identity and difference, or existence and non-existence. By means of skillful expedients, one causes sentient beings to enter this Dharma according to their mental dispositions; this is called the "characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma."
"You and all the bodhisattvas should diligently practice and study.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The ultimate meaning and verbal expression, Self-realization and the teaching of the Dharma,"
If one can skillfully know and see, one will not follow the deluded interpretations of others.
That which is discriminated by the foolish is not the true characteristic;
how could they not seek liberation? Yet there is no dharma that can be attained.
Observing all conditioned phenomena, which continue in a succession of arising and ceasing;
they increase the two views, being inverted and devoid of true knowledge.
Nirvāṇa is free from mind and intellect; this alone is the one true reality.
Observing that all things in the world are entirely illusory, Like a phantom, a dream, or a plantain tree;
Therein is no greed, hatred, or delusion, Nor is there any person at all;
The aggregates arise from craving, Just like what is seen in a dream.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of false discrimination."
How does this false discrimination arise?
From what does it arise?
By what cause does it arise?
"By whom is it produced?
For what reason is it called 'false conceptualization'?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati!
Out of compassion for the world of devas and humans, you have asked about this meaning; it will bring great benefit and great peace and happiness.
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said:
"Yes," replied Mahāmati. The Buddha said: "Mahāmati!"

All sentient beings, regarding various objects, are unable to comprehend that these are manifestations of their own minds; they falsely cling to the duality of grasper and grasped, giving rise to various discriminations and falling into views of existence and non-existence. They increase the habitual tendencies of the false views of externalists, and when the mind and mental factors arise in conjunction, they cling to the notion that external objects exist as something to be apprehended in their various forms. They then become attached to a self and what belongs to a self; for this reason, it is called "false discrimination."
Mahāmati said:
"If it is so, then the various external objects are devoid of the nature of existence and non-existence, yet they give rise to the characteristics of all views.
World-Honored One!"
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is likewise so: it is free from the measures of the sense faculties, as well as propositions, reasons, and examples.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak of the arising of conceptual discrimination regarding various meanings, yet not say that such arises within the ultimate truth?
"Could it be that what the World-Honored One has said contradicts reason, since in one instance you speak of 'arising' while in another you do not?

World-Honored One, you have also said that false discrimination falls into the views of existence and non-existence; for example, just as illusory phenomena are manifold yet unreal, so too is discrimination, being devoid of the characteristics of both existence and non-existence. How then can you say that it falls into these two views?"
"Does this teaching not fall into worldly views?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
Discrimination does not arise nor does it cease.

Why is this? Because it does not give rise to the marks of discrimination regarding existence or non-existence; because all external phenomena that are perceived are non-existent; and because one realizes that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind. It is only because foolish people discriminate among the various phenomena of their own minds and become attached to various marks that they speak in such a manner.

To cause them to know that all that is seen is nothing but one’s own mind, to sever all views and attachments regarding "self" and "what belongs to self," to depart from the various evil causes and conditions of agent and action, and because they realize it is "mind-only," to transform their mental disposition; to clearly illuminate the various stages (*bhūmi*) and enter the realm of the Buddhas; to abandon the five dharmas, the intrinsic natures, and all views of conceptual discrimination—it is for this reason that I say: "Various objects manifested by one's own mind arise through the attachment of false discrimination; if one understands this as it truly is, one attains liberation."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“From various causes and conditions, this world arises;
Those who engage with the four propositions do not understand my Dharma.”
The world is not born from existence or non-existence, nor from both, nor from neither.
Why do the foolish discriminate regarding dependent origination?
It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent.
Observing the world in this way, the mind turns toward the realization of non-self.
All phenomena are unarisen, because they arise from conditions;
that which is produced by various conditions is a phenomenon that is not truly born.
An effect does not produce itself as an effect, for that would entail the fallacy of two effects;
since there are no two effects, no intrinsic nature can be found.
When one contemplates all conditioned phenomena, they are seen to be devoid of the subject and object of cognition.
It is determined that this is mind alone; therefore, I speak of the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*).
The nature of that measure is a state where both conditions and dharmas are abandoned;
this ultimate, wondrously pure reality—I call it the "measure of mind."
The "self" is a conventional designation, yet in reality it cannot be found;
the aggregates and the designation of "aggregates" likewise lack any substantial entity.
There are four kinds of equality: that of characteristics, causes, and those produced [therefrom].
Non-self is the fourth, which the practitioner contemplates.
Free from all views, as well as the discrimination of subject and object;
without attainment and without arising—this I call the measure of mind (cittamātra).
Neither existent nor non-existent, Free from both existence and non-existence;
The mind is likewise free from these— This, I say, is the measure of the mind (cittamātra).
Suchness, emptiness, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), Nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);
The various bodies produced by thought—I declare these to be the measure of mind (cittamātra).
Bound by the habitual tendencies of false imagination, various things arise from the mind;
that sentient beings perceive them as external—I declare this to be the measure of mind.
"What is seen externally does not exist; yet the mind manifests in various ways.
The body, its requisites, and its dwelling place—I declare these to be the measure of the mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Tathāgata has said:
‘As I have taught, you and all the bodhisattvas should not grasp the meaning based on the literal words.’”
"World-Honored One!
For what reason should one not rely on the words to grasp the meaning?
What constitutes 'words'?"
"What is meant by 'the meaning'?
The Buddha said,
"Listen attentively!"
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said, "Yes."
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!

As for ‘speech,’ it has the habitual tendencies of discrimination as its cause; depending upon the throat, tongue, lips, palate, teeth, and cheeks, it produces various sounds and characters through mutual discourse. This is what is called speech.”
What is meant by "meaning" (artha)?

It refers to when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in a solitary and quiet place, using the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation to contemplate and observe the path toward nirvāṇa—the realm of their own intrinsic gnosis—thereby transforming all habitual tendencies and practicing the various modes of conduct throughout the stages; this is called "meaning."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is skilled in words and their meaning, knowing that words and meaning are neither identical nor different; the same applies to meaning and words.
If meaning were different from words, then meaning could not be manifested by means of words; yet one perceives meaning through words, just as a lamp illuminates forms.
Mahāmati!
It is like a person holding a lamp to illuminate an object, thereby knowing that the object is such and exists in such a place;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who, by means of the lamp of language, enters the realm of self-realization that transcends verbal expression.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

If there are those who grasp at the literal meaning within the non-arising and non-ceasing, the self-nature of nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the five dharmas, the various minds, and the self-nature of phenomena, they fall into the views of superimposition and denial. Because they give rise to conceptual discrimination by treating these as something other than they are—just as one perceives a magical illusion and reckons it to be real—this is the vision of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“If one grasps at the meaning according to the words, One establishes [views] regarding all phenomena;
Because of those established views, Upon death, one falls into hell.”
Within the aggregates there is no self, nor is the non-aggregate the self;
it is not as they conceptualize, yet it is not that it does not exist.
Just as the ignorant conceptualize, [they hold that] all things possess an intrinsic nature.
If things were as they are perceived, then everyone should perceive reality.
All phenomena, whether defiled or pure, are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature;
yet they are not as they are perceived, nor are they non-existent.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

I shall now explain for you the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). If you and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly understand the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness, you will be able to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Mahāmati!
There are three kinds of knowledge:
namely, worldly knowledge, supramundane knowledge, and the supreme-superior supramundane knowledge.
What is mundane knowledge?
It refers to the conceptualization of existence and non-existence by all heterodox teachers and ordinary fools.
What is supramundane knowledge?
This refers to how all followers of the two vehicles are attached to self-characteristics and common characteristics.
What is the supreme supramundane wisdom?

It is when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate all phenomena as being entirely without characteristics—neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent—and by realizing the selflessness of phenomena, they enter the stage of the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are three kinds of knowledge:
namely, the knowledge that knows specific and general characteristics; the knowledge that knows arising and ceasing; and the knowledge that knows non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Arising and ceasing are consciousness; non-arising and non-ceasing are wisdom.

That which falls into the various characteristics of signs and signlessness, as well as existence and non-existence, and which is caused by them, is consciousness; that which is free from signs and signlessness, as well as the causes of existence and non-existence, is wisdom.
That which has the characteristic of accumulation is consciousness; that which lacks the characteristic of accumulation is wisdom.
That which clings to the characteristics of objects is consciousness; that which does not cling to the characteristics of objects is wisdom.
That which arises from the correspondence of the threefold conjunction is consciousness; that which has the characteristic of an unimpeded corresponding self-nature is wisdom.
The characteristic of attainment is consciousness; the characteristic of non-attainment is wisdom.
Realizing the sphere of activity of one’s own noble wisdom is like the moon in water, for it neither enters nor exits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Gathering karma is the mind; Examining phenomena is wisdom.
Wisdom can realize the signless, Attaining sovereign majesty and radiance."
The bondage of objective realms constitutes the mind; the arising of awakened conceptualization constitutes wisdom.
Within that which is signless and preeminent, wisdom arises.
When the mental faculty, the intellect, and consciousness are free from all conceptual discriminations, [wisdom is realized].
Attaining the non-conceptual dharma, these sons of the Buddha are not śrāvakas.
With the sublime patience of tranquility and the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom,
they are born into the excellent ultimate truth, far removed from all conditioned activities.
I possess three kinds of wisdom, which the Noble Ones can clearly illuminate;
they discern all characteristics and reveal all phenomena.
My wisdom is free from all characteristics and transcends the two vehicles.
"Because the śrāvakas and others cling to the existence of all phenomena;
the Tathāgata’s wisdom is stainless, for he thoroughly realizes that there is only mind.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
The various non-Buddhists hold nine kinds of views regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*), namely:

transformation of form, transformation of characteristics, transformation of cause, transformation of correspondence, transformation of view, transformation of birth, transformation of substance, transformation of the manifestation of conditions, and transformation of the manifestation of what is produced;
these are the nine.
Because of this view, all non-Buddhists give rise to theories of existence, non-existence, and transformation.

Among these, "transformation of form" refers to the perception of distinct differences in form; for example, when gold is fashioned into various ornaments such as rings, bracelets, and necklaces, although their shapes differ, the essence of the gold remains unchanged. The transformation of all phenomena is likewise so.
The various conceptual attachments of other non-Buddhists are neither like this nor different from it; rather, all transformations arise solely through discrimination—thus should it be understood.
For example, when milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth have matured, non-Buddhists claim that these all undergo transformation;
yet in reality, there is neither existence nor non-existence, for what is seen is one's own mind and no external objects exist.

All such things are merely the delusions of ignorant ordinary beings, arising from the habitual tendencies of their own conceptual discrimination; in reality, not a single dharma is born or extinguished. They are like the various forms seen in illusions and dreams, or like speaking of birth and death for the son of a barren woman.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Form, location, and temporal transformation, The primary elements and the sense faculties;
The intermediate state arises gradually— Such are false imaginings, not the wisdom of the enlightened.”
"The Buddhas do not discriminate between dependent origination and the world;
the world of all conditions is like a city of the Gandharvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will explain for us the profound and secret meaning of all dharmas and the characteristics of their interpretation.

May I and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly understand these teachings so as not to fall into the deep-seated attachment of grasping at the literal meaning, but rather to transcend false discrimination regarding words and language, universally enter all Buddha-lands, be sealed by the power of the superknowledges, mastery, and dhāraṇīs, and have our awakened wisdom well-established in the ten inexhaustible vows.”

Through various manifestations performed without effort, his radiance shines like the sun, moon, mani-jewels, earth, water, fire, and wind; abiding in the stages, he is free from discriminatory views.

Knowing all phenomena to be like illusions and dreams, he enters the rank of the Tathāgata to universally transform sentient beings, causing them to realize that all phenomena are false and unreal. Freeing them from the categories of existence and non-existence and severing attachment to arising and ceasing, he causes them to transcend verbal expression and transform their basis of reliance.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati! Regarding all dharmas, there are immeasurable attachments to meanings as they are expressed in words, which are profound and subtle.

These are: attachment to marks; attachment to conditions; attachment to existence and non-existence; attachment to arising and non-arising; attachment to cessation and non-cessation; attachment to vehicles and non-vehicles; attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned; attachment to the specific characteristics of each stage; attachment to the realization of one's own discrimination; attachment to the categories of existence and non-existence in the doctrines of external paths; and attachment to the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
Mahāmati!

These various secret attachments are of immeasurable kinds; they are all secret attachments arising from the self-discriminating grasping of the foolish and ignorant. These discriminations are like a silkworm making a cocoon, binding themselves and others with the threads of their own false imaginings, clinging to existence and non-existence with a firm and dense desire for pleasure.
Mahāmati!

In this regard, there is truly no characteristic of secrecy or non-secrecy, because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive all dharmas as abiding in tranquility and being free from conceptual discrimination.

If one realizes that all phenomena are seen only by the mind and that there are no external objects—all being identical in their signlessness—and accordingly observes them, then all subtle attachments to the conceptual distinctions of existence and non-existence are seen to be quiescent; therefore, there is neither the characteristic of the subtle nor the characteristic of the non-subtle.
Mahāmati! In this, there is neither bondage nor liberation; it is only those who do not understand reality who perceive bondage and liberation. Why is this so?
Because the essential nature of all phenomena— whether existent or non-existent— cannot be found when sought.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
ignorant ordinary beings have three kinds of secret bonds, namely:

Greed, hatred, delusion, and the craving for future existence, together with the delight of greed—by these subtle fetters, all sentient beings are made to continue their births within the five destinies.
If these subtle fetters are severed, then there will be neither the mark of the subtle nor the mark of the non-subtle.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
If there is attachment to the conditions of the conjunction of the three, the various consciousnesses will arise in succession, bound by secret fetters.

Because of attachment, there are secret fetters; however, if one perceives the three liberations as being free from the consciousness of the conjunction of the three, all secret fetters will utterly not arise.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Unreal and false conceptualization—this is called the subtle mark;
If one can know it according to reality, all subtle nets will be severed."
“Ordinary fools cannot comprehend this; they grasp at meaning according to the words alone.
Like a silkworm dwelling within its cocoon, they entangle themselves with their own deluded thoughts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said:
‘One discriminates all phenomena by means of various minds; these phenomena do not possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva); this is merely a false conceptualization.’”
“World-Honored One!
If one were merely to falsely conceptualize that all phenomena do not exist, would it not follow that all phenomena—both defiled and pure—are utterly destroyed?
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! So it is, so it is!
It is just as you have said.”

All ordinary, ignorant people conceptually differentiate all phenomena, yet the nature of phenomena does not exist in such a way; this is merely a false attachment to that which lacks intrinsic nature or characteristics. However, the noble ones, by means of their noble eye of wisdom, perceive and know the self-nature of phenomena as it truly is.
Mahāmati said:

"If the noble ones perceive the nature of all phenomena with the eye of noble wisdom, rather than with the divine or fleshly eyes, it is not the same as the conceptual discriminations of ordinary, ignorant people."
"How can ordinary, ignorant people be freed from conceptual discrimination?
Because they are unable to awaken to and comprehend the dharmas of the noble ones,
World-Honored One!"
That is neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why?

Because they do not perceive the dharmas perceived by the noble ones; because the vision of the noble ones is far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence; because the noble ones do not attain things through the conceptual constructions of ordinary people; and because it is not a mark within the sphere of their own activity.

They also perceive the intrinsic nature and characteristics of phenomena as manifesting according to their false attachments; because they do not speak of them as having causes or being causeless, they fall into the view of the intrinsic nature and characteristics of phenomena.
World-Honored One!
Since other realms are not like this, such a case would lead to the fault of infinite regress; who then could thoroughly understand the nature and characteristics of dharmas?
World-Honored One!
Since the nature and characteristics of all dharmas do not arise from conceptual discrimination, why do you say that all dharmas exist because of conceptual discrimination?
World-Honored One!
Since the characteristics of conceptualization differ from the characteristics of the various phenomena, and their causes are not similar, how can phenomena arise through conceptualization?
Furthermore, for what reason do ordinary, ignorant people conceptualize that things exist in such a way, when they speak thus:
"In order to cause sentient beings to abandon conceptualization, it is taught that the characteristics of phenomena as they appear through conceptualization do not exist as such phenomena"?
“World-Honored One!

For what reason do you cause all sentient beings to leave behind the dharmas clung to through views of existence and non-existence, yet again cause them to cling to the realm of noble wisdom and fall into the view of existence?”
"For what reason do you not speak of the dharma of quiescent emptiness and non-existence, but instead speak of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
It is not that I do not teach the dharma of tranquil emptiness, for one would otherwise fall into the view of existence. Why is this?
Because I have already explained the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom.

For sentient beings who, since beginningless time, have been attached to existence, I have taught the Dharma of tranquility through the discourse of the noble ones. Now that they have heard it, they do not give rise to fear; they are able to realize the Dharma of tranquil emptiness as it truly is, depart from the signs of delusion and confusion to enter the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), and know that what is perceived contains no external phenomena. They awaken to the three gates of liberation and attain the seal of reality (*yathābhūta-mudrā*), seeing the self-nature of dharmas and comprehending the realm of the noble ones, thereby remaining far removed from all attachments to existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not establish the position that all dharmas are entirely non-arising. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, and because their own tenets are characterized by the mark of arising.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the statement that "all phenomena are unarisen" is self-contradictory.
Why is this? Because that school [of thought] maintains that things arise dependently;
furthermore, because that school is itself included within all phenomena, and even the characteristic of non-arising does not arise.
Furthermore, because that school asserts that things are established through the combination of various parts;

and because in that school all existent and non-existent phenomena are unarisen, whereas in this school one enters into all phenomena precisely because both existent and non-existent marks are unarisen;
therefore, since all phenomena are unarisen, that school’s own position collapses.
It should not be established in this manner, because the various members [of the argument] entail many fallacies and because they are mutually dependent on distinct characteristics.
Just as there is no arising, so too all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature.
Mahāmati!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should declare that all phenomena are like illusions and like dreams, because they are seen and yet not seen, and because everything is a manifestation of delusive confusion—except when it would cause fear in the foolish.
“Mahāmati!
Ordinary people are ignorant and fall into the views of existence and non-existence; do not cause them to become terrified and abandon the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Without intrinsic nature and without expression, without objective entities and without a basis;
the foolish and ignorant falsely discriminate, their evil conceptions like a corpse.
All phenomena are unarisen—this is what is established by the non-Buddhists.”
Because whatever arises therein is not established by conditions, all phenomena are unarisen; the wise do not conceptualize them.
Since their own position relies on arising, that realization [of theirs] is thereby undermined.
Just as one with cataracts in the eyes Perceives illusory hair-tufts through false imagination, So too are all phenomena:
The foolish and ignorant falsely discriminate them.
The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; They possess no real, intrinsic substance.
Based on these provisional designations, one discriminates and falsely conceptualizes.
These various signs of phenomena, established by mere names, agitate the mind and consciousness;
yet the sons of the Buddha completely transcend them, wandering in non-discrimination.
The perception of water where there is no water arises from craving;
ordinary fools see things in this way, but the noble ones do not.
The noble ones see purity, which gives rise to the three gates of liberation.
Far removed from arising and ceasing, one constantly dwells in the realm of signlessness.
By practicing in the realm of signlessness, there is likewise neither existence nor non-existence;
since existence and non-existence are entirely equal, one thereby gives birth to the fruit of sainthood.
What is the existence or non-existence of phenomena?
How are they established as equal?
If the mind does not comprehend phenomena, then both the internal and external will be agitated and disturbed.
"Once [this] is realized, there is equality, and at that time, the signs of disorder are extinguished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

As the Buddha has taught: if one knows that objects are merely provisional designations and are ultimately unapprehendable, then there is nothing to be grasped. Because there is nothing to be grasped, there is also no grasper. Since both the grasper and the grasped are absent, conceptual discrimination does not arise; this is what is called wisdom.
World-Honored One!

For what reason does that wisdom not apprehend its object? Is it said that it does not apprehend because it is unable to comprehend the meaning of the self-characteristics and common characteristics, as well as their identity and difference, regarding all phenomena?

Is it because they are mutually obscured by the various differences between the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena that they cannot be perceived?
Or is it because they are covered and separated by mountains, crags, stone walls, curtains, and canopies that they cannot be perceived?
Is it because they are extremely distant or extremely near, or because they are old, young, blind, or have impaired faculties that one does not perceive?

If you say one does not perceive because one does not understand the meaning of the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as well as their identity and difference regarding all phenomena, this is not called wisdom; it must be non-wisdom, for there is an object present yet it is not known.

If one fails to apprehend because the various self-characteristics and common characteristics of all phenomena mutually obscure one another, this too is not wisdom; for it is called wisdom because of knowing the object, not because of not knowing it.

If one does not know because of being obstructed by mountains, rocks, walls, curtains, or screens, or because of being extremely distant or extremely near, or because of being old, young, blind, or ignorant, that too is not wisdom; for it is due to the presence of objects and the incompleteness of wisdom that one does not know.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! This is indeed wisdom; it is not as you have described. What I have taught is not a teaching given with concealment."

When I say that objects of perception are merely provisional names and are unattainable, it is because one realizes they are but what is seen by one's own mind; as for the existence or non-existence of external phenomena, wisdom finds nothing at all therein. Because nothing is attained, cognitive objects (*jñeya*) do not arise, and upon entering the three gates of liberation, even the essence of wisdom is forgotten.

This is not like ordinary people of discursive thought who, due to the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation since beginningless time, cling to various forms and characteristics of external phenomena—whether as existing or non-existing. To know in such a way is called "not knowing," for they fail to realize that all phenomena are but what is seen by the mind alone; they are attached to the self and what belongs to the self, discriminating between object and wisdom, and do not know whether external phenomena exist or not, because their minds abide in the view of nihilism.
"In order to cause them to abandon such conceptual discrimination, it is taught that all phenomena are established as being mind-only.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"If there is an object of perception, And wisdom does not perceive it; [then it is mind-only]."
That which is neither wisdom nor non-wisdom is called the one who engages in false conceptualization.
Boundless mutual concealment, obstruction, and distance—
when wisdom cannot perceive these, it is called distorted wisdom.
"The faculties of the old and the young are dull, yet there truly exists an objective realm;
that they cannot give rise to wisdom is what is called false wisdom.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"

Foolish ordinary beings, deluded by the false discriminations of beginningless hypocrisy and evil views, do not understand reality as it is nor the teachings expressed through words. They conceive of external signs apart from the mind and cling to expedient teachings, unable to cultivate the pure, true Dharma that transcends the four propositions.
Mahāmati said: “So it is, so it is!
It is truly as Your Reverence has taught.”

I pray that you will expound for me the Dharma of suchness and the Dharma of verbal expression, so that I and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may attain skillfulness in these two types of Dharma, which is inaccessible to non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati!
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharmas, namely:
the dharma of verbal expression and the dharma of suchness.
The "teaching of the Dharma" refers to the various skillful means taught in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.

The "Dharma as it truly is" refers to that which practitioners perceive within their own minds as free from all conceptual discrimination; it does not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither. It transcends the entire domain of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), and is the sphere of activity for the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). It is free from the characteristics of causal conditions and the duality of subject and object (*nimitta*), and cannot be known by any heterodox teachers, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas* who have fallen into the two extremes; this is called the Dharma as it truly is.
"You and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should skillfully train yourselves in these two kinds of dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"I have taught two kinds of dharmas: The verbal instruction and the reality as it is; Thus, the Tathāgata has spoken of two kinds of dharmas: The dharma of words and the dharma of suchness."
"The teaching is shown for the sake of ordinary beings, while in reality it is for the practitioner.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

At one time, the Tathāgata taught the spells, incantations, and treatises of the Lokāyata; these can only secure worldly wealth and profit, but cannot secure the benefit of the Dharma. Since they do not secure the benefit of the Dharma, one should not associate with, serve, or make offerings to them.
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak thus?
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!”

The doctrines and treatises of the Lokāyata merely adorn words and phrases to deceive the ignorant and foolish; they conform to worldly, false speech, do not accord with reality, nor are they consistent with principle. They cannot lead one to enter the realm of ultimate truth, nor can they bring about the awakening to all phenomena. They cause one to perpetually fall into the two extremes, thereby losing the right path oneself, and likewise cause others to lose it, so that they wander through the various realms of saṃsāra without ever attaining liberation.
Why is this? Because they do not understand that all phenomena are seen only as the mind’s own projections, and because they cling to external objects, their conceptual discrimination increases.

Therefore, I say that the sentences, causes, and examples used to adorn worldly treatises merely deceive the foolish; they cannot bring liberation from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, grief, and so forth.
“Mahāmati!
Śakra Devendra has extensively mastered various treatises and composed many of his own.
A disciple of that worldly philosopher (Lokāyatika) manifested the body of a nāga, went to the palace of Śakra, and established a philosophical tenet, making this essential statement:”
