"Kauśika! Let us debate together;
if you are not as capable as I, I shall shatter your thousand-spoked wheel;
if I am not as capable as you, I shall cut off each of my own heads to atone for my defeat."
Having spoken these words, he immediately subdued Śakra by means of the methods of debate and destroyed his thousand-spoked wheel, returning once more to the human realm.

Mahāmati! Worldly discourse is adorned with causes and similes, even to the point of manifesting the form of a nāga; through its exquisite phrasing, it deludes the devas and asuras, causing them to cling to views such as arising and ceasing—how much more so for humans?
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should not associate with,
serve, or make offerings to them, because they can act as a cause for the arising of suffering. Mahāmati!
The worldly treatises speak only of the body and the objects of sensory perception. Mahāmati!

Those worldly treatises consist of hundreds of thousands of words and phrases; in the future degenerate age, those with evil views will become estranged, and the heterodox assemblies will collapse and disperse, splitting into many sects, each clinging to its own cause.
Mahāmati!

No other non-Buddhist teachers are able to establish a true teaching; only the Lokāyata, with its hundreds of thousands of phrases, extensively expounds immeasurable varieties of causal characteristics that do not accord with reality, yet they themselves do not realize that this is a delusive worldly doctrine.
At that time, Mahāmati said to the World-Honored One:
“World-Honored One,

if the treatises composed by the Lokāyatas— which are adorned with various words, causes, and examples, yet cling to their own tenets rather than the Dharma as it truly is— are called ‘non-Buddhists’ (tīrthika), [then what of these?].”

The World-Honored One also speaks of worldly matters, meaning that he extensively explains, through various phrases and expressions, how the multitudes of devas and humans from all lands throughout the ten directions have gathered together; this is not a dharma realized by his own wisdom.
“Does the World-Honored One also teach the same as the non-Buddhists?
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!”
I do not speak according to worldly conventions, nor is there coming or going; I teach that all dharmas neither come nor go.
Mahāmati! That which comes is accumulation and birth; that which goes is destruction and cessation. Neither coming nor going—this is what is called non-arising and non-ceasing.
Mahāmati!
What I have taught is not like that of the non-Buddhists who fall into conceptual discrimination. Why is this?

Because one is without attachment to the existence or non-existence of external phenomena, one realizes that there is only one's own mind and does not perceive the duality of grasper and grasped; by not engaging with objective characteristics and not giving rise to discrimination, one enters the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, thereby attaining liberation.
“Mahāmati!
I recall that once, while I was dwelling in a certain place, a world-theorizing brāhmaṇa came to me and suddenly asked me:
‘Gautama!’”
"Is everything that which is created?
To this, I replied: "Brahmin!"
"Everything is created; this is the first worldly doctrine. He then asked me:
"Is everything uncreated?"
I then replied:
"That 'everything is uncreated' is the second worldly doctrine.
He asked again:
"Is everything eternal?
Is everything impermanent?
Does everything arise?"
"Are all things non-arisen?
I replied at that time:
"This is the sixth worldly doctrine."
He asked again:
"Are all things one?
Or are all things different?"
Are all things simultaneous?
Are all things not simultaneous?
Do all things arise through various causes and conditions?
I then replied: "This is the eleventh worldly doctrine. He asked again:
"Are all things determinate?
Are all things indeterminate?
Does a self exist?"
Is there no self?
Does this world exist?
Does this world not exist?
Is there a future world?
Is there no future world?
Is there liberation?
Is there no liberation?
Is it momentary?
Or is it non-momentary?
Are space, nirvāṇa, and non-analytical cessation conditioned phenomena?
Are they unconditioned phenomena?
Do they exist or not exist?
"Is there no intermediate state? I then replied to him: "Brahmin!"
All such views as these belong to your worldly philosophy; they are not what I have taught. O Brahmin!

I teach that the three realms of existence arise from beginningless conceptual proliferation and the habitual tendencies of evil. Failing to realize that these are merely what is seen by one's own mind, one grasps at external phenomena, though in reality nothing can be apprehended.
As the non-Buddhists claim, consciousness arises from the conjunction of the three—self, sense faculties, and objects;

I do not hold such a view. I do not say there is a cause, nor do I say there is no cause; rather, I speak of dependent origination as the deluded mind appearing as the grasping subject and the grasped object. This is beyond the comprehension of you and others who are attached to a self.

"Mahāmati! Space, nirvāṇa, and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) possess only the number three and have no intrinsic nature (svabhāva); how much less can one speak of their being created or uncreated?"
“Mahāmati! At that time, the Lokāyatika Brahmin again asked me:
‘Is it because of ignorance, craving, and karma as causes and conditions that the three realms of existence arise?’”
"Is it without cause?
I replied: "These two views are also worldly theories."
He further asked me:
"Do all dharmas enter into both their own-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and common-characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)? I then replied:
"This too is worldly discourse, O Brahmin!
Even the slightest movement of consciousness that discriminates external objects is all worldly discourse."
"Mahāmati! At that time, that brahmin again asked me:
'Is there anything that is not worldly discourse (lokāyata)?"'"
"All the discourses and treatises of all non-Buddhists, adorned with various phrases, causes, and analogies, do not fail to emerge from within my own Dharma. I replied, "There are."

"It is not that which you accept, nor is it that which the world does not accept; it is not that various phrases and sentences are not spoken in accordance with their meaning and principle, nor is it that they are not so accordant.
He asked again: "Is there anything that is accepted by the world yet is not the worldly discourse?"
I replied: "There is.
However, it cannot be known by you or by any of the non-Buddhists."
Why is this? It is because one gives rise to attachment through false conceptualization regarding external phenomena.

If one can thoroughly understand that all phenomena, such as existence and non-existence, are entirely what is seen by one's own mind, then one will not give rise to conceptualization nor grasp at external objects, but will abide in one's own state.
To abide in one's own state is the meaning of non-arising. From what does it not arise?
It does not arise from conceptual discrimination. This is my dharma; it is not yours.

"Brahmin! To speak briefly, wherever the mind and consciousness go, come, die, or are born, seeking and clinging—whether through feeling, seeing, contact, or abiding; wherever they grasp at various signs and continue in conjunction with them, giving rise to attachment toward craving and its causes—all such views belong to your worldly doctrines and are not my Dharma."
“Mahāmati! When the world-discussing Brahmin asked such questions, I answered him in this way. He did not inquire about the true Dharma of my own school, but departed in silence, thinking to himself:

‘The śramaṇa Gautama has nothing worthy of respect; he teaches that all dharmas are unarisen, signless, causeless, and conditionless, being merely what is seen through the discrimination of one’s own mind. If one can thoroughly understand this, such discrimination will not arise.’”
"Mahāmati! You now likewise ask me about this same matter: for what reason do those who associate with worldly scholars obtain only material gain and not the gain of the Dharma?"
Mahāmati said: "What is the meaning of what you have called 'wealth' and 'Dharma'?
The Buddha replied:
“Excellent! You are indeed able to contemplate this meaning for the sake of future sentient beings.
Listen attentively!”
Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you, Mahāmati.

That which is called "wealth" (dhana) is tangible, graspable, receivable, and flavorful; it causes one to become attached to external objects and fall into the two extremes, increasing craving and leading to birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. I and all the Buddhas call this "profitable wealth," which is obtained by those who frequent worldly treatises.
What is the benefit of the Dharma?

It means realizing that all phenomena are mind, seeing the two kinds of selflessness, not grasping at signs, and being free from conceptual discrimination. It means skillfully knowing the various stages (*bhūmi*) as being apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness; receiving the collective empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of all Buddhas; fully undertaking and practicing the ten inexhaustible vows; and attaining complete mastery over all phenomena. This is called the benefit of the Dharma;
by means of this, one does not fall into the conceptual proliferation of views or the dual extremes of eternalism and nihilism.
Mahāmati! The worldly discourses of the non-Buddhists cause ignorant people to fall into the two extremes, namely, eternalism and nihilism.
By accepting the doctrine of no-cause, they give rise to the view of eternalism; because they perceive the destruction of causes, they produce the view of nihilism.

I say that one who does not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing is said to have attained the benefit of the Dharma; this is called the distinguishing characteristic between material wealth and the Dharma.
You and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently investigate this.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Taming and gathering sentient beings, Subduing all evils through the precepts;
Wisdom extinguishes all views, And liberation attains increase.”
The false teachings of the non-Buddhists are all merely worldly discourses;
their arbitrary conceptualizations of agent and action cannot establish themselves.
Only my own unique school is free from attachment to subject and object.
For the sake of all disciples, I teach so that they may leave behind worldly discourse.
The phenomena of the grasper and the grasped are but mind; nothing exists apart from it.
Both modes appear as manifestations of the mind; neither permanence nor annihilation can be found.
As long as the mind continues to fluctuate, this is merely worldly discourse;
for one who does not give rise to such conceptual discrimination, that person perceives their own mind.
When things come, they appear to arise; when they go, those things do not manifest.
Clearly understanding coming and going, one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination.
Permanence and impermanence, the conditioned and the unconditioned,
this world and the next world, and so forth— all these are the doctrines of worldly treatises.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the Buddha speaks of *nirvāṇa*, what dharma does he designate as *nirvāṇa*?”
"Yet the various non-Buddhists engage in manifold conceptual discriminations.
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
The various external paths conceptualize nirvana in ways that do not accord with the true nature of nirvana.
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you, Mahāmati.

There are certain non-Buddhists who say that by seeing the impermanence of phenomena, they no longer crave sense objects; the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) cease, and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not manifest before them. They do not dwell upon objects of the past, present, or future, and like the extinguishing of a lamp, the rotting of a seed, or the going out of a fire, their various graspings do not arise and discrimination does not occur; thus, they give rise to the notion of *nirvāṇa*.
“Mahāmati!
It is not by the destruction of views that one calls it nirvāṇa;
nor is it called attaining nirvāṇa upon reaching a certain place, where the perception of objective realms ceases like the stilling of the wind.”
Some claim that not perceiving the grasper and the grasped is called *nirvāṇa*;
others claim that not giving rise to the conceptualization of permanence and impermanence is called attaining *nirvāṇa*.

Still others say that the conceptualization of various marks gives rise to suffering, yet they fail to realize that these are manifestations of their own minds; because they do not know this, they fear marks and seek the markless, developing a deep fondness for it and clinging to it as *nirvāṇa*.

Some claim that by perceiving the intrinsic and common characteristics of all internal and external phenomena as having an indestructible nature throughout the past, future, and present, they conceive of this as nirvana.
Others reckon that the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, and all phenomena are subject to neither destruction nor cessation, and thus conceive of this as nirvana.

Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists lacking wisdom who reckon that there is a primal nature (*svabhāva*), and that through the transformation of the *puruṣa* and the *guṇas*, all things are produced; they take this to be nirvana.

Some non-Buddhists reckon that the exhaustion of merit and demerit constitutes [nirvana]; some reckon that the exhaustion of all afflictions occurs not through wisdom; some reckon that Īśvara is the true creator and consider this to be nirvana;

some claim that sentient beings arise from one another in succession, taking this as the sole cause with no other cause, and because they lack wisdom, they fail to realize it, and due to this lack of realization, they cling to it as nirvana;
or some reckon that the realization of the path of the truths through false discrimination constitutes nirvana.
Or they calculate that *guṇas* and the possessor of *guṇas* are in union, whether as identical, distinct, both, or neither, and cling to this as *nirvāṇa*;

or they calculate that all things arise spontaneously—that the patterns on a peacock’s feathers, the sharpness of a thorn, and the various jewels produced from jewel-mines—by whom could such things have been made?
They immediately grasp at spontaneity (*svabhāva*) as *nirvāṇa*;
or they claim that by being able to understand the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*), one attains *nirvāṇa*;
or some say that by being able to receive the six parts and protect sentient beings, one attains *nirvāṇa*.
Some say that time gives rise to the world and time itself is nirvāṇa;
some cling to the existence of a thing as being nirvāṇa;
others reckon the non-existence of a thing as being nirvāṇa.
Some conceive of nirvana as being either the existence of things or the non-existence of things;
others conceive that all things are no different from nirvana, and thus form the notion of nirvana [regarding those things]. Mahāmati!

Furthermore, there is another teaching that differs from what is propounded by those non-Buddhists: it is the Great Lion’s Roar of the Omniscient One, which enables one to thoroughly comprehend that all is a manifestation of mind-only and not to grasp at external objects. It involves remaining far removed from the four extremes and abiding in the vision of reality as it is; it does not fall into the two extremes and is free from the grasped and the grasper. It does not enter into the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor cling to [the notion of] ultimate reality. Abiding in the Dharma realized through noble wisdom, one awakens to the two kinds of selflessness, abandons the two afflictions, purifies the two types of obstructions, and proceeds through the successive stages (*bhūmi*) until entering the Buddha-stage. Attaining great samādhis such as the "illusion-like," one forever transcends the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); this is called attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Mahāmati!

Those various non-Buddhists engage in false conceptualizations that do not accord with reason; they are rejected by the wise, for they all fall into the two extremes while imagining them to be nirvana.

In this, there is neither abiding nor emerging; those various non-Buddhists all give rise to false cognitions based on their own tenets, which contradict reason and achieve nothing, merely causing the mind and consciousness to wander and fluctuate, such that none among them attain nirvana.
"You and all other bodhisattvas should remain far removed from them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"The views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists are each distinguished by their own various conceptualizations; [they are like the tracks of birds in the sky, or like the tracks of fish in the water. The wise do not rely upon them."
That is merely deluded imagination; there is no skillful means for liberation.
Having abandoned all skillful means, one does not reach the state beyond bondage;
though one falsely conceives the idea of liberation, in reality there is no liberation.
Established by the non-Buddhists, various cognitions each grasp differently;
they all lack liberation, for they are deluded and engage in false discrimination.
All foolish non-Buddhists falsely perceive the agent and the acted-upon.
All things are established within the doctrine of non-existence; therefore, there is no liberation.
The ignorant delight in conceptual discrimination and do not give rise to true wisdom.
Verbal expression is the root of the triple world; true reality is the cause for the cessation of suffering.
Just as an image in a mirror, though appearing, is not real;
so within the mind-mirror of habitual tendencies, the ignorant perceive duality.
Failing to understand that these are but manifestations of mind alone, they give rise to dualistic discrimination.
If one knows that it is merely mind, conceptual discrimination will not arise.
Mind itself is the manifold; it is far removed from both the perceiving thought and the perceived object.
As the ignorant discriminate, things appear even as they are not seen.
The three realms of existence are merely conceptual construction; external objects do not exist at all.
Various delusive thoughts manifest, yet the ignorant and foolish fail to realize this.
The sūtras repeatedly explain that "conceptual construction" is nothing but a different name for the same thing.
If one is apart from language, its meaning cannot be apprehended.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Four;
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Zhou Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
The Remainder of Chapter Three, "On Impermanence. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will explain for us the self-awakened nature of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, so that I and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may attain skillfulness in awakening ourselves and awakening others.”
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! Regarding what you have asked, I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said:
“Yes, World-Honored One!”

Are the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the agent and the non-agent, the fruit and the cause, the characteristic and the characterized, the speaker and the spoken, the awakening and the awakened—such things as these different or not different?
The Buddha said: “Mahāmati!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither an agent nor a non-agent; neither an effect nor a cause; neither a characteristic nor that which is characterized; neither speech nor that which is spoken; neither awakening nor that which is awakened.”
Why is this? Because both [positions] entail faults, Mahāmati!
If the Tathāgata were a conditioned product, he would be impermanent; if he were impermanent, then all conditioned phenomena would be the Tathāgata, which neither I nor any of the Buddhas can accept.

If there were no nature by way of being produced through action, then the skillful means one cultivates would all be empty and useless, identical to a rabbit’s horns or the son of a barren woman, because they would not be established through the cause of action.
That which is neither cause nor effect is neither existent nor non-existent; that which is neither existent nor non-existent transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
As for these "four propositions," they are merely conventional expressions following worldly usage;
if one transcends the four propositions yet remains with mere verbal expression, it is like the son of a barren woman.

Mahāmati! The son of a barren woman exists only as a verbal expression and does not fall within the four propositions; because it does not so fall, it cannot be measured. All wise ones should understand all the meanings of the Tathāgata’s words in this same way.
Mahāmati!

As I have taught that all dharmas are without self, it is because there is no self-nature within all dharmas that they are said to be "without self"; it is not that the self-nature of all dharmas does not exist.
You should know that the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words is likewise so.
Mahāmati!

Just as a cow lacks the nature of a horse and a horse lacks the nature of a cow, yet it is not that they lack their own-nature (*svabhāva*), so too it is with all phenomena (*dharma*): they have no self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet they are neither non-existent nor existent; this is not something that can be known by ordinary, ignorant people.
Why is it not known?
Because of conceptual discrimination.
All phenomena are empty, all phenomena are unarisen, and all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; everything is likewise so.
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates (skandhas). If they were non-different, he would be impermanent, for the phenomena of the five aggregates are produced by causes.

If they were different, it would be like the two horns of an ox, which are both different and not different: they are not different because they resemble each other, yet they are different because they differ in length; just as the right horn of an ox differs from the left and the left horn differs from the right, their lengths are not the same and their color and characteristics are distinct;
nevertheless, they are also not different.
As it is with the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases, so it is with all phenomena.
"Mahāmati, the Tathāgata speaks in reliance upon liberation; the Tathāgata and liberation are neither different nor not different."
If they were different, the Tathāgata would be associated with the characteristics of form, and being associated with the characteristics of form is impermanent.
If they were not different, the practitioner’s vision would have no distinction; yet, since there is a distinction, they are not non-different.
In this way, wisdom and the object of knowledge are neither different nor not different;

because they are neither different nor not different, they are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither agent nor action, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither the awakener nor the awakened, neither the characteristic nor the characterized, neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates, neither the teaching nor the taught, neither one nor different, and neither both nor not both.

For this reason, they transcend all measures (*pramāṇa*). Because they transcend all measures, there is only verbal expression; because there is only verbal expression, there is no arising; because there is no arising, there is no cessation; and because there is no cessation, they are like space.

Mahāmati! Space is neither a creator nor a created thing; because it is neither a creator nor a created thing, it is free from objective conceptualization (*ālambana*). Being free from objective conceptualization, it transcends all phenomena of discursive proliferation (*prapañca*). That which transcends all phenomena of discursive proliferation is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the essence of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). One who is perfectly enlightened is eternally detached from the spheres of all sense faculties.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Transcending the measure of all faculties, Neither fruit nor cause;
Characteristics and the characterized— All such things are utterly abandoned."
The conditions for the aggregates and perfect awakening—neither their identity nor their difference can be perceived;
since there is no perceiver, how could conceptualization arise?
It is neither created nor uncreated, neither caused nor uncaused.
Neither aggregates nor non-aggregates, Nor distinct from other things;
There is no single dharma-essence As it is perceived through conceptual construction;
Nor is it non-existent— Such is the nature of all phenomena.
Depending on existence, non-existence is established; depending on non-existence, existence is established.
Since non-existence cannot be grasped, existence likewise should not be asserted.
Failing to understand self and non-self, one clings merely to words.
They are submerged in the two extremes, destroying themselves and destroying the world.
If one can see this Dharma, then one is free from all faults;
this is called right contemplation, and one does not disparage the Great Teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As analyzed and taught in the Buddha’s sūtras, the non-arising and non-ceasing are grasped as being none other than another name for the Tathāgata.”
"Bhagavān!
May you please explain for me that which is neither born nor extinguished—this being a non-existent dharma—how can it be said to be another name for the Tathāgata?
According to what the Bhagavān has taught, if all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, one should know that this falls into the view of existence and non-existence."
“World-Honored One!
If dharmas are unarisen, they cannot be grasped; there is not even the slightest dharma. Who, then, is the Tathāgata?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.”
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati!
I say that the Tathāgata is not a non-existent thing, nor is he a grasping at that which is neither born nor extinguished; he does not depend on conditions, nor is he without meaning.

What I call "non-arising" is a distinct name for the Tathāgata’s mind-made Dharma-body; its meaning is not understood by any of the non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage.
Mahāmati!

It is like Śakra, the earth, space, and even hands and feet; each individual thing has many names according to its various aspects, yet it does not possess multiple entities because of the multiplicity of names, nor is it without an entity.
Mahāmati! I am also like this: within this Sahā world, I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names.
Although all foolish ordinary people hear them and speak of them, they do not know that these are alternative names for the Tathāgata. As for those...
Among them, some recognized him as the Tathāgata; some recognized him as the One Without Teacher; some recognized him as the Guide; some recognized him as the Supreme Guide;
some recognized him as the Universal Guide; some recognized him as the Buddha; some recognized him as the Bull-King (Vṛṣabha); some recognized him as the Brahmā-King;
some recognized him as Viṣṇu; some recognized him as Īśvara; some recognized him as the Victorious One (Jina); some recognized him as Kā...
Vīra is one who knows the limit of reality, who knows the inexhaustible, who knows auspicious signs,
who knows that which is like the wind, who knows that which is like fire, who knows that which is like the *kubera*, who knows that which is like the moon,
who knows that which is like the sun, who knows that which is like a king, who knows that which is like a seer (*ṛṣi*), and who knows *śuka*.
One who knows Indra, who knows the Morning Star, who knows Great Power, who knows that which is like water,
who knows non-extinction, who knows non-arising, who knows the emptiness of nature,
who knows True Suchness, who knows this truth, who knows the real nature, who knows the limit of reality, and who knows the Dharma.
As for the "realms" (dhātu): it is knowing nirvāṇa, knowing the eternally abiding, knowing equality, knowing non-duality,
knowing signlessness, knowing quiescence, knowing that which possesses marks,
knowing causes and conditions, knowing the Buddha-nature, knowing the teacher, knowing liberation, and knowing the Path.
The "Path" refers to the Knower of All-Knowledge, the Knower of the Most Supreme, the Knower of the Mind-made Body, and so forth;
these and other such names, numbering three hundred thousand asaṃkhyeyas, are complete, neither more nor less.

In this and other worlds, there are those who know me to be like the moon in water—neither entering nor exiting—yet ordinary, foolish people, their minds submerged in the two extremes, cannot comprehend this. Nevertheless, they honor, serve, and make offerings to me; however, they do not skillfully understand the meaning of names and phrases. Clinging to the literal teachings, they are obscured regarding the ultimate reality, claiming that "non-arising" and "non-ceasing" mean a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), failing to recognize these as the Buddha’s various epithets—just as with Indra, Śakra, and so forth.

Because they obscure the truth by relying on faith in the literal teachings, they grasp at the meaning of all phenomena according to the words alone. Those ordinary, foolish people speak thus: "The meaning is exactly as the expression; the meaning and the expression are no different."
Why is this? Because meaning has no intrinsic substance.
This person does not understand the intrinsic nature of speech and sound, asserting that speech itself is the meaning and that there is no separate substance for meaning.
"Mahāmati!
Those people are deluded; they do not know that while speech arises and ceases, the meaning does not arise or cease.
Mahāmati!"
All verbal expressions fall within the realm of words, but their meaning does not; for meaning is free from existence and non-existence, and is without arising or essence.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall within words, because the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended, except for those things that do not fall within words.
Mahāmati!
If a person preaches the Dharma while falling into the trap of words and letters, this is false and deceptive speech. Why is that?
Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is free from words. Therefore, Mahāmati,
I have said in my sūtras that I, along with all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, do not speak a single word nor answer a single word.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are free from words; it is not that one does not analytically explain them in accordance with their meaning.
Mahāmati!

If it were not taught, the Dharma would be severed; if the Dharma were severed, there would be no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas. If these were all non-existent, who would teach and for whom?
Therefore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not cling to words but should preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.

I and all the Buddhas manifest and expound the teachings in accordance with the various differences in the afflictions, understandings, and desires of sentient beings, so that they may know all phenomena are but what is seen by their own minds and have no external objects; thereby they may abandon dualistic discrimination and transform the mind, intellect, and consciousness, rather than for the purpose of establishing a realm of the noble ones' self-realization.

“Mahāmati! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should follow the meaning and not rely on the words; for those who rely on the words fall into evil views, clinging to their own tenets and engaging in verbal discourse. They cannot skillfully comprehend the characteristics of all phenomena, nor the phrasing and sentences [of the teachings]; thus, they harm themselves and others alike, and are unable to cause the minds of others to attain realization.”

If one can skillfully know the characteristics of all phenomena and achieve complete mastery of their phrasing, terminology, and meanings, then one will be able to cause oneself to experience the bliss of signlessness and also enable others to dwell securely in the Mahāyāna.
If one can cause others to dwell securely in the Mahāyāna, one will receive the protection and acceptance of all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
if one receives the protection and acceptance of all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, one will be able to embrace all sentient beings;
if one is able to embrace all sentient beings, one will be able to embrace all the true Dharma.
If one can embrace all the true teachings, then the lineage of the Buddhas will not be severed;
if the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, then one will attain the supreme and wondrous state. Mahāmati!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born in sublime and excellent realms, desiring to cause sentient beings to dwell securely in the Mahāyāna; by means of the ten powers of mastery, they manifest various forms and appearances, preaching the true Dharma according to what is appropriate for each.
The true Dharma is without difference or distinction, neither coming nor going; all conceptual proliferations are completely stilled.
Therefore, Mahāmati, sons and daughters of good family should not cling to the meaning according to the literal expression.
Why is this? Because the true Dharma is free from words. "Mahāmati!
For example, it is like a person pointing at an object with a finger; a child looks at the finger and does not look at the object.

Foolish ordinary people are just like this: following the finger of verbal expression, they give rise to attachment, and even until the end of their lives, they are unable to discard the finger of words to grasp the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Mahāmati! It is like an infant who should eat cooked food; if someone, not understanding the skillful means of cooking it, eats it raw, they will fall into madness and confusion.

Non-arising and non-ceasing are also like this: if one does not practice them with skillful means, it is unwholesome. Therefore, one should properly cultivate skillful means and not follow mere words, just as one would not look at the tip of a finger.

Mahāmati! Ultimate reality is subtle, wondrous, and tranquil; it is the cause of nirvāṇa. Discursive speech, however, accords with false conceptualization and causes one to circulate through birth and death.
Mahāmati!

True meaning is obtained from extensive learning; "extensive learning" refers to being skilled in the meaning rather than skilled in mere verbal expression. Being skilled in the meaning means not following any of the evil views of external paths, neither following them oneself nor causing others to follow them. This is what is called "extensive learning in the meaning. Those who seek the meaning should draw near to such persons; those who are the opposite—those who cling to the literal letter—should be swiftly abandoned.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
it is not extraordinary for the Tathāgata to proclaim that there is neither arising nor ceasing.”

Why is this? All non-Buddhists also speak of a creator that is neither born nor extinguished; the World-Honored One also speaks of space, nirvāṇa, and analytical cessation as being neither born nor extinguished.

Non-Buddhists also say that the world arises from the causes and conditions of a creator; the World-Honored One also says that all worlds arise from ignorance, craving, and karma. Both are causes and conditions, differing only in name.
The causes and conditions of external objects are likewise thus; therefore, there is no difference between what the Buddha teaches and what the non-Buddhists teach.
The non-Buddhists say that the nine entities—such as atoms, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the supreme lord (*īśvara*), and the creator (*puruṣa*)—are neither born nor extinguished;
the World-Honored One also says that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, for whether they exist or do not exist, they are both unattainable.
"World-Honored One!

The great elements are indestructible because, by virtue of their own characteristics, they are neither born nor extinguished; they circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their intrinsic nature.

World-Honored One, although there may be slight variations in their differentiation, everything is nothing other than what has already been taught by the non-Buddhists. Therefore, the Buddha-dharma is identical to that of the non-Buddhists."
If there is any difference, we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us: on what basis does the Buddha say his teaching is superior?
If there is no distinction, then non-Buddhists are themselves Buddhas, because they also speak of non-arising and non-ceasing.
“The World-Honored One has always taught that there are not many Buddhas in a single world; yet according to what was just said, there would have to be. The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!
The non-arising and non-ceasing that I teach is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the non-Buddhists, nor is it their doctrine of the non-arising of impermanence.
Why is this? Because what the non-Buddhists teach is that there exists a real nature and characteristic that does not arise and does not change.
I do not fall into such categories of existence or non-existence.
The Dharma I teach is neither existent nor non-existent, transcending both arising and ceasing.
Why is it not non-existent?
Because forms are seen in various ways like illusions and dreams;
why are they not existent?
Because the self-nature of the characteristics of form is not existent, because they are seen and yet not seen, and because they are grasped and yet not grasped.
Therefore, I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent.

If one awakens to the fact that these are merely what is seen by one's own mind, and abides in suchness so that self-nature discrimination does not arise, then all worldly activities will forever cease.
Discrimination is the business of the foolish and ignorant; it is not that of the noble ones.
Mahāmati!
The discriminating mind conceptualizes unreal objects, like a city of the gandharvas or a person created by illusion.
Mahāmati!

For example, it is like a child who, seeing a city of Gandharvas or illusory merchants entering and exiting, deludedly discriminates that there are real things; what is seen by the ignorant—whether arising or non-arising, conditioned or unconditioned—is entirely like this.
As an illusory person is born and an illusory person ceases, yet that illusory person in reality neither arises nor ceases, so too are all phenomena; they are free from arising and ceasing.
Mahāmati!
Ordinary beings give rise to views of arising and ceasing through delusion, whereas the noble ones do not.

To speak of "delusion" means to give rise to inverted views contrary to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Those with inverted views cling to the notion that phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and fail to perceive their quiescence. Because they do not perceive this quiescence, they are unable to distance themselves from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness is superior, not the vision of signs.
Signs are the cause of birth; if there are no signs, there is no conceptual differentiation. That which is neither born nor extinguished is nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!

What is called nirvāṇa is the relinquishing of the mind and mental factors through seeing the state of reality as it is; it is the attainment of the Tathāgata’s internally realized noble wisdom. This, I say, is the quiescent nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"To eliminate attachment to existence, I establish the meaning of non-arising;
The doctrine of causelessness that I teach Is not something the ignorant can comprehend."
All phenomena are unborn, yet they are not non-existent;
like a city of the gandharvas, a phantom, or a dream, they exist though they lack a cause.
They are empty, unborn, and without intrinsic nature—how can you explain this to me?
Apart from the conditions of combination, wisdom cannot perceive them.
For this reason, I teach that they are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature;
though each appears through the combination of conditions, it does not truly exist.
Upon analysis, there is no combination; it is not as the non-Buddhists perceive.
Like a dream, falling hairs, a mirage, and a city of the Gandharvas—these appear falsely without cause; all worldly phenomena are just like this.
I refute the proponents of causality and expound the principle of non-arising.
If the meaning of non-arising is preserved, the Dharma-eye shall never perish;
when I preach this doctrine of no-cause, all non-Buddhists are struck with awe and terror.
What is it? What is its cause? For what reason does it arise?
In what place does it come together?
Yet they propound the doctrine of causelessness.
When one observes conditioned phenomena as being neither caused nor uncaused,
the views of those who argue for arising and ceasing are thereby extinguished.
Is it because they do not exist that they do not arise?
Is it because they depend upon various conditions?
Or is it that they have names but no referents?
I pray that you will explain for me:
it is not that non-existent things do not arise, nor is it that they wait for conditions;
it is not that there are entities that possess names, nor is it that names are without meaning.
All non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas—this is not the sphere of those on the ten stages; this is the characteristic of non-arising.
It is far removed from all causes and conditions, and there is no creator whatsoever.
Established solely by the mind, I declare these to be non-arising.
All phenomena do not arise from causes; they are neither non-existent nor existent.
Free from the duality of subject and object, I declare these to be non-arising.
Mind-only is without anything seen, and it is also free from the two natures;
when the basis is thus transformed, I call this "non-arising.
Whether external objects exist or do not exist, the mind has nothing to grasp.
All views are completely severed; this is the characteristic of non-arising.
Such is the meaning of phrases like "emptiness" and "absence of intrinsic nature":
it is not empty because of emptiness, but is said to be empty because of non-arising.
Through the gathering together of causes and conditions, there is thus arising and ceasing;
when causes and conditions are dispersed, arising and ceasing do not exist.
Apart from all causes and conditions, there is no further phenomenon whatsoever.
Identity and difference are conceptualized by the ignorant.
The dharmas of existence and non-existence do not arise; the same applies to that which is neither.
Except for the convergence of various conditions, within them one perceives arising and ceasing.
Following worldly convention, we employ provisional designations; through causes and conditions, they link together like a chain.
If one were to separate from this causal chain, the meaning of "arising" could not be established.
I teach that it is merely a chain: since there is no arising, there is no birth.
Free from the errors of all non-Buddhists, this is not understood by the foolish.
If there were a phenomenon of arising apart from the chain of conditions,
then it would be a doctrine of causelessness, which destroys the meaning of the causal chain.
Just as a lamp can illuminate objects, so too do the links of dependent origination appear;
yet if these were separate from the links of dependent origination, there would be other phenomena existing apart from them.
Since there is no arising, there is no intrinsic nature; their essence and characteristics are like empty space.
To seek the Dharma apart from the chain of dependent origination is the conceptualization of the foolish.
Furthermore, there is another non-arising, the Dharma attained by the various sages;
that which is both arising and non-arising is precisely the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
All worlds are nothing other than chains of links;
if one can understand them thus, this person’s mind attains concentration.
Ignorance, craving, and karma—these are the internal chains of links.
Seeds, clay, wheels, and so forth— these are called "external.
If one claims that there exists some other phenomenon produced from causes and conditions,
yet divorced from the principle of causal linkage (*saṃkalana*), this is contrary to the scriptural teachings and logical reasoning.
If the phenomena that arise did not exist, for whom would they be causes and conditions?
That they arise in mutual succession—this is the meaning of causes and conditions.
Solidity, moisture, heat, motion, and so forth, are merely conceptualized by the ignorant.
Because all phenomena lack any intrinsic existence, they are said to be without self-nature.
Just as a physician treats various ailments, his medical discourse remains undifferentiated;
yet because the illnesses differ, the prescriptions and medicines vary accordingly.
For the sake of all sentient beings, I eliminate the disease of afflictions;
knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I expound the various Dharma gates.
It is not that the afflictions or the faculties differ, yet there are diverse teachings.
"There is only the One Great Vehicle, the cool eightfold path.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All non-Buddhists falsely proclaim impermanence, and the World-Honored One also says that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing.
We do not yet know whether this teaching is erroneous or correct.
"How many kinds of impermanence are there?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
The non-Buddhists speak of seven kinds of impermanence, which are not part of my teaching.
What are these seven? They are as follows:
Some say that the very moment of initial arising is abandonment, which is called impermanence, because once produced, there is no further production;
some say that the transformation and disintegration of form and location is called impermanence;
and some say that form itself is impermanent.

Some say that the transformation of form (*rūpa*) is called impermanence (*anitya*); all phenomena (*dharma*) continue in an uninterrupted succession, capable of undergoing transformation and naturally returning to extinction, just as milk transforms into curd over time. Although this is invisible, it exists within phenomena and destroys all things.
Some say that "things" (*bhāva*) are impermanent;
some say that "things" and "non-things" (*abhāva*) are impermanent.
Some say that non-arising impermanence pervades all phenomena. Regarding the "impermanence of things and non-things" therein:

it refers to the destruction of the characteristics of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), while the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the great elements is fundamentally unarisen.

Regarding "non-arising impermanence": this refers to phenomena such as permanence and impermanence, existence and non-existence, and so forth; all such things lack any arising. Even when analyzed down to the level of subtle atoms, nothing is perceived. Because they do not arise, they are called "unborn" (*anutpāda*).
This is the characteristic of non-arising impermanence; if one does not understand this, one falls into the heterodox view of the impermanence of arising.

As for the meaning of "the impermanence of existing things" and "the impermanence of non-existing things," it refers to the spontaneous generation of conceptual discrimination regarding that which is neither permanent nor impermanent.
What is the meaning of this?

They establish that impermanence itself does not perish or disintegrate, yet it is capable of destroying all phenomena. If there were no impermanence to destroy all phenomena, then phenomena would never cease and would thus become non-existent. It is just as a staff, a mallet, or a stone can destroy an object while remaining undestroyed themselves; this case is also like that.

Mahāmati! It is directly perceived that there is no distinction between impermanence and all phenomena in terms of agent and object; since there is no difference such that "this is impermanence" and "this is the produced," both the agent and the object would have to be eternal. This is because no cause can be found that could render all phenomena non-existent.
"Mahāmati!
Although all phenomena indeed have causes for their disintegration and cessation, these cannot be understood by the ignorant and foolish. Mahāmati!"

A different cause should not produce a different effect; if it could so produce them, then all distinct phenomena would arise from one another simultaneously, and there would be no distinction between those phenomena as producer and produced.
Since we clearly perceive distinct differences, how could a different cause produce a different effect? Mahāmati!

If the nature of impermanence were an existing entity (*bhāva*), it would be identical to that which is produced and thus itself impermanent; because it is itself impermanent, all impermanent phenomena would consequently have to be permanent.
Mahāmati!

If the nature of impermanence were to abide within all phenomena, it would likewise fall into the three periods of time along with those phenomena; it would have already perished simultaneously with past form, it would not arise in the future, and it would perish together with the present.

All non-Buddhists reckon that the essential nature of the four great elements does not destroy form; for they hold that these are merely distinctions of the great elements and derivative forms of the great elements, which, being neither different nor non-different, possess a self-nature that likewise does not perish or cease.
Mahāmati!

Within the three realms of existence, there is nothing among the primary elements and their derivatives that does not possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. How could there be any other nature of impermanence apart from these, which could produce things and yet itself not cease?

Regarding the claim that "that which is created at the very beginning is immediately abandoned and thus impermanent": it is not the case that the primary elements (mahābhūtas) create other primary elements, because they are distinct from one another.
Nor is it the case that they create themselves, because they lack differentiation.
It is not created anew, because of its separation.
One should know that this is not the impermanence of initial creation.
Regarding the impermanence of the destruction of shape: this is not the destruction of the creator or the created, but merely the destruction of the shape.
What is the meaning of this?

It means that when matter is analyzed down to its subtlest particles (paramāṇu), one merely eliminates the perception of shapes such as long and short, but does not eliminate the essential substance of the primary and derived elements.
This view falls within the Sāṃkhya school.

As for the claim that "form is impermanent," this means that it is the shape that is impermanent, not the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). If the nature of the primary elements were also impermanent, then there would be no worldly affairs;
one should know that such a position falls into the Lokāyata view, because it perceives all phenomena as being merely verbal designations for the appearance of their own characteristics.

Regarding "impermanence through transformation," this means that it is the substance of form (*rūpa*) that changes, not the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). For example, when gold is fashioned into an ornament, the ornament undergoes change while the gold itself remains unaltered; this case is likewise.

“Mahāmati! Such various non-Buddhists, through false discrimination, perceive the nature of impermanence and speak thus: ‘Fire cannot burn its own characteristics; rather, they merely disperse. If it were able to burn them, then both the primary elements and their derivatives would all be annihilated.’”
Mahāmati!
I teach that all dharmas are neither eternal nor impermanent. Why is this?

Because external dharmas are not grasped; because the three realms are mind-only; because various characteristics are not spoken of; because the great elements, their natures, and their locations, in all their various distinctions, are neither born nor extinguished; because there is no distinction between the creator and the created; because the two natures of the grasper and the grasped all arise from discrimination; because one knows the nature of these two graspings as they truly are; because one realizes that they are merely manifestations of one's own mind; because one is free from the two views of external existence and non-existence; and because, being free from the view of existence and non-existence, one does not discriminate between the creator and the created.
Mahāmati!

Regarding all dharmas—mundane, supramundane, and supremely supramundane—they are solely one's own mind, neither eternal nor non-eternal. Failing to realize this, one falls into the evil views of the two extremes held by the externalists.
Mahāmati!
All non-Buddhists are unable to understand these three kinds of dharmas; relying on their own conceptual discrimination, they give rise to verbal expressions that proclaim the nature of impermanence.
Mahāmati!
"These three kinds of phenomena, with all their linguistic designations and conceptual domains, are not something that ordinary, ignorant people can understand.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Created at first, they are then abandoned; Their forms undergo transformation."
Form and material things are impermanent; this is the false discrimination of the non-Buddhists.
All dharmas are without destruction or cessation; the primary elements abide in their own intrinsic nature.
Yet the various views of the non-Buddhists describe them as being impermanent.
Those various followers of external paths all proclaim non-arising and non-ceasing;
they claim that the nature of the great elements is inherently eternal—what, then, could be an impermanent dharma?
Both the grasper and the grasped are entirely nothing but mind.
The two kinds [of existence] manifest from the mind; there is no self or what belongs to a self.
The various phenomena such as the Brahmā heavens—I say they are nothing but mind.
If one is separated from the mind, nothing at all can be found.
Chapter 4: Direct Realization (5). The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Four: Direct Realization. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I pray that you will explain to me the characteristics of the sequential continuity of entry into cessation for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, so that I and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having thoroughly understood this, may have no confusion regarding the bliss of the samādhi of cessation, and shall not fall into the errors of the two vehicles or the various non-Buddhist paths.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."

“Mahāmati! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas reach the sixth stage, as well as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they enter the samādhi of cessation; however, Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage enter it constantly in every thought-moment because they have abandoned the self-nature characteristics of all dharmas, which is not the case for those of the two vehicles.”

The followers of the two vehicles possess effortful activity and thus fall into the duality of subject and object; they fail to attain the undifferentiated characteristic of all phenomena. Although they understand the specific and general characteristics of the wholesome and unwholesome and enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), for this reason they are unable to enter it constantly at every moment.
Mahāmati!

For Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, as well as for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the conceptualizations of mind, intellect, and consciousness are extinguished. From the first stage through the sixth stage, they observe that all things within the triple world arise solely from the self-discrimination of mind, intellect, and consciousness; they are detached from "self" and "what belongs to self," and they do not perceive the various marks of external phenomena.

Ordinary fools do not understand this; due to the habitual perfuming of faults and evils from beginningless time, they manifest within their own minds the appearances of grasper and grasped, and thereby give rise to attachment.
Mahāmati!

The samādhis attained by Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are identical to the nirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; however, through the empowerment of the Buddhas' power, they do not enter nirvāṇa within those gates of samādhi.

If one does not uphold it, one will fail to transform and deliver all sentient beings, will be unable to fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata, and will likewise sever the lineage of the Tathāgatas. For this reason, the Buddhas expound for them the inconceivable great merits of a Tathāgata, so that they may ultimately never enter nirvana.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are attached to the bliss of samādhi; therefore, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa within that state. Mahāmati!

Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage are well able to discern the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness, as well as the grasping at "self" and "mine," the selflessness of persons and phenomena, and the specific and general characteristics of arising and ceasing. They possess skillful certainty regarding the four unhindered analytical knowledges and attain mastery over the gates of samādhi, gradually entering the successive stages while being endowed with the factors of enlightenment.
"Mahāmati!

I have spoken thus because I fear that bodhisattvas might not skillfully understand specific and general characteristics, and failing to know the sequential progression of the stages, would fall into the various evil views of the non-Buddhists."
Mahāmati!
In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing; the progression through the stages, the succession of the three realms, and all coming and going are entirely what is seen by one's own mind.
Yet ordinary, ignorant people are unable to understand this; because they do not know it, I and the Buddhas speak thus. "Mahāmati!

From the stage of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas up to the eighth stage of the Bodhisattvas, they become intoxicated by the bliss of samādhi and are unable to thoroughly comprehend that what is seen is but the manifestation of mind alone. Their minds are entangled and shrouded by the habitual tendencies of self-characteristics and common characteristics; they conceive the realization of Nirvana through attachment to the two kinds of selflessness, yet this is not the wisdom of ultimate cessation."

Mahāmati! When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas behold the gate of the bliss of the samādhi of cessation, they immediately recollect their original vows and great compassion, and fully cultivate the ten inexhaustible phrases. For this reason, they do not immediately enter nirvāṇa; because entering nirvāṇa would result in no further fruit; because they are free from the grasping of subject and object; because they have realized that all is but mind; because they are without discrimination regarding all phenomena; and because they do not fall into the attachment to the characteristics and natures of external dharmas within the mind, thought, or consciousness.

However, it is not that they fail to give rise to the true cause of the Buddha-dharma, for they arise in accordance with the movement of wisdom in this manner, thereby attaining the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

Mahāmati! It is like a person who, while dreaming, employs skillful means to cross a river; before having crossed, he awakens. Having awakened, he reflects upon what he saw previously: "Was this real?"
Is this a delusion?
He further thought to himself:

"It is neither real nor false; it is merely what has been seen, heard, sensed, and known—a manifestation within the consciousness-dream arising from the habitual tendencies of past experiences and the conceptualization of existence and non-existence."

"Mahāmati! It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas: from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh, and further progressing into the eighth where they attain non-conceptuality, they see all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth, free from the grasped and the grasper. They perceive the vast and powerful functioning of the mind and mental factors; they diligently cultivate the Buddha-dharma to realize what has not yet been realized; and by departing from the false conceptualizations of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). This is the nirvāṇa attained by Bodhisattvas; it is not a state of annihilation."
Mahāmati!

Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is neither sequence nor continuity; it is far removed from all objective realms and conceptual discrimination—this is what is called the dharma of quiescence (nirvāṇa).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The various stages and the Buddha-ground Are mind-only, without images;
This is what has been taught by all The Buddhas of the past, future, and present.”
The seventh stage is with mind; the eighth stage is without images.
These two stages are called "abiding"; the rest is what I have attained.
Self-realization and purity—this is my own ground.
In the most supreme realm of Maheśvara, adorned by Akaniṣṭha,
Like a great mass of fire with blazing, radiant flames,
He manifests throughout the three realms of existence, Delightful and refreshing.
Some manifest transformations, while others are transformed beforehand;
the various vehicles taught therein are all the stage of the Tathāgata.
The tenth stage is the first, and the first is the eighth stage.
The ninth is the seventh, and the seventh is again the eighth.
The second is the third, and the fourth is the fifth;
the third is the sixth—when there is no characteristic, what sequence can there be?
Chapter Five: On the Permanence and Impermanence of the Tathāgata. At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, permanent or impermanent?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither eternal nor impermanent. Why?
Because both positions entail faults.
What is the fault? Mahāmati!
If the Tathāgata were eternal, there would be the fault of being a creator; for all non-Buddhists assert that the creator is eternal.

If it were impermanent, it would entail the fault of being something produced, sharing the same nature as the aggregates in being characterized and characterized; it would ultimately be subject to total annihilation and thus become non-existent. However, the Buddha-Tathāgata is truly not subject to annihilation.
Mahāmati!

All created things, such as jars, garments, and the like, are impermanent; if this were so, the Tathāgata would incur the fault of impermanence, and the merit and wisdom he has cultivated would all be empty and of no benefit.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena should be the Tathāgata, because there is no other cause; therefore, the Tathāgata is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Moreover, Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata is not eternal; if he were eternal, he would be like space, which is established without depending on causes.
Mahāmati!
For example, space is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Why is this? Because it would entail all the faults of being either identical to or different from permanence and impermanence, as well as being both or neither, and so forth.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata is not eternal; if he were eternal, he would be unarisen and thus identical to the horns of rabbits, horses, fish, snakes, and so forth.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
From another perspective, it may also be said that [the Tathāgata] is permanent. Why is this?
Because he realizes the permanent Dharma through direct knowledge; since the realizing wisdom is permanent, the Tathāgata is also permanent.
Mahāmati!

The nature of phenomena realized by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas—the abiding of phenomena and the fixed position of phenomena—remains eternally constant and unchanging whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear. It exists within the dharmas attained by all those of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists; it is not a mere void or nothingness, yet it is not something that can be known by the ignorant and foolish.

Mahāmati! As for the Tathāgata, he receives his name because he has internally realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through pure wisdom; it is not by means of the mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, or the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, nor through false habitual tendencies, that he is so named.
All three realms arise from false conceptualization, but the Tathāgata does not arise from false conceptualization.
Mahāmati!

If there were duality regarding permanence and impermanence, the Tathāgata would not be non-dual; however, because he has realized that all dharmas have the characteristic of non-arising, he is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Mahāmati!

As long as there is even the slightest arising of verbal conceptualization, there will be the faults of permanence and impermanence; therefore, you should eliminate these two types of dualistic discrimination so that not even a trace remains.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Far removed from permanence and impermanence, yet manifesting permanence and impermanence;
Thus constantly contemplating the Buddha, one does not give rise to wrong views."
If one holds that things are either eternal or non-eternal, all that has been accumulated will be of no benefit;
to eliminate such discriminative cognition, I do not speak of eternity or non-eternity.
As long as there is anything established, everything is delusive.
"If one perceives that it is only one's own mind, then there will be no conflict or dispute.
Chapter Six: On Moments (*Kṣaṇavarga*) At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I only pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. If there is no self, who is it that arises and who is it that ceases?
Yet all ordinary beings rely upon this arising and ceasing; they do not seek the exhaustion of suffering nor do they realize nirvana.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! Listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you, Mahāmati.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, capable of universally producing all realms of existence.

It is like an actor who manifests various roles; though devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self," through the lack of awakening, the three conditions harmonize to bring about the arising of fruits.

The non-Buddhists do not understand this and cling to it as a creator; permeated by beginningless false and evil habits, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*. It gives rise to the seven consciousnesses upon the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*), like the waves upon the great ocean. Its substance is a continuous succession that flows perpetually without interruption; its fundamental nature is pure, free from the fault of impermanence and free from the doctrine of a self.

The remaining seven consciousnesses—the mental consciousness and so forth—arise and perish moment by moment, produced through the conjunction of deluded conceptualization as the cause and objective appearances as the condition. Failing to realize that form and other phenomena are manifestations of one’s own mind, they cling to names and signs, giving rise to sensations of pleasure and pain. Bound by these names and signs, they arise from craving and further produce craving. If the causes, the objects of perception, and the roots of grasping cease and no longer continue to arise, and one uses self-insight to discern the sensations of pleasure and pain, one may attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the four dhyānas, or skillfully enter the liberation of the Truths; yet, one falsely conceives the thought of having attained liberation, while in reality one has neither abandoned nor transformed the name "store-consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*) within the Tathāgata-garbha.
If the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) did not exist, the seven consciousnesses would cease. Why is this?
Because they arise depending upon it and their respective objects of perception.

However, this is not the sphere of experience known by all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or practitioners of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), for they only realize the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) while still grasping at the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields (*skandha*, *dhātu*, and *āyatana*). If one perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the selflessness of all phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), these [graspings] will gradually be transformed and extinguished according to the sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*). One is no longer moved by the evil views of non-Buddhists; abiding in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), one attains the ten gates of the bliss of samādhi. Sustained by the power of samādhi and upheld by all Buddhas, one contemplates the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas and the power of original vows. Not dwelling in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) or the bliss of samādhi, one attains the wisdom of personal realization (*pratyātma-jñāna*), which is not shared with the two vehicles or non-Buddhists. Thus, one attains the path of the ten noble lineages (*āryagotra*) and the mind-made body of wisdom (*manomaya-jñānakāya*), becoming free from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, Mahāmati,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to attain the supreme dharma should purify the designations "tathāgatagarbha" and "ālayavijñāna. Mahāmati!
If there were no such thing as the Tathāgatagarbha, which is called the Ālayavijñāna, then there would be no arising and ceasing.

Yet, both ordinary beings and noble ones alike experience arising and ceasing; therefore, all practitioners, even though they perceive internal objects and abide in the bliss of the present life, do not relinquish their courageous diligence.

Mahāmati! This Tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, is pure by nature; it becomes impure only when defiled by adventitious dust. All followers of the two vehicles and the various non-Buddhists speculate and give rise to views regarding it, yet they cannot realize it through direct perception. The Tathāgata perceives this clearly and directly, as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand.

“Mahāmati! For the sake of Queen Śrīmālā and other bodhisattvas of profound, subtle, and pure wisdom, I have taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is called the ālayavijñāna, which arises together with the seven consciousnesses, so as to enable all śrāvakas to perceive the selflessness of phenomena.”
Mahāmati!
It was for the sake of Queen Śrīmālā that I spoke of the realm of the Buddha; it is not the realm of the non-Buddhists or the followers of the two vehicles.
Mahāmati!

This Tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, is the realm of the Buddhas and the sphere of activity for you, Bodhisattvas of Pure Wisdom, who accord with the true meaning; it is not the sphere of activity for any non-Buddhists who cling to words or for those of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, you and all other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently investigate the Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna; do not merely become complacent upon having heard of them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The profound Tathāgatagarbha coexists with the seven consciousnesses;
Through attachment, the two kinds of birth arise; When fully understood, one is far removed from them."
Perfumed by habitual tendencies since beginningless time, Objects appear in the mind like reflections;
If one can contemplate according to reality, The characteristics of objects will all be non-existent.
It is like a fool looking at the finger pointing at the moon: He gazes at the finger and does not see the moon.
Those who are attached to words do not see my true reality.
The mind is like an actor, the intellect is like the stage manager;
the five consciousnesses are its companions, while false discrimination watches the performance.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
I pray that you will explain to me the characteristics of the distinctions between the five dharmas, the self-natures, the various consciousnesses, and the absence of self."

Once I and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have thoroughly understood this, we shall gradually cultivate the stages, fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas, and reach the state of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.
The Buddha said:
“Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you.”
Mahāmati!
The five dharmas, the self-natures, the various consciousnesses, and the absence of self are as follows:
namely, name, appearance, discrimination, correct knowledge, and suchness.

If a practitioner contemplates this Dharma, they will enter the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, remain far removed from views such as permanence, annihilation, existence, or non-existence, and attain the profound samādhi of happiness in the present life.
Mahāmati!

Ordinary, ignorant people do not understand the five dharmas, the self-natures, the various consciousnesses, and non-self; they perceive external objects manifested by the mind and give rise to discrimination, whereas this is not the case for the noble ones.
Mahāmati said:
“How does one give rise to conceptual discrimination without understanding?
The Buddha said:

“Mahāmati! The ignorant and foolish do not know that names are merely provisional designations; their minds follow after movement and perceive various marks. They conceive of ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self,’ becoming defiled and attached to form. This obscures noble wisdom, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, whereby they create all manner of karma like a silkworm spinning its cocoon. Bound by their own false imaginings, they fall into the great ocean of birth and death across the various realms of existence, circling incessantly like a waterwheel drawing up water. They do not understand that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, or like the moon reflected in water; rather, they give rise to false discrimination regarding what is seen by their own minds. Detached from the grasped and the grasper, as well as from arising, abiding, and ceasing, they claim that things arise from Īśvara, time, atoms, or primordial nature (pradhāna), following the flow of names and marks.”
Mahāmati! In this context,
"characteristic" refers to that which is seen by the visual consciousness, which is designated as form (*rūpa*).
That which is apprehended by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness is termed sound, odor, flavor, tangibility, and phenomena; such things, I say, are characteristics.

Discrimination (*vikalpa*) refers to the establishment of various names to manifest various characteristics; that is, manifesting their characteristics through names such as elephant, horse, chariot, infantry, man, or woman. When these matters are thus determined to be non-different [from those names], this is called discrimination.

Right Knowledge means observing that names and characteristics are mutually adventitious, such that the consciousness-mind neither arises nor ceases, and is neither eternal nor annihilated; not falling into the stages of external paths or the two vehicles is called Right Knowledge.
Mahāmati!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe names and characteristics with their correct wisdom, they realize that these are neither existent nor non-existent, thereby remaining far removed from the two extremes of harmful and beneficial views. Since names, characteristics, and consciousness have never arisen from the beginning, I declare this Dharma to be called "Tathatā" (Suchness).

“Mahāmati! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in suchness (tathatā), they attain the non-manifestation of objective realms, ascend to the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), and leave behind the evil destinies of external paths. They enter the supramundane dharma, whereby their realization of the characteristics of dharmas (dharma-lakṣaṇa) matures; they know that all dharmas are like illusions and so forth, realize the dharma traversed by their own noble wisdom (sva-āryajñāna), and depart from speculative views. Proceeding in this sequence, they reach up to the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi).”

Upon reaching the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), through the power of samādhis, various strengths, and sovereign supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), one fully blossoms and becomes a Tathāgata. Having become a Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, one manifests the body everywhere like the moon in water, preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations and desires.

His body is pure, transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness; he is clad in the armor of the great vows and has fully perfected the ten inexhaustible aspirations—this is called the attainment of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva upon entering suchness.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do the three natures enter into the five dharmas?”
"Does each have its own specific characteristic?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"

The three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are all subsumed within the five dharmas. Among these, name and appearance constitute the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
