because they arise simultaneously with the mind and mental factors that depend upon them—just as the sun and its light constitute the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
and because correct gnosis and suchness are indestructible, they constitute the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Mahāmati!

When attachment arises toward what is manifested by one's own mind, eight kinds of discrimination emerge; these various characteristics are all unreal and consist solely of the nature of false conceptualization.
If one can abandon the two kinds of self-grasping, the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness will arise and grow.
Mahāmati! The stages of self-realized noble wisdom for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas—all the Buddha-dharmas—are entirely subsumed within these five dharmas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are as follows:
namely, appearance (*nimitta*), name (*nāman*), discrimination (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Among these, "appearance" refers to the distinct shapes of perceived objects such as forms; this is called appearance.
Based on those various characteristics, one establishes names such as "vase"; that "this is thus" and "this is not otherwise" is called "name.
The application of various names to manifest the characteristics of mind and mental factors is called "conceptualization."

Those names and those marks are ultimately non-existent; they are merely the successive conceptualizations of the deluded mind. To observe in this manner until even awakening ceases is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Mahāmati!
The ultimate, definitive, and fundamental self-nature that can be attained is the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*).
I and all the Buddhas have entered into realization in accordance with it, and we reveal and expound it according to its true nature.

If one can accord with and awaken to this understanding, remaining free from both annihilationism and eternalism, not giving rise to conceptual discrimination, and entering the realm of self-realization—thereby transcending the spheres of the non-Buddhists and the two vehicles—this is called right knowledge.
Mahāmati!
These five kinds of dharmas—the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—comprehensively encompass all Buddha-dharmas.
Mahāmati!

Within this Dharma, you should skillfully penetrate it through your own wisdom and also exhort others to penetrate it; having penetrated it, your mind will become resolute and no longer follow after others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The five dharmas, the three natures, And the eight kinds of consciousness;
The two kinds of selflessness— These universally encompass the Mahāyāna."
"Name, mark, and discrimination are subsumed under the two natures;
correct knowledge and suchness constitute the characteristic of the perfected nature.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As it is said in the sūtras that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, how should this be understood?
Should one accept it exactly as it is stated?”
"Is it for the sake of a distinct meaning?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Do not accept [the teaching] according to the literal expression."
Mahāmati!
The Buddhas of the three periods of time are not like the sands of the Ganges. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is most supreme, transcending all worlds; there is no one equal to him, and he cannot be reached by analogy, yet I employ a small portion as a metaphor for his sake.

For those who are ordinary, foolish, or among the non-Buddhists—their minds constantly clinging to permanence or impermanence, their evil views increasing as they wander through the cycle of birth and death—I say that the Buddha is easy to realize and easy to encounter, so that they may develop weariness [with saṃsāra] and give rise to superior aspiration.

If I were to say that he is difficult to meet, like the udumbara flower, they would become discouraged and fail to apply themselves with diligence; therefore, I say that [the Buddhas] are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are times when I observe those to be converted and say that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower. Mahāmati,
while no one has ever seen, does see, or will see the udumbara flower, the Tathāgata has already been seen, is being seen, and will be seen.
Mahāmati! Such metaphors do not describe my own Dharma.

My own Dharma is the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom realized within; it is peerless in the world and transcends all metaphors, such that all ordinary and ignorant people are unable to believe or accept it.
Mahāmati!
The true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by mind, intellect, and consciousness; therefore, no analogy can be established for him.
Nevertheless, there are times when analogies are established, such as saying he is like the sands of the Ganges, which is not contradictory.
Mahāmati!
It is like the sands of the Ganges, which, though trampled by turtles, fish, elephants, and horses, do not give rise to discrimination and remain eternally pure and stainless;

the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata is like that Ganges, with its powers, superknowledges, and masteries serving as its sands. Although non-Buddhists and others come in competition to disturb it, the Buddha does not give rise to a single thought of discrimination.

Why is this? Because it is the original vow of the Tathāgata to universally settle all sentient beings in the bliss of samādhi, like the sands of the Ganges, being without love or hatred and free from discrimination.
Mahāmati!

It is like the sands of the Ganges, which are the very nature of earth. When the kalpa comes to an end and all the earth is consumed by fire, that element of earth does not abandon its own nature, for it arises simultaneously with the element of fire. Fools and ordinary people say that the earth is being burned, but in reality it is not burned, as it is the cause upon which the fire depends.
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is also like this; it is like the sands of the Ganges, never to be destroyed or extinguished.
Mahāmati! Just as the sands of the Ganges are without limit, so too are the radiances of the Tathāgata;
desiring to bring immeasurable sentient beings to fulfillment, they universally illumine all the great assemblies of the Buddhas.
Mahāmati! Just as the sands of the Ganges abide in their own nature, remaining unchanged and never transforming into other things;
so too is the Tathāgata in the world—neither born nor extinguished—for all causes of birth have been utterly severed.
Mahāmati! It is like the sands of the Ganges: though one takes them away, they do not diminish; though one throws more in, no increase is seen.
So it is with the Buddhas: through the wisdom of skillful means, they bring sentient beings to maturity without decrease or increase.
Why is this? Because, Mahāmati,
the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body has no physical body.
Because there is a body, there is disintegration; because the Dharma-body has no body, it is without disintegration. Mahāmati!
It is like the sands of the Ganges: though one might press and treat them with hardship in an attempt to obtain ghee or oil, they can never be obtained.

The Tathāgata is likewise: although he is oppressed by the manifold sufferings of sentient beings until even the most minute creatures have attained nirvāṇa, he desires to cause them to abandon [suffering] within the dharmadhātu; yet, even his profound aspiration and delight therein cannot be apprehended as a grasped object.
Why is this? Because they have fully accomplished the mind of great compassion. Mahāmati!
For example, just as the sands of the Ganges flow along with the water and not without it, so too it is with the Tathāgata:
all his teachings accord with the current of nirvāṇa. For this reason, it is said that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are like the sands of the Ganges.
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma does not follow after the realms of existence (*gati*). "Realm" carries the meaning of destruction; since the original limit of birth and death cannot be known, and it being unknowable, how could one speak of realms?
"Mahāmati!
The pursuit of meaning is nihilistic, yet ordinary fools do not realize this.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If the original limit of birth and death cannot be known, how can sentient beings within birth and death attain liberation?
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!

When the causes of beginningless habitual tendencies toward falsehood are extinguished, one realizes that external objects are manifestations of one's own mind; this transformation of the basis of conceptualization is called liberation.
It is not a state of annihilation, and therefore it cannot be said to be without limit.
Mahāmati! "Limitlessness" is merely another name for discrimination. Mahāmati!

Apart from the discriminating mind, there are no separate sentient beings. By observing all internal and external phenomena with wisdom, one knows that both the subject and the object are entirely quiescent. Mahāmati!
"All dharmas are seen only through the conceptualization of one's own mind; because they are not understood, the conceptualizing mind arises, but when the mind is understood, it ceases.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Observe all the Teachers, Who are like the sands of the Ganges River;"
Neither perishing nor proceeding—such a person can see the Buddha.
Like the sands of the Ganges, entirely free from all faults, yet ever flowing along with the current; such is the nature of the Buddha’s body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain to me the characteristic of the momentary destruction of all dharmas.”
“What dharmas are said to possess moments?
The Buddha said,
“Listen attentively!”
I shall explain this for you, Mahāmati.
"All dharmas" refers to the following:

Wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas; conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas; mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas; tainted dharmas and untainted dharmas; dharmas associated with grasping and dharmas not associated with grasping.
Mahāmati! To state the essentials:

the phenomena of the five aggregates of grasping increase by taking the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of mind, intellect, and mentation as their cause. In this regard, the ignorant and foolish give rise to discrimination, labeling them as "wholesome" or "unwholesome."
The noble ones directly realize the dwelling in the bliss of samādhi; this is what is called the wholesome, untainted dharma.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the wholesome and the unwholesome refer to the eight consciousnesses.
What are these eight?
They are the Tathāgatagarbha, which is called the ālayavijñāna, along with the manas, the manovijñāna, and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses. Mahāmati!

Those five bodies of consciousness coexist with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); their wholesome and unwholesome characteristics arise in mutual distinction, continuing in an uninterrupted succession. They do not possess distinct substantial entities, but perish immediately after arising; they do not comprehend that objects are manifestations of one's own mind. As they perish in succession, other cognitions arise. The mental consciousness coexists with those five consciousnesses, grasping various differentiated forms and appearances, remaining for no more than a moment. I call these "momentary phenomena" (*kṣaṇadharma*).

Mahāmati! The Tathāgatagarbha is named the ālayavijñāna. That which is associated with the mental faculty (*manas*) and other habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is a momentary dharma; however, the untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are not momentary dharmas. This is not something that can be known by the foolish and ignorant proponents of momentariness.

Because they cannot know that among all phenomena there are some that are momentary and others that are non-momentary, they conceive of the unconditioned as being subject to destruction like all other phenomena, thereby falling into the view of nihilism.

Mahāmati! The five bodies of consciousness do not undergo transmigration; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa. It is the Tathāgatagarbha that experiences suffering and pleasure, which, together with its causes, possesses arising and ceasing. It is obscured by the four kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and because the deluded minds of ordinary fools are permeated by discrimination, they are unable to understand it and give rise to the view of momentariness (*kṣaṇika-dṛṣṭi*).
Mahāmati! Just as gold, vajra, and the relics of the Buddha possess extraordinary characteristics that are never destroyed;

if the realization of the Dharma were subject to momentariness, then the noble ones would cease to be noble, yet those noble ones have never been anything other than noble. It is like gold and vajra, which remain for kalpas without their weight diminishing.
"Why is it that ordinary, ignorant people do not understand my secret teaching and instead conceive of all phenomena as being momentary?
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have often said that if one fulfills the six pāramitās, one will attain perfect enlightenment."
“What are these six?
How are they fulfilled?
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! There are three distinctions regarding the pāramitās.
They are as follows:”
"Worldly, supramundane, and supremely supramundane. Mahāmati, as for the worldly pāramitās:

this refers to those ordinary, deluded beings who are attached to 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' who grasp at the two extremes, and who, seeking the bodies of existence, crave objects such as forms. Thus they practice the pāramitā of dāna (generosity), śīla (ethical discipline), kṣānti (patience), vīrya (diligence), and dhyāna (meditative concentration), and having accomplished the supernormal powers, they are born in the Brahma world."
Mahāmati!
As for the supramundane pāramitās, this refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who, being attached to nirvāṇa and seeking their own pleasure, practice the various pāramitās in such a manner.

Mahāmati! Regarding the supramundane, unsurpassed *pāramitā*: it means that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas realize that the two dharmas within their own minds are merely manifestations of discrimination, they do not give rise to deluded thoughts nor produce attachments; they do not grasp at the marks of form (*rūpa*), yet for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they constantly practice the *dāna-pāramitā*.
When they do not give rise to discrimination regarding any objective realm, this is the practice of the *śīla-pāramitā*.
At the very moment when conceptual discrimination does not arise, to patiently realize the intrinsic nature of both the grasper and the grasped is called the *kṣānti-pāramitā*;

to practice diligently without indolence during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, conforming to true understanding and not giving rise to discrimination, is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*;
and not giving rise to discrimination and not conceiving the views of non-Buddhists regarding *nirvāṇa* is called the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.

Observing with wisdom that the mind is without conceptual differentiation and does not fall into the two extremes, one transforms the basis of existence into purity without destroying it; thus attaining the realm of internal realization through noble wisdom, this is called Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The fool discriminates the conditioned as empty, impermanent, and momentary;
yet he discriminates the meaning of 'moment' [as being real], like a river, a lamp, or a seed."
All phenomena are unarisen, Quiescent and devoid of activity;
The nature of all things is utterly transcendent— This is the meaning of my "moment" (kṣaṇa).
Arising and ceasing in immediate succession, It is not taught to the foolish and ignorant.
The dharmas of uninterrupted continuity arise through the differentiation of the various realms of existence.
Ignorance is their cause, and the mind is born from it;
since one has not yet understood where form comes from, where could it abide in the interim?
When there is cessation in uninterrupted succession, another mind arises;
while it does not abide in form, from what object of perception does it arise?
If it arises by taking that [form] as its object, then its cause is false.
Since the essence of delusion is not established, how can it be subject to momentary extinction?
The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of practitioners, the diamond relics of the Buddha,
and the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven— these are things in the world that do not perish.
The Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom and the realization attained by the bhikṣus—
since the nature of all phenomena is eternally abiding, how can they be seen as momentary?
Why are forms such as those in a city of the gandharvas or illusions not momentary?
Since the great elements lack intrinsic reality, how can they be said to be the creators?
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Five; *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of the Great Zhou Dynasty at Khotan, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seven: Transformations (6). Chapter Seven: Transformations. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Tathāgata bestow upon arhats the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
And for what reason do you further say that sentient beings who lack the dharma of parinirvāṇa shall attain the path to Buddhahood?”
Furthermore, for what reason do you say that from the initial attainment of Buddhahood until Parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken in the interval?
Again, you say that the Tathāgata is always in meditative concentration, without vitarka or vicāra;
and you say that all Buddha-activities are merely transformations.
Furthermore, you state that all consciousnesses undergo momentary transformation and decay;
yet you also state that the Vajra deity constantly follows and protects one;
and you state that while the prior limit is unknowable, there exists parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are currently Māras and the deeds of Māra;
there are also other karmic retributions, namely:

the incident with the Brahmin woman Ciñcā, the heretical woman Sundarī, and returning with an empty bowl. Since the World-Honored One possesses such karmic obstructions, how can he have attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
“Since you have already perfected all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), why do you not remain free from such faults?
The Buddha said,
“Listen attentively!”
I shall explain this for you, Mahāmati.

For the sake of the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, I have secretly exhorted them to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva. There are bodhisattvas in this world and in other lands whose minds delight in seeking the *nirvāṇa* of śrāvakas; therefore, I have made this statement in order to cause them to abandon such a mind and advance in the cultivation of the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, it is the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) who bestows predictions upon transformed śrāvakas, not the Dharma-nature Buddha (dharmatā-buddha).
Mahāmati! The bestowing of predictions upon śrāvakas is a teaching of intentional secrecy (saṃdhyābhāṣya).
Mahāmati!

That there is no difference between the Buddha and the followers of the two vehicles is based on the single flavor of liberation through the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*); it does not refer to the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), for the cognitive hindrance is purified only upon realizing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Regarding the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*): when one abandons the consciousness that perceives a self in persons, at that time the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are first severed and extinguished; only then is liberation from the obstacle to phenomena (*dharmāvaraṇa*) attained, resulting in ultimate purity.
Mahāmati!

I have uttered this esoteric teaching based on the principle of primordial abiding; it is not different from what was taught by previous Buddhas, for they previously possessed all such syllables and characters.
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgata possesses correct knowledge and is free from delusive thoughts; he does not require deliberation before preaching the Dharma. Having long since severed the four kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he is liberated from the two kinds of death and has eliminated the two kinds of obstructions.
Mahāmati!

The manas, the mental consciousness, and the seven [consciousnesses] beginning with the visual consciousness have habitual tendencies as their cause and are momentary in nature; they are apart from untainted goodness and are not dharmas of transmigration.
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of the cycle of birth and death as well as of nirvāṇa, and the cause of both suffering and happiness; yet ordinary fools, not knowing this, falsely cling to emptiness.
Mahāmati! A transformation Tathāgata is constantly guarded and protected by Vajrapāṇi; he is not a true Buddha.

A true Tathāgata transcends all limitations and is unknowable to those of the two vehicles or to non-Buddhists. Abiding in the bliss of the present dharma, he has perfected the patience of wisdom (*jñāna-kṣānti*) and does not rely on the protection of Vajrapāṇi.

All transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) are not born of karma; they are neither identical to the Buddha nor are they non-Buddhas. Just as a potter produces various objects through the combination of many conditions, so too is it with the transformation Buddha: though endowed with all marks, he expounds the Dharma, yet he cannot speak of the realm traversed by the noble wisdom of self-realization (*svasaṃvedya-āryajñāna*).
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

All foolish ordinary people, seeing the cessation of the six consciousnesses, give rise to the view of annihilationism; failing to understand the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of eternalism.
Mahāmati!"

The conceptualization of one's own mind is its fundamental limit; therefore, it cannot be apprehended. By departing from this conceptualization, one attains liberation, severing the four kinds of habitual tendencies and becoming free from all faults.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“In the three vehicles and that which is not a vehicle, there is no nirvana for a Buddha;
All are granted the prophecy of the Tathāgata, And it is taught that they are free from all faults and evils.”
Having attained ultimate wisdom and nirvana without remainder,
he spoke with this underlying intention to encourage those who are timid and inferior:
"The wisdom attained by all Buddhas is explained through such a path."
This alone is it, and nothing else; therefore, for them, there is no nirvāṇa.
Desire, form, existence, and various views—these are the four kinds of habitual tendencies;
from these the mental consciousness arises, and the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the manas are also contained therein.
"Seeing that the eye-consciousness and so forth are impermanent, they speak of their cessation;
yet, deluded regarding the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the notion of permanence, and with false wisdom, they call this Nirvāṇa.

Chapter 8: On Abstaining from Eating Meat (6). The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Eight: On Abstaining from Eating Meat. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will explain for us the merits and faults of eating or not eating meat. Having understood their meaning, I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas shall expound them for the sake of sentient beings who eat meat—those currently living or those yet to come—who are conditioned by the habitual tendencies of past retribution. This shall cause them to renounce the flavor of meat and seek the flavor of the Dharma;
to give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, to love one another as if they were an only child, to abide in the stages of a Bodhisattva, and to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Or perhaps they may temporarily rest upon the stages of the two vehicles, yet ultimately shall attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
World-Honored One!

Even among the various non-Buddhist practitioners such as the Lokāyatas, who give rise to views of existence and non-existence and cling to the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, there are still prohibitions that forbid the eating of meat. How much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who nurtures all with great compassion and is the refuge of the world—how could he permit both oneself and others to eat meat?"
Excellent, World-Honored One!

You possess great compassion and take pity upon the world, regarding all sentient beings equally as if they were your only child. We pray that you will explain for us the faults and evils of eating meat and the merits of not eating it, so that I and the other bodhisattvas, having heard this, may practice it and widely proclaim it to others.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva spoke again in verse:
“Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, Aspiring to seek supreme enlightenment—
Regarding wine, meat, and onions, Are they to be eaten or not?”
Fools crave meat, which is foul-smelling, filthy, and devoid of renown;
it is the same as that of evil beasts—how could it be fit for consumption?
What fault is there in eating it?
"What merit is there in not eating?
I pray that the Most Victorious Honored One will fully explain this for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"Mahāmati! Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
Reflect upon this well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you, Mahāmati.
All meats have immeasurable causes and conditions; within these, a bodhisattva should give rise to compassion and must not consume them. I shall now explain a small portion of these for you.

Mahāmati! All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been revolving incessantly in the cycle of birth and death; there has never been one who has not served as their father, mother, brother, son, daughter, or relative, nor even as a friend, a loved one, or a servant. Having passed through various births, they have even received the bodies of birds and beasts; how, then, could one take them and eat them?
Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva regards all sentient beings as identical to his own self; considering that meat comes from the life-force of living beings, how could he eat it?
"Mahāmati!
Even rākṣasas and the like, upon hearing this teaching of mine, should cease eating meat; how much more so those who delight in the Dharma?
Mahāmati!"

Wherever a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is born, they regard all sentient beings as their own kin, even cherishing them with a mind of loving-kindness as if they were an only child; for this reason, one should not eat any kind of meat.
Mahāmati!
At crossroads and marketplaces, there are meat-sellers who, for the sake of profit, hawk the flesh of dogs, horses, humans, oxen, and so forth; how could such impure things be fit for consumption?
“Mahāmati! All meats are produced from semen, blood, and impurities; how could one who seeks purity consume them?
Mahāmati!”
When sentient beings see those who eat meat, they are all struck with fear and alarm. How can one who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) consume meat? Mahāmati!

It is like hunters, *caṇḍālas*, fishermen, bird-catchers, and other such evil persons; when dogs see them, they bark in alarm, and when wild beasts see them, they flee. All beings—whether flying in the air, dwelling in the water, or on land—think this very thought upon seeing them: [“This person is one of us!”]
"This person's breath is like that of a rākṣasa; having come here now, he will surely kill me.
For the sake of protecting their lives, they all flee and hide away.
It is the same for those who eat meat. Therefore, a bodhisattva practicing the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) should not eat meat.
"Mahāmati!

Those who eat meat have foul-smelling and impure bodies, and their ill repute spreads far and wide; thus, the wise and virtuous do not associate with them. For this reason, a bodhisattva should not eat meat."
"Mahāmati!
As for flesh and blood, they are rejected by the various ṛṣis and not consumed by the multitude of sages; therefore, a bodhisattva should not eat meat.
Mahāmati!"
To protect the faith of sentient beings and prevent them from giving rise to slander toward the Buddha-dharma, a bodhisattva, out of compassion, should not eat meat.
Mahāmati!
If my disciples were to eat meat, it would cause all people in the world to harbor slander, saying:

"How can these śramaṇas, practitioners of pure conduct, having abandoned the flavors consumed by celestial beings and sages, still roam the world with bellies full of meat like wicked beasts, causing all sentient beings to feel terror, destroying their pure conduct, and losing the path of a śramaṇa?"
"Therefore, you should know that within the Buddha-dharma there is no practice of subduing.
Out of compassion and for the sake of protecting sentient beings, the Bodhisattva causes them not to give rise to such thoughts; thus, one should not eat meat.
Mahāmati!
Just as the foul stench of burning human flesh is no different from that of burning other kinds of meat, why would there be any distinction between eating and not eating it?
Therefore, those who seek purity in all things should not eat meat. Mahāmati!

Whether they are virtuous men or women practicing in silence among graves, under trees, or in forest hermitages; whether they abide in a mind of loving-kindness, maintain incantations, seek liberation, or aspire to the Mahāyāna—because of eating meat, all such obstacles will prevent their accomplishments. For this reason, a Bodhisattva who wishes to benefit both self and others should not eat meat.
"Mahāmati!

As for those who eat meat, the mere sight of its form and color gives rise to a mind that craves its flavor. Since a Bodhisattva regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own body, how could he look upon them and conceive the thought of eating them?"
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not eat meat.

Mahāmati! Those who eat meat are shunned by the devas; their breath is perpetually foul; they experience unrest in sleep and anxiety upon waking; yakṣas and malevolent spirits steal away their vital energy; their minds are filled with frequent terror; they lack satiety in eating; they increase their illnesses and easily develop sores and scabs; they are constantly nibbled at by various insects; and they are unable to develop a deep sense of revulsion toward food.
"Mahāmati!
I have always said:
'In whatever one eats or consumes, one should conceive of it as the flesh of one's own child.'"
"If even leftover food is thus [prohibited], how can you permit your disciples to eat meat?
Mahāmati! Meat is not wholesome;
meat is impure. It gives rise to all manner of evils and ruins all virtues. Since it is something abandoned by all the seers and holy ones, how could you allow your disciples to eat it?"
If one were to say that eating is permitted, such a person slanders me.

Mahāmati, you should know that pure, excellent food consists of non-glutinous rice, millet, large and small wheat, beans, ghee, oil, and rock honey; such categories as these were permitted by the Buddhas of the past and are what I proclaim.

Those sons and daughters of good family within my lineage, who harbor pure faith and have long planted roots of goodness, who do not give rise to greedy attachment toward body, life, or wealth, and who regard all beings with compassion as they would themselves—the food appropriate for such persons is not what those of evil habits and the nature of tigers or wolves cherish.

“Mahāmati! In the past there was a king named Siṃhaprabha who was addicted to the taste of meat and ate various kinds of flesh. Not ceasing in this way, he eventually came to eat human beings; his ministers and subjects could no longer endure it and all rebelled against him, so that he lost his throne and suffered great affliction.”
Mahāmati!
Śakra Devendra, while occupying the position of the Heavenly King, because of residual habits from eating meat in the past, transformed himself into a hawk and pursued a dove.
"At that time, I was a king named Śibi; out of compassion for the pigeon, I cut flesh from my own body to spare its life.
Mahāmati, if even Śakra’s residual habits still afflict sentient beings, how much more so those who lack shame and constantly eat meat?"
You should know that eating meat brings suffering to oneself and distress to others; therefore, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati! Long ago, there was a king who went hunting on horseback.

His horse became startled and bolted, fleeing into a perilous mountain wilderness where there were no paths for return and no human habitation. There, he encountered a female lion with whom he lived together and committed lewd acts, subsequently fathering several sons. The eldest was named Pāṇḍu-pāda (斑足). Later, he became king and ruled over seven hundred million households. Due to the lingering habit of eating meat, he would not eat anything but flesh; first he ate birds and beasts, and later even humans. All the sons and daughters born to him were rākṣasas.

After this body has transmigrated, one will again be born among lions, jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, eagles, vultures, and the like; though one seeks a human body, it can never be obtained, let alone the path to nirvana that transcends birth and death.

“Mahāmati! Those who eat meat have such immeasurable faults as these; by renouncing it and not eating it, one attains great merit. Yet the ignorant and foolish do not understand such benefits and harms. Therefore, I now expound for you that all kinds of meat whatsoever should not be eaten.”
Mahāmati!
Those who take life do so mostly for human consumption; if humans did not eat it, there would be no killing. Therefore, eating meat is a sin equal to that of killing.

How strange it is that those in the world are so attached to the taste of flesh that they even take to eating the flesh of human beings; how much more so for birds and beasts, of which there are none who do not eat it? Driven by this craving for flavor, they employ a vast array of expedient means—setting out snares, nets, and traps everywhere—so that all creatures of water, land, and air are slaughtered. Even if they do not eat it themselves, they perform these deeds out of greed for its price.

“Mahāmati! Furthermore, there are people in the world who lack a heart of compassion and exclusively practice cruelty like rākṣasas; if they see a sentient being with a flourishing body, they immediately conceive the thought of meat and say, ‘This may be eaten.’”
"Mahāmati!

In this world, there is no meat that has not been killed by oneself or killed by another, nor is there any that one could eat without the mind harboring suspicion of its being killed for one's sake. For this reason, I permit the śrāvakas to eat such meat."
Mahāmati!

In future ages there will be foolish people who leave the household life within my Dharma, yet falsely proclaim the Vinaya to subvert and disorder the True Dharma; they will slander me, saying that I permit the eating of meat and have myself eaten it as well.
Mahāmati!

If I were to permit the śrāvakas to eat meat, I would not be one who dwells in a mind of loving-kindness, one who practices meditative cultivation, one who observes the dhūta ascetic practices, or one who is intent upon the Mahāyāna. How then could I exhort all sons and daughters of good family to conceive the thought of all sentient beings as their only child and to abstain from all meat?
"Mahāmati!
When I have taught in various places that ten kinds [of meat] are prohibited while permitting three kinds, it was for the purpose of gradual restriction so that they might practice and train;
however, in this sutra, all meat—whether from animals that died naturally or were killed by others—is entirely forbidden."
Mahāmati!
I have never permitted my disciples to eat meat; nor do I permit it now, nor shall I ever permit it in the future. Mahāmati!
"Whatever constitutes meat is entirely impure for renunciants. Mahāmati!

If there are deluded people who slanderously claim that the Tathāgata permits the eating of meat and even eats it himself, you should know that such persons are entangled by evil karma and will inevitably fall forever into states of no benefit."
Mahāmati!
Even my noble disciples do not consume the coarse food of ordinary beings, much less the impure food of flesh and blood.
Mahāmati!
If even śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas subsist solely on the food of dharma, how much more so the Tathāgata?
Mahāmati!
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a body sustained by impure food.

Mahāmati! I have severed all afflictions; I have washed away all habitual tendencies; I have skillfully discerned all mental states through wisdom; and with great compassion, I impartially regard all sentient beings as if they were my only child.
"How could you permit the śrāvaka disciples to eat the flesh of their own children,
let alone eat it themselves?
To speak in such a manner is impossible."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"All have once been our kin; They grow from a multitude of impurities.
They terrify all sentient beings; Therefore, one should not eat them."
All meats and onions, leeks, garlic, and various wines—
such impure things as these, the practitioner should avoid.
One should also always stay away from sesame oil and beds with perforated slats.
Because of those minute insects, one should feel great alarm and fear within;
food gives rise to negligence, and negligence gives rise to wrong thoughts;
from such thoughts arises craving—therefore, one should not eat.
Because false perceptions give rise to greed, the mind becomes intoxicated by craving;
with the mind intoxicated, one’s desire for existence grows long, and one is not liberated from birth and death.
To profit, one kills sentient beings, taking their flesh for the sake of wealth.
Both are evil karmas; upon death, one falls into the Raurava hell.
Not seeking, not commanding, and not requesting—these three types are called pure.
Such meat does not exist in the world; those who eat it, I condemn.
They devour one another, and upon death they fall among the evil beasts;
foul-smelling and insane—therefore, one should not eat [meat].
Hunters, caṇḍālas, butchers, and rākṣasas [arise from such acts].
Born from among these various species, all are the retribution for eating meat.
Having eaten it without shame or remorse, one shall be perpetually insane in every birth;
such persons are loathed by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas.
In the *Gajapramardana*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Aṅgulimālīya*,
and this *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I have in all cases prohibited the eating of meat.
First, regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, all meat-eating has already been abandoned;
yet because of their evil habits, the foolish engage in false discrimination.
Just as craving obstructs liberation, so too do meat and other such things.
If there are those who eat it, they shall not enter the Noble Path.
Beings of future ages will speak out of ignorance regarding meat, saying:
"This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it."
Even pure food is like medicine, And should be regarded as the flesh of one's own son;
Therefore, the practitioner Should know moderation when begging for alms.
Eating meat turns one away from liberation And violates the outward signs of a sage.
They cause living beings to feel fear; therefore, one should not eat them.
For those who abide in a mind of loving-kindness, I say they should always maintain a sense of weary detachment;
even with lions, tigers, and wolves, they should dwell and travel together.
"If one does not eat any [of these], such as alcohol, meat, and so forth, one will surely be born among the worthy and holy ones, possessing abundant wealth and wisdom.
Chapter 9: Dhāraṇī (6) The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra on Entering the Mahāyāna, Chapter Nine: Dhāraṇī At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:

“Mahāmati! The Buddhas of the past, future, and present, desiring to protect those who uphold this sutra, have all expounded the *Laṅkāvatāra* mantra; I now speak it as well, which you should receive and uphold.”
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

In future ages, if there are good men or good women who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this dhāraṇī for others, you should know that such persons shall not be harmed by any humans, non-humans, or various spirits.
Furthermore, if someone is suddenly struck by evil, and one recites it one hundred and eight times for them, the malevolent spirit will immediately flee in haste.”
"Mahāmati!
I shall further explain a dhāraṇī for you.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

If there are good men or good women who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this dhāraṇī for others, they shall not be taken advantage of by any evil ghosts or spirits, such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, or non-humans.

I have spoken this divine mantra for the purpose of restraining all rākṣasas; if one upholds this mantra, it is equivalent to upholding the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, with all its phrases and sentences fully complete.

Chapter Ten: The Chapter on Verses (6–7) The Tenth Chapter of the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra: The Beginning of the Chapter on Verses At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate the extensive meanings contained within this sūtra, spoke these verses:
"All dharmas are not solid; They all arise from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Since conceptual discrimination is itself empty, That which is discriminated does not exist."
Through false conceptualization, consciousnesses arise;
the eight or nine consciousnesses in their various forms are like the many waves upon the ocean.
Habitual tendencies constantly increase, rooted firmly and supported by a solid foundation.
The mind flows toward objects, like iron to a magnet.
The nature upon which sentient beings rely is free from all conceptual constructions and detached from both cognition and its objects;
through this transformation of the basis, one attains liberation.
Attaining the illusion-like samādhi, one transcends the ten stages;
when observing the mind-king, both conceptualization and consciousness are left far behind.
At that time, the mind undergoes transformation and reliance (āśraya-parāvṛtti), which is itself eternal abiding.
Abiding in the Lotus Palace, which arises from the realm of illusion,
once established in that palace, one acts with mastery and effortless spontaneity;
benefiting all sentient beings like a mani jewel reflecting myriad colors.

All phenomena are without arising; they are also not non-existent.

Due to the accumulation of beginningless [tendencies], one discriminates various conceptual proliferations;

Because of the false conceptualization of self-nature, all phenomena are unborn;
yet, relying upon dependent origination, sentient beings are deluded by discrimination.
When discrimination does not correspond [to reality], that which is dependent on others is itself pure.
The abode is free from conceptual construction; the transformation of the basis is suchness itself.

Regarding the various external objects of wrong views: there are no objects, for they are but mind.
When observed correctly and with right insight, both the grasped object and the grasping subject are extinguished.
Just as the ignorant conceptualize, external objects do not truly exist;

Having extinguished the two types of conceptualization, wisdom accords with suchness;
arising from the absence of images, it is the inconceivable sphere of the noble ones.
Depending on the union of father and mother, it is like ghee contained within a vessel.

Five, five, and five; there are nine types of orifices and wounds.

to eliminate this delusion, names and conventions are established.
Fools discriminate among all phenomena and become confused by these names.
And those produced through various conditions—these are the three kinds of conceptualization.

since their intrinsic nature is non-existent, this is called the characteristic of false imagination (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).
Like an illusion, a mirage, a reflection, a dream, or a fire-wheel;
like an echo or a city of the gandharvas—this is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Suchness, emptiness, non-duality, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and the dharma-nature (dharmatā);
All are devoid of conceptual discrimination; I call this the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The range of speech and the activity of the mind are false and fall into the two extremes;
when wisdom discriminates the ultimate truth, that wisdom is non-conceptual.
It appears to the wise, yet does not appear to the foolish;
thus, that which appears to wisdom is that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*).
Like a golden necklace made of imitation gold, it is not gold, yet the foolish call it gold.
All phenomena are likewise thus, yet non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize them.
All phenomena have neither beginning nor end; they abide in the mark of reality.
The world is entirely without agency, yet through false conceptualization, people cannot comprehend this.
All phenomena of the past, those of the future, and those of the present—
all such phenomena are entirely without arising.
Because they arise from the conjunction of various conditions, they are therefore said to exist.
If separated from their combination, they neither arise nor cease.

briefly described, they are "arising," and explained in detail, they are "ceasing."
One is the emptiness of non-arising, and one is the emptiness of arising;

Suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, nirvana, and the dharma-realm—these are likewise so.
The various types of mind-made bodies—these I say are all but different names.

Sentient beings engage in false discrimination, and what they perceive is like a rabbit's horn.
Discrimination is itself delusion, like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage.
Due to false attachment, discrimination arises.
If one is free from the causes of deluded attachment, then conceptual discrimination does not arise.
This profound, vast, and extensive [teaching], which knows all lands with mastery—

For the sake of the śrāvakas, I have thus explained these general characteristics.
Non-attached to all phenomena, Tranquil, pure, and practiced in solitude;
Thinking of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, I speak for the sake of such persons:

All conditions are without arising, and all sense faculties are non-existent.

There is no time and no nirvana; the nature of dharmas cannot be apprehended.
There is no Buddha and no ultimate truth; there is neither cause nor fruit.
Neither inversion nor nirvāṇa, neither birth nor cessation;
There are no twelve links, and neither the finite nor the infinite exists.
All views are severed—this I declare to be Mind-only.
Afflictions, karma, and the body, As well as the fruits obtained from karma—
All are like a flame, like a dream, And like a city of the gandharvas.
Because they abide in mind-only, All phenomenal marks are relinquished.
Because one abides in mind-only, one is able to see [the extremes of] annihilation and permanence.
In nirvāṇa there are no aggregates; there is no self and no marks.
By entering into mind-only, one effects the transformation of the basis and attains liberation.
Because of the cause of evil habitual tendencies, the external world appears as the great earth and all sentient beings;
yet it is only mind, with nothing to be seen.
The images of bodies, possessions, and lands are what appear through the habitual tendencies of sentient beings.
The mind is neither existent nor non-existent; habitual tendencies cause it not to manifest.
Defilements appear within purity, yet purity does not appear within defilement;
just as clouds obscure the void sky, so too the mind fails to manifest.
The imagined nature is held to exist, yet it does not exist within dependent origination;
because of deluded attachment to the imagined, dependent origination is without conceptual differentiation.
Not all that is produced is form, yet there is form that is not produced.
Like a dream, an illusion, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas, these things are not created.
If one regards dependently arisen phenomena as either real or unreal,
that person will certainly rely on views such as identity and difference.
There are three kinds of śrāvakas: those who aspire for rebirth, those who are emanations, and those who are free from greed, hatred, and so forth, arising from the Dharma.
There are likewise three kinds of bodhisattvas: those who do not yet possess the marks of a Buddha;
Thinking of sentient beings, he manifests in the form of a Buddha.
What appears to the minds of sentient beings arises entirely from habitual tendencies;
these various images are like stars, clouds, the sun, and the moon.
If the primary elements (mahābhūta) existed, then the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) could arise;
but because the primary elements lack intrinsic nature, there is neither the characteristic nor that which is characterized.
The primary elements are the creators, while earth and the others are the created.
The great elements are fundamentally unarisen; therefore, there are no derived forms.
Whether they be conventional or substantial forms, or forms created by illusion;
the forms of dreams, the forms of the city of the gandharvas, and the forms of mirages as the fifth.
There are five kinds of icchantikas, and likewise five kinds of spiritual lineages;
there are the five vehicles and that which is not a vehicle, and six kinds of nirvana;
there are twenty-four aggregates and eight kinds of form.
There are twenty-four Buddhas, and two kinds of sons of the Buddha.
There are one hundred and eight Dharma gates, and three kinds of śrāvakas.
The buddha-fields of all Buddhas are but one, and the single Buddha is likewise so.
There are three kinds of liberation, four streams of the mind,
six kinds of selflessness, and likewise four objects of knowledge;
they are far removed from an agent and free from all views of extremes.
Internally self-realized and immovable, this is the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
Regarding birth and non-birth, there are eight kinds and nine kinds;
whether attained in a single thought-moment or through gradual stages, the principle of realization is one alone.
The formless realm has eight types; the distinctions of dhyāna are six;
for pratyekabuddhas and the sons of the Buddhas, there are seven modes of renunciation.
In the three times, none of these exist; neither permanence nor impermanence exists either.
Karma and its retribution are all like matters within a dream.

The Buddhas are fundamentally unborn; for the sake of the sons of the Buddha who are śrāvakas, their minds are constantly unable to perceive them, because [the Buddhas] are like illusory phenomena and the like.
Therefore, in all lands, he descends from Tuṣita into the womb;
at his birth and renunciation, he does not arise from a place of birth.
For the sake of wandering sentient beings, he speaks of nirvāṇa.
The various truths and lands are made to be awakened to according to the capacities of beings.
The world, its continents, trees, and forests; the non-self and the practices of external paths;
dhyāna-yāna and the ālayavijñāna; the fruit and the inconceivable realm.
The various classes of lunar mansions, the lineages of kings and devas,
the gandharvas and yakṣas— all are born from karma and craving.
Even the inconceivable death of transformation is still accompanied by habitual tendencies.
When death has reached its ultimate end and the net of afflictions is severed, one should not possess wealth, grain, gold, or silver; fields, houses, or servants;
nor elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and the like.
One should not sleep on a perforated bed, nor on ground smeared with mud;
bowls made of gold, silver, or copper—none of these should be kept.
[Bows] made of earth, stone, iron, conch, or crystal [are permitted].
To the extent that it fills the Magadha measure, one is permitted to keep it for the sake of the bowl.
One should always use colors such as blue, or cow-dung mud and fruit leaves,
to dye white *kṣaumpaka* cloth and other materials into the color of the *kāṣāya*.
A knife four finger-widths long, shaped like a half-moon,
for the purpose of cutting and tailoring robes— this the practitioner is permitted to keep.
One should not study the arts and crafts, nor should one engage in buying or selling.
If one must employ a *kappiya-kāraka*, this is the method I have taught:
always guarding the sense faculties, being well-versed in the meaning of the Sūtras and Vinaya,
and not associating with worldly people— such a person is called a practitioner.
Beneath trees and in mountain caves, in wilderness huts and among burial mounds,
in grass huts and in the open air— there the practitioner should dwell.
Whether at a cemetery or elsewhere, the three robes should always remain close at hand.
If one is lacking robes, one should accept what is offered.
When going out on alms-round, look ahead only a fathom’s distance;
collecting mindfulness while begging for food, like a bee gathering nectar from flowers.
In places where crowds gather, where various bhikṣuṇīs congregate,
where one makes a living by socializing with the laity— in all such places, one should not beg for alms.
This includes the presence of kings and princes, ministers and elders.
When a practitioner begs for alms, they should not approach any of these:
the homes of those recently born or recently deceased, the homes of close friends or loved ones, and households where monks and nuns mingle. A practitioner does not eat from such places.
In the monastery, the smoke never ceases; They constantly prepare various kinds of food, Whether made by themselves or commissioned by others— The practitioner does not eat such things.
The practitioner contemplates the world: The characteristic and that which is characterized;
All are entirely free from arising and ceasing, and likewise free from existence and non-existence.
*The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Six;
*The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Zhou Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Ten: Verses in Praise, Part Two. "If practitioners do not give rise to conceptual discrimination;..."
Before long, one attains samādhi, as well as powers, superknowledges, and mastery.
A practitioner should not falsely cling to the notions that the world arises from atoms, from time, from primordial nature (prakṛti), or from a creator; rather, it is born of dependent origination.
The world arises from one's own conceptualization, produced by various habitual tendencies;
the practitioner should contemplate that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions.
One should constantly see them as being free from both deprecation and reification.
Regarding the body, its requisites, and its dwelling, one does not discriminate among the three realms of existence.
Without thoughts of food or drink, one dwells with right mindfulness and an upright body;
repeatedly and with reverence, one pays homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Skillfully understanding the true principles within the sūtras and vinaya—
the five dharmas and the two kinds of selflessness— and likewise contemplating one's own mind;
internally realizing the pure nature of phenomena (dharmatā), as well as the various stages (bhūmis) and the stage of Buddhahood.
The practitioner cultivates this, receiving the consecration amidst lotuses;
sinking through the various realms of existence, they grow weary of all conditioned being;
going to cemeteries and secluded places, they cultivate various meditative practices.
To claim that things arise without cause, while falsely asserting this is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence,
and further claiming it is free from existence and non-existence, recklessly designating it as the Middle Way—
this false reckoning of a theory of no-cause is itself the view of annihilationism.
Because they do not understand external objects, they destroy the Middle Way.
Fearing they might fall into the view of nihilism, they do not relinquish their grasped dharmas;
through their establishment and denigration, they falsely claim [their views] to be the Middle Way.
By awakening to the fact that there is only mind, one abandons external phenomena;
by further abandoning false discrimination, this practice accords with the Middle Way.
Since there is only mind, there are no objects; since there are no objects, the mind does not arise.
I and all the Tathāgatas declare this to be the Middle Way:
whether arising or non-arising, having intrinsic nature or lacking intrinsic nature;
existence, non-existence, and so forth are all empty, and one should not differentiate between these two.
Unable to give rise to discernment, the foolish claim they have attained liberation;
yet when no wisdom arises in the mind, how can one sever the two types of grasping?
By awakening to one’s own mind, one is able to sever the two objects of grasping.
Through thorough understanding, one is able to sever [delusion]; it is not through a lack of discernment.
By thoroughly knowing that which is manifested by the mind, discrimination no longer arises;
because discrimination does not arise, the mind undergoes the transformation of the basis into True Suchness (*tathatā*).
If one perceives the dharmas that arise, free from the errors of all non-Buddhists;
this is what the wise grasp: Nirvāṇa is not annihilation.
I and all Buddhas declare: awakening to this is itself Buddhahood.
If one were to engage in further conceptual differentiation, this would be the discourse of non-Buddhists.
Without arising, there is apparent arising; without ceasing, there is apparent cessation.
Throughout billions of lands, it appears instantaneously, like the moon reflected in water.
A single body becomes many bodies; emitting fire and pouring down rain—these appear within the mind according to its conditions;
therefore, it is said that "it is mind alone.
Mind itself is also mind-alone; even that which is not mind arises from the mind.
The various kinds of forms and appearances— All are understood to be but mind alone.
The images of the Buddhas and Śrāvakas, As well as those of the Pratyekabuddhas,
And all other diverse forms— All are said to be but mind alone.
From the formless realm down to the depths of hell,
they manifest everywhere for the sake of sentient beings— all of which are created by mind alone.
Such are the various illusory samādhis and the mind-made bodies.
The ten stages and spiritual mastery are all attained through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Fools are bound by signs; they follow what is seen, heard, sensed, and known.
Driven by their own inverted conceptualizations, they are moved by idle proliferation (*prapañca*).
All things are empty and unarisen; I truly do not enter nirvana.
Emanated Buddhas in all lands proclaim the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
There are thirty-six Buddhas, each further possessing ten kinds.
According to the mental capacities of sentient beings, He manifests various buddha-fields.
The Dharma-Buddha in the world Is like the nature of false conceptualization;
Though various forms appear to be seen, In reality, nothing exists at all.
The Dharma-Buddha is the true Buddha; all others are transformation Buddhas.
According to the seeds of sentient beings, they perceive the bodies manifested by the Buddha.
Because they are deluded regarding various marks, they give rise to conceptual discrimination.
Discrimination is not different from reality, yet the characteristics are not identical to discrimination.
The nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), and the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) further manifest transformations;
these thirty-six Buddha-qualities are all accomplished by the nature body.
From seeds perfumed by external objects, discrimination arises;
one does not grasp at reality, but grasps at what is falsely imagined.
Delusion relies upon the internal mind and takes external objects as its conditions.
It arises solely from these two, with no third condition.
Once delusion has arisen, depending on the internal and external, it becomes sixty, twenty-eight, and so forth; therefore, I call it "mind."
Knowing that there are only faculties and objects, one is then free from the grasping at a self;
realizing that the mind has no objective realm, one is then free from the grasping at phenomena.
Because they rely upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the various consciousnesses arise.
Due to reliance upon the internal sense bases, there appear external-like reflections;
through the constant conceptualization of the ignorant,
both the conditioned and the unconditioned are entirely unattainable, like a dream, a star, or a mass of falling hairs.
Like a city of Gandharvas, like an illusion, a mirage, or water in a flame—though non-existent, they appear to exist; so too is the nature of dependently arisen phenomena.
Based on the three types of mind, I provisionally designate the sense faculties, objects, and the self.
Yet that mind, thought, and consciousness have no self-nature whatsoever.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness—non-selfhood is of two kinds;
the five dharmas and the self-natures: these are the realm of the Buddhas.
The habit-energy, being a single cause, gives rise to the three characteristics;
just as with a single color, one sees various forms upon a painted wall.
The five dharmas, the two kinds of selflessness, the intrinsic nature, mind, thought, and consciousness;
Within the Buddha-lineage, nothing at all can be found.
It is far removed from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and likewise free from the five dharmas;
further, it is detached from intrinsic nature—this is the Buddha-lineage.
If one does not cultivate pure and white dharmas through the actions of body, speech,
and mind, then the Tathāgata’s pure lineage will be separated from manifest activity.
With mastery over the power of supernatural faculties and adorned by the purity of samādhi, [one attains liberation].
The various kinds of mind-born bodies are the Buddha’s pure lineage;
internally self-realized and stainless, they are far removed from causal characteristics.
These, belonging to the eighth stage and the Buddha-stage, are accomplished through the nature of the Tathāgata.
The stage of Far-Reaching, the stage of Good Wisdom, The stage of Dharma-Cloud, and the Buddha-stage— These are all the lineage of the Buddhas;
All others are subsumed within the two vehicles.
The Tathāgata’s mind is sovereign, yet for the sake of all foolish beings,
Due to the distinctions in the characteristics of the mind, seven stages are taught.
In the seventh stage, the faults of body, speech, and mind do not arise;
the support for the eighth stage is like crossing a river in a dream and so forth.
On the eighth and fifth stages, they master the science of arts and crafts;
these sons of the Buddhas are able to act as kings among all beings.
The wise do not discriminate between whether things arise or do not arise.
Emptiness and non-emptiness, intrinsic nature and the absence of intrinsic nature—
all these are merely the measure of the mind, and in reality they cannot be apprehended.
For the sake of those of the two vehicles, it is said that "this is real" and "that is false."
It is not for the sake of the sons of the Buddha that one should engage in conceptual differentiation.
Both existence and non-existence are entirely non-existent; there is also no characteristic of momentariness.
Neither provisional nor substantial dharmas exist; mind alone cannot be apprehended.
The existence of phenomena is conventional truth; the absence of intrinsic nature is the ultimate meaning.
To be deluded regarding this absence of intrinsic nature is precisely what constitutes the conventional.
All phenomena are empty; it is for the sake of all the ignorant and foolish that I [teach].
Following worldly convention, they are provisionally designated, yet they possess no reality.
Because phenomena arise from speech, there is the meaning of their activity;
yet when one observes that which is produced by speech, all of it is found to be unobtainable.
Just as there is no painting apart from a wall, nor a reflection apart from its substance;
if the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is purified, the waves of the various consciousnesses will not arise.
Based on the dharma-body (dharmakāya), there is the reward-body (sambhogakāya); from the reward-body, the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) arises.
This is the fundamental Buddha; all others are manifestations of transformation.
One should not engage in false discrimination regarding emptiness or non-emptiness;
by falsely conceptualizing existence and non-existence, the meaning of words cannot be found.
Ordinary fools engage in false discrimination, [thinking] that the aggregates of atoms are real forms;
yet each and every atom is non-existent, and for this reason there are no objective realms.
That sentient beings perceive external appearances is entirely due to the manifestation of their own minds.
Since that which is perceived is not existent, there are thus no external objects.
Like an elephant mired in deep mud, unable to move again;
so it is with the Śrāvakas dwelling in samādhi, submerged in darkness and delusion.
If one perceives all worlds as having habitual tendencies as their cause,
One is liberated through the selflessness of phenomena, which is free from existence, non-existence, and both.
Intrinsic nature is called "imagined construction," while dependent origination is the "other-dependent."
Suchness is the perfected nature; this I have constantly taught in my sūtras.

Mind, mentation, and consciousness, as well as discrimination and representation—the foundational consciousness that produces the three realms of existence—are all merely different names for the mind.
Life-span, warmth, and consciousness; the ālaya and the life-faculty;
the manas and the mental consciousness—these are all distinct names for the same thing.
The mind (citta) is able to sustain the body, while the manas constantly engages in deliberation.
The mental consciousness arises together with all the [other] consciousnesses, cognizing the objects of its own mind.
If a real self-entity existed— whether distinct from the aggregates or within the aggregates—
one would seek that self-entity therein, yet it could never be found.
Observing each and every world, one sees that all are manifestations of one's own mind;
by regarding the latent tendencies of affliction as such, one attains liberation from suffering.
For the Śrāvaka, this is the knowledge of exhaustion; for the Pratyekabuddha, it is the wisdom of tranquility.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata arises without end.
Externally there is no such thing as form; it is merely what is manifested by one's own mind.
Fools do not realize this, and thus they falsely discriminate conditioned phenomena.
Not knowing that external objects are in every way but one's own mind,
the deluded use causes and analogies to establish them through the four logical alternatives.
The wise fully understand that objects are manifestations of one's own mind.
It is not established by means of propositions, reasons, or examples;
the distinction between the subject and the object of cognition is the characteristic of false conceptualization.
Relying upon this false conceptualization, further conceptualization arises.
Arising in succession and mutually dependent, all are caused by a single habitual tendency (*vāsanā*);
these two are both adventitious and do not arise from the mind of a sentient being.
Abiding within the three realms, they are the conceptualizations of mind and mental factors.
That which arises appearing as an objective realm is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The images and their seeds combined constitute the twelve bases (*āyatana*);
the union of the support and the object is said to constitute the performance of activity.
Just as an image appears in a mirror, Or as one with cataracts sees floating hairs;
So too, obscured by habitual tendencies, Ordinary beings give rise to false views.
Regarding the objects of their own conceptualization, They further give rise to discrimination.
Just as non-Buddhists discriminate, external objects cannot be found.
Just as a fool who does not recognize a rope mistakenly grasps it as a snake;
failing to understand that what appears is the manifestation of one's own mind, one falsely discriminates external objects.
Thus, the self-nature of the rope is devoid of both unity and difference;
it is only through the delusions of one's own mind that the false discrimination of a "rope" arises.
When one falsely discriminates and conceptualizes, its nature does not exist.
How can one perceive what does not exist and yet give rise to conceptual construction?
The nature of form is non-existent, and the same is true for jars, garments, and so forth;
they arise merely from conceptual construction, and that which is perceived ultimately has no existence.
“In the beginningless conditioned realm, delusion gives rise to discrimination;
by what cause does this delusion arise?
I pray that the Buddha will explain this to me.”
"All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; they are manifested solely by the mind.
Failing to understand that they are one's own mind, one therefore gives rise to conceptual discrimination."
As is conceptually constructed by the foolish, that which is falsely imagined does not exist in reality;
yet they cannot know that which exists apart from this.
That which belongs to the noble ones is not what is conceptually constructed by the foolish.
If the noble were the same as the ordinary, the noble would possess falsehood.
Because the noble purify the mind, they are free from delusion;
because the minds of the foolish and ignorant are impure, they harbor false discrimination.
As a mother says to her infant: "Do not weep;
there are fruits in the sky, of every variety, for you to take as you please.
So do I speak to sentient beings of various fruits of false conceptualization.
Having caused them to take delight [in this], [one explains that] the reality of phenomena is free from existence and non-existence.
All phenomena did not previously exist; the various conditions were not in conjunction.
Originally unarisen yet arising, their intrinsic nature is non-existent.
Unarisen phenomena do not arise; apart from conditions, there is no place for arising.
Presently arising phenomena are likewise; apart from conditions, they cannot be found.
Contemplating the essential principle of actual dependent origination, one finds it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Neither existence nor non-existence, nor both, nor neither— The wise do not engage in such conceptualization.
Foolish outsiders falsely speak of identity and difference;
They fail to understand that all dependent arisings Are like illusions and dreams in this world.
My unsurpassed Mahāyāna transcends names and expressions;
its meaning is exceedingly clear, yet the foolish do not perceive it.
What is spoken by the śrāvakas and the non-Buddhists is all characterized by stinginess.
All meanings are completely transformed, arising entirely from false conceptualization.
Regarding characteristics and intrinsic nature, as well as form and name—
by clinging to these four kinds, various discriminations arise.
Even if one calculates that Brahmā or Maheśvara created them— whether as a single body or many bodies—
or even the movement of the sun and moon, they are not my sons.
They are endowed with noble vision and have attained mastery over the Dharma as it truly is.
Skillfully transforming all perceptions, one reaches the further shore of consciousness.
By means of this seal of liberation, one is forever free from existence and non-existence, as well as from coming and going; such a person is a child of my Dharma.
If the consciousness of form were to cease and all karmas were to perish,
then there would be neither birth and death, nor permanence and impermanence.
Yet, at the time of that cessation, although the sphere of form is abandoned;
Karma abides in the ālayavijñāna, free from the faults of existence and non-existence.
Although form and consciousness undergo transformation and cessation, karma is neither lost nor destroyed;
it causes form and consciousness to continue in succession throughout all states of existence.
If those sentient beings were to lose the karma they have initiated,
then there would be neither birth and death nor nirvāṇa.
If karma, form, and consciousness were to perish simultaneously;
If birth were to occur within the cycle of birth and death, then form and karma would have no distinction.
Form, mind, and discrimination are neither different nor not different;
fools claim they are subject to destruction, yet in reality they are free from existence and non-existence.
Dependent origination and false conceptualization are mutually devoid of distinct characteristics;
just as form and impermanence are related through mutual production, so it is here.
Since they are neither different nor non-different, false conceptualization cannot be known.
Just as form has the nature of impermanence, how can one speak of its existence or non-existence?
One who thoroughly understands false conceptualization finds that dependent origination is non-arising;
by seeing dependent origination, false conceptualization is itself suchness.
If one were to negate the nature of false conceptualization, This would destroy the eye of the Dharma;
Consequently, within my teaching, One would engage in both establishment and slander.
Persons of such a kind Shall revile and slander the True Dharma.
They all, by means of what is not the Dharma, destroy my eye of the Dharma.
The wise should not converse with them, nor should they attend to the affairs of such bhikṣus;
for they destroy right reflection and establish slander.
If one follows after conceptual discrimination, giving rise to views of existence and non-existence,
that person is like a phantom, a net of hair, a dream, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas.
Such a person does not study the Buddha-dharma and should not dwell together with them.
Because one falls into the two extremes oneself and also ruins others; therefore,
if there is a practitioner who contemplates the nature of false conceptualization—
tranquil and free from existence and non-existence— one should embrace them and dwell together with them.
Just as there are places in the world where gold and mani-jewels are found;
though they are not produced by any deliberate effort, sentient beings nevertheless enjoy them.
The nature of karma is likewise: it is utterly free from any manifold nature.
The karma that is perceived does not exist, yet it is not that the various realms of existence do not arise.
As the Noble Ones realize, all phenomena are non-existent;
yet what is conceptualized by the foolish, their false imputations, are not non-existent.
If those phenomena discriminated by the ignorant do not exist,
then since all phenomena are absent, sentient beings would have no defilement.
Yet because there are phenomena that cause defilement, they are bound by ignorance and craving.
It can give rise to the body of birth and death, with all its faculties fully complete.
If one claims that these dharmas are all non-existent due to the discrimination of the ignorant, then the faculties would not arise; such a person is not practicing correctly.
If these dharmas did not exist as the cause of birth and death,
the foolish would be liberated spontaneously without needing cultivation.
If those dharmas did not exist, how could there be a distinction between the ordinary person and the sage?
Thus there would be no noble ones practicing the three liberations;
the aggregates, persons, and dharmas, as well as their specific and general characteristics and lack of characteristics,
along with all conditions and sense faculties— these I have taught for the sake of the śrāvakas.
Mind-only and the absence of external causes, the various stages and sovereign mastery;
the inner realization of pure *tathatā*—these I have taught for the sake of my sons.
In future ages, there will be those who wear the saffron robes;
Those who falsely speak of existence and non-existence destroy my true Dharma.
The natureless nature of dependent origination is the sphere of activity for the noble ones;
the imagined nature is a non-entity, yet those who engage in conceptualization discriminate it.
In the future, there will be ignorant ones, the Keṇa heretics, who propound theories of non-causality;
with their evil views, they will destroy the world.
They falsely claim that all worlds arise from atoms.
Yet those objects are without cause; the nine kinds of substantial entities are eternal.
From substance, substance is produced; from quality, quality can arise.
True dharmatā is different from this; they slander it by saying it does not exist.
If that which was originally non-existent were to arise, then the world would have a beginning;
yet I have taught that birth and death have no prior limit.
That all things within the three realms arise from what was originally non-existent—[this is my teaching].
If camels, donkeys, and dogs were to grow horns, there would likewise be no cause for doubt.
Since the eye, forms, and visual consciousness are fundamentally non-existent, yet now they arise;
then clothes, caps, mats, and the like should likewise be produced from a lump of clay.
Just as there is no mat within the threads, nor is there a mat within the reeds;
why then does the mat not arise from each and every one of its conditions?
If that life-principle and the body were originally non-existent and then came into being;
I have already stated before that those [views] are all the doctrines of non-Buddhists;
my previously stated tenets were intended to refute their positions.
Having refuted them, I shall then explain my own school’s doctrine.
Fearing that my disciples might become deluded by the tenets of existence and non-existence,
I therefore first taught them the treatises of the non-Buddhists.
Kāpila, with his evil intellect, taught these to his own disciples.
The world arises from Primal Nature (Prakṛti), which undergoes transformation through its qualities (guṇas).
Since conditions do not exist, there is nothing that has already arisen nor anything currently arising;
since conditions are not truly conditions, there is neither arising nor non-arising.
