Our school is free from existence and non-existence, and likewise free from all causes and conditions;
it is utterly remote from arising and ceasing, as well as from the characterized and its characteristics.
The world is like a phantom or a dream; all causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature.
Constantly practicing such contemplation, Discrimination will never arise again.
If one can contemplate all modes of existence As being like a flame or a mass of floating hairs,
And like a city of Gandharvas, One will forever be free from both existence and non-existence.
When causes and conditions are both abandoned, the mind is made entirely pure;
yet if one says that external objects do not exist and that there is only mind,
then in the absence of objects there is no mind— how, then, can "consciousness-only" be established?
Because there is an objective referent, the minds of sentient beings arise.
Without a cause, the mind would not be produced; how then could it be established as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*)?
Suchness (*tathatā*) and mere consciousness are the sphere of activity for all the Noble Ones.
To say that this exists when it does not exist—such people do not understand my Dharma.
Because of the grasped and the grasper, the mind arises.
Since the worldly mind is thus, it is not "mind-only."
The body, its requisites, the land, and reflected images—like a dream, they arise from the mind.
Although the mind appears as two parts, the mind itself possesses no duality;
it is like a blade that cannot cut itself, or a finger that cannot touch itself.
Yet the mind does not see itself, and its objects are likewise so;
where there is no locus for reflected images, there is no dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
The imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is also non-existent; thus the five dharmas and the two minds are exhausted.
The producer and the produced are both manifestations of one’s own mind.
It is with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that they are called "producers," yet in reality they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
for various objective forms arise from false conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
Space and the horns of a rabbit should also constitute objective appearances;
since objects arise from the mind, these objects are not false imaginings.
Yet those falsely imagined objects cannot be found apart from the mind.
Within beginningless birth and death, objects do not exist at all.
Since the mind has no place of arising, how could it form images?
If things could arise without existing, then even a rabbit’s horns should arise.
Nothing can arise without an object, yet it originates from conceptual construction;
just as the appearing object does not exist, so too did it not exist previously.
How, then, could the mind arise by taking an object as its focal point within a state where no object exists?
Suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, Nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm—
The non-arising of all phenomena Is the nature of the ultimate truth;
Fools fall into existence and non-existence, And conceptualize various causes and conditions.
"One cannot know the various realms of existence, for they are without birth and without an agent;
the causes of the mind from beginningless time are but mind itself, with nothing to be seen.
"Since there are no objects from beginningless time, from what could the mind arise?"
If something could arise without any entity, then a poor person would surely be rich.
If the mind arises without an object, I pray that the Buddha will explain this to me;
for if everything were without cause, there would be neither mind nor object.
"Since the mind has nothing from which it arises, it is free from the activities of the three realms of existence;
yet, based on things such as jars, garments, and horns, one speaks of the non-existence of a rabbit's horn."
Therefore, one should not say that there are no phenomena caused by those marks;
for if something exists without a cause, its non-existence cannot be established as non-existent.
The same applies to dependent non-existence: they arise through mutual dependence on one another.
If, depending on a small dharma, a small dharma arises,
then that which was previously depended upon would exist of itself without a cause;
if that [first] support has another support, then that support must likewise have a support.
In this way, there would be no end, nor would there be even the slightest phenomenon;
just as various illusory forms appear based on wood, leaves, and so forth,
so too do sentient beings appear in various ways based on things.
Relying on the power of a magician, The deluded perceive illusory forms;
Yet within the wood, leaves, and so forth, No illusion can actually be found.
If one relies upon [the existence of] things, Then this Dharma will be destroyed.
Since that which is seen is non-dual, how could there be even the slightest discrimination?
When discrimination is free from false conceptualization, discrimination itself does not exist.
Because discrimination is absent, there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
Because there is no conceptualization, conceptualization does not arise.
How can it be that the mind does not arise, yet "mind-only" exists?
The various distinctions of the mental faculty are immeasurable, yet none possess any truly real dharma.
There is no reality and no liberation, nor are there any worlds;
as the ignorant discriminate, all that is seen externally does not exist.
The mind, turbid by habitual tendencies, appears like a reflected image.
All phenomena, such as existence and non-existence, are entirely unarisen.
They are merely manifestations of one's own mind and are free from conceptual discrimination;
to say that phenomena arise from conditions is for the sake of the ignorant, not for the wise.
The nature of the mind is liberated by itself; it is the pure mind in which the noble ones dwell.
Those who follow the systems of Saṃkhya, Jaina nudity, Brahmanism, and Īśvara—all fall into the view of non-existence and remain far removed from the meaning of tranquility.
"Unborn and without intrinsic nature, Stainless, empty, and like an illusion.
"For whom did the Buddhas of the past and the present Buddha speak thus?"
"The practitioner of pure mind Is free from all views and conceptual constructions.
"The Buddhas have taught this for them, And I likewise teach it:
If everything is but mind, Where does the world abide?"
For what reason do we see the great earth, and sentient beings coming and going?
Like birds soaring through the void, they follow their conceptualizations as they go.
Without support and without dwelling, they move like one walking upon the ground.
Sentient beings are likewise; following deluded discrimination, they roam within their own minds like birds in the sky.
The bodies, requisites, and lands are but shadows; the Buddha taught that they arise solely from the mind.
“Please explain how reflections are but mind; by what cause do they arise, and in what manner?
The reflections of body, possessions, and the land all arise through the transformation of habitual tendencies.”
It also arises from improper mental construction;
external objects are mere false imaginings, and the mind arises by taking those objects as its condition.
When one realizes that objects are merely mind, such mental construction no longer arises.
If one perceives that the nature of false conceptualization is the non-union of name and referent,
and remains far removed from the perceiver and the perceived, one is liberated from all conditioned phenomena;
having relinquished both name and referent— this is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
If one seeks awakening apart from this, there is no awareness of self or other;
if one can see the world as free from the subject that perceives and the object perceived,
then at that time, the conceptualization of "name" and "named" will not arise.
By seeing one's own mind, the false construction of names and concepts ceases.
Failing to see one's own mind, one gives rise to that discrimination;
yet the four aggregates have no form or characteristics, and their number cannot be apprehended.
The great elements (mahābhūta) each have distinct natures; how could they together produce form?
Since they are devoid of all characteristics, neither the primary nor the derived exist.
If form had a separate characteristic apart from them, why would the aggregates (skandha) not also arise?
If one perceives the signless, one abandons all aggregates and sense-bases.
At that time, the mind is also liberated, because one perceives the selflessness of phenomena;
due to the distinctions between faculties and objects, the eight kinds of consciousness arise.
Within that signlessness, these three characteristics are all absent;
the mind, taking the ālaya as its object, gives rise to grasping at "I" and "mine.
Furthermore, regarding the two types of grasping by consciousness, one should understand that they are all utterly transcended.
Observing that which is free from unity and difference, one is then unmoved.
Free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," as well as the two kinds of false conceptualization;
there is no arising and no growth, nor does it serve as a cause for consciousness.
"Since it is free from agent and action, having ceased, it does not arise again;
the world has no creator, and is devoid of the characteristics of agent and object.
"Regarding false conceptualization and 'mind-only,' how should I explain this for you?"
"Various things manifest from one's own mind; one discriminates their various forms and characteristics.
Failing to understand what is manifested by the mind, one falsely grasps at them as being external to the mind.
Because of a lack of wisdom and awakening, the view of non-existence arises."
How can one not give rise to attachment toward existence?
By discerning that neither existence nor non-existence truly exists, one does not give rise to [the notion of] existence.
Realizing that what is seen is but mind, conceptualization then does not arise.
Because conceptual discrimination does not arise, the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is free from attachment.
Thus, one negates the four tenets—namely, that phenomena have causes and so forth;
these are merely different names for the same thing, and what they establish is entirely unestablished.
One should know that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is likewise not established;
it is to negate such an efficient cause that the "conjunction of conditions" (*pratyaya-sāmagrī*) is taught.
To negate the fault of permanence, it is said that conditions are impermanent.
Fools say there is impermanence, yet in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Without perceiving the nature of disintegration, one is able to perform actions;
how could there be an impermanent dharma that is capable of being produced?
Devas, humans, and asuras, ghosts, animals, and those in Yama’s realm;
sentient beings born within these— I call them the six realms.
According to karma that is superior, middling, or inferior, they take birth therein.
"By guarding all wholesome dharmas, one attains supreme liberation.
"The Buddha has taught the monks concerning their rebirths;
that every thought-moment arises and perishes—please explain this for me."
“Form does not remain for even a moment, and the mind likewise arises and perishes;
I have taught my disciples that the aggregates arise and pass away with every thought.”
In each and every form there is discrimination; arising and ceasing are likewise so.
Discrimination belongs to sentient beings; apart from discrimination, nothing exists.
For this reason, I say that [all things] arise in every moment of thought.
If one is free from grasping at form, there is neither arising nor ceasing.

Whether through dependent origination or non-dependent origination—whether it be ignorance, true suchness, or the like—the two dharmas give rise to manifestation; yet in the absence of duality, there is true suchness.
If those conditions and non-conditions, and the produced phenomena, were distinct;
and if there were a relationship of agent and acted between the eternal and other such [causes] and their conditions—
this would indeed be what is taught by the Great Muni and all the Buddhas.
To posit an agent and an object of action is no different from the non-Buddhists.
For my disciples, I have taught that the body is suffering and the world;
it is also the origin of the world, and it is fully endowed with cessation and the path.
Ordinary beings engage in false discrimination because they grasp at the three natures;
thus they perceive the existence of grasper and grasped, as well as mundane and supramundane phenomena.
It is because I have previously considered these dependencies that I speak of grasping at intrinsic nature.
Now, in order to block all views, one should not engage in false conceptualization.
Seeking faults constitutes what is not the Dharma, and it also causes the mind to be unsettled;
all these arise from the two-fold grasping, while non-duality is suchness itself.
If ignorance, craving, and karma give rise to consciousness and the other factors,
and these in turn have further causes through wrong mindfulness, then there would be the fault of infinite regress.
One who lacks wisdom speaks of the four kinds of cessation and destruction regarding all phenomena;
Delusively giving rise to the two types of discrimination, While phenomena in reality transcend existence and non-existence.
Far removed from the four extremes, And likewise free from the two views;
Once one thoroughly understands the duality arisen from discrimination, It will no longer arise.
"In non-arising one knows arising; in arising one knows non-arising.
Because those phenomena are equal, one should not give rise to discrimination.
"I pray that the Buddha will explain for me the principle of negating these two views."
May I and the rest of the assembly never fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence.
May we not be mixed with the various non-Buddhists, but remain free from the two vehicles;
may we abide in the sphere realized by all Buddhas, the stage from which the sons of the Buddha never regress.
The causes and non-causes of liberation are identical in their mark of non-arising;
yet, due to delusion, they are grasped as distinct names—this the wise should always avoid.
Phenomena arise from conceptual construction, like the appearance of falling hairs, illusions, or mirages.
The non-Buddhists falsely discriminate, claiming that the world arises from a primal nature (*svabhāva*).
Non-arising, suchness (*tathatā*), the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—these are spoken of as different names;
one should not cling to them as being non-existent.
Just as the hand has many names, so too are the names of Śakra;
all phenomena are likewise thus, and one should not grasp them as non-existent.
Form and emptiness are no different, and the same is true for non-arising.
One should not grasp [them] as distinct, for that would result in the faults of various views;
because of the discrimination between the general and the particular, and because of pervasive discrimination,
one becomes attached to the characteristics of all things, such as long and short, square and round.
General discernment is the mind (*citta*); pervasive discernment is the intellect (*manas*);
specific discernment is consciousness (*vijñāna*). All are devoid of the characteristics of subject and object.
Views arising within the self and phenomena, as well as the "non-arising" of the non-Buddhists;
All these are false conceptualizations; their faults are equal and no different.
If there is one who can understand what I have taught regarding non-arising, as well as that for which non-arising is intended, such a person understands my Dharma.
To destroy all views, [I teach] that there is neither arising nor a place of abiding;
to make known these two meanings, I therefore speak of non-arising.
If the Dharma of non-arising taught by the Buddha were either existent or non-existent;
This would be identical to the various non-Buddhist outsiders who maintain the doctrine that nothing arises without a cause.
I teach that all is but mind-only, which is far removed from existence and non-existence;
whether regarding arising or non-arising, one should abandon all such views.
The theory of no-cause results in non-arising; if there is arising, one clings to an agent.
If there is an agent, it is mixed with various views; if there is no agent, things arise spontaneously.
"The Buddha taught various skillful means, such as right view and the great vow."
"If all phenomena were non-existent, what would the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) be established upon?
Free from the grasper and the grasped, neither arising nor ceasing;
the perceived phenomena and non-phenomena all arise from one's own mind."
“What the Muni has taught is self-contradictory from beginning to end;
how can he speak of all phenomena and yet say they are unarisen?”
Sentient beings are unable to know this; I pray that the Buddha will explain it for me—how one may leave behind the faults of non-Buddhists and their causes of perversion.
I only pray that the Supreme Speaker will explain both arising and cessation.
"Free from both existence and non-existence, yet not destroying cause and effect.
"The world falls into two extremes, deluded by various views;
I pray that you, with your blue-lotus eyes, will explain the sequence of the stages."
Grasping at arising and non-arising, etc., one does not understand the cause of quiescence;
in the place of awakening there is nothing to be attained, and I likewise have nothing to say.
All phenomena are empty in a single instant; they are without arising and without intrinsic nature.
“The Buddhas have already purified duality; to have duality is to incur error.
Covered by evil views, you discriminate [the Buddha] as not being the Tathāgata;
you falsely reckon in terms of arising and ceasing—please explain this for our sake.”
"Accumulated through conceptual proliferation, born from the conjunction [of conditions];
appearing according to their respective types, the objects of form are all fully present."
Having seen external forms, one gives rise to conceptual discrimination;
if one can thoroughly understand this, then one sees the true meaning.
If separated from the great elements, all things are not established.
Since the great elements are but mind, one should know that nothing is produced.
This mind, too, is unproduced; thus one accords with the lineage of the noble ones.
Do not conceptualize conceptualization; non-conceptualization is wisdom.
To differentiate between differentiation—these two are not nirvāṇa.
If one establishes the thesis of non-arising, then one destroys the nature of illusory phenomena.
Furthermore, to claim that illusions arise without a cause is to undermine one's own school.

Just like a reflection in a mirror, Though it is free from the nature of being either identical to or different [from its cause], What is seen is not non-existent; The characteristic of arising is likewise so.
Like a city of the gandharvas or illusions, All exist in dependence upon causes and conditions.
All phenomena are likewise thus: they arise and do not fail to arise;
yet through the discrimination of persons and dharmas, two kinds of self are conceived.
This is merely conventional discourse, which the foolish do not perceive.
Through the convergence of aspiration and conditions, By one's own power and by the supreme [Buddha],
The fifth is the Śrāvaka-dharma, In which there are Arhats and others;
There is the separation of time and destruction, The ultimate truth and successive transition.
These four kinds of impermanence are conceptualized by the ignorant, not by the wise;
the fool falls into the two extremes, constructing the self-nature of virtues and defilements.
By grasping at the tenets of existence and non-existence, he does not know the cause of liberation.
The primary elements are mutually contradictory; how could they give rise to form?
There is only the nature of the primary elements, and no form produced by them;
fire burns form, and water causes it to rot and decay.
The wind can cause them to scatter and perish; how then could form arise?
The aggregate of form and the aggregate of consciousness—these two alone, and not five.
The rest are merely different names; I describe them as being like enemies.
The distinctions between mind and mental factors arise within the present life.
When analyzing all forms, one finds only mind with nothing created therein;
just as blue and white exist in mutual dependence, so too do the agent and the action.
That which is produced and its emptiness of intrinsic nature, the characteristics and the characterized,
existence and non-existence— all such things are not established through false conceptualization.
The mind, the intellect, and the other six consciousnesses are all associated in mutual correspondence.
All arise from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), being neither identical nor different. Those who calculate the number of categories,
the supreme self, or the naked ascetics, as well as those who reckon the Lord (*Īśvara*) as the creator—
all fall into the dogmas of existence and non-existence, and remain far removed from the meaning of tranquility.
The great elements produce form, yet they are not produced from the great elements;
the non-Buddhists claim that the great elements produce both further great elements and form.
Apart from these dharmas of non-arising, the non-Buddhists postulate a creator.
Relying on the doctrines of existence and non-existence, the foolish do not perceive it;
the pure and true nature is conjoined with great wisdom,
yet it corresponds only with the mind and is not a composite of the mental faculty and its objects.
If all karma were to produce form, it would contradict the causes of the aggregates;
sentient beings would have no grasping, and there would be no abiding in the formless.
If one says that form does not exist, then sentient beings would likewise not exist.
The formless realm is cessation; no consciousnesses should arise there.
Since consciousness abides in four ways, how could it be established in the formless?
When the internal and external are not established, consciousness likewise should not arise.
If the consciousness of sentient beings did not exist, they would naturally attain liberation;
this must be the doctrine of the non-Buddhists, which those who engage in false conceptualization do not understand.
Or there may be those who, following their own inclinations, cling to the existence of the various aggregates within the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Just as one is born in the formless realm, how could form exist there?
That "form within the formless" is not something visible;
to claim formlessness [in this sense] contradicts your own tenet, for there would be neither the vehicle nor the traveler.
Consciousness arises from habitual tendencies and is in conjunction with the sense faculties;
in a single moment, these eight kinds cannot be apprehended.
If material forms do not arise, the sense faculties are no longer faculties.
Therefore the World-Honored One said: "The sense-faculties, forms, and kṣaṇikas.
How can consciousness arise without apprehending form?
"How can consciousness not arise, yet still undergo birth and death?
"The noble ones understand the true meaning of the sense faculties and their objects;
the ignorant and witless falsely cling to their names."
One should not cling to the sixth [consciousness] as having grasping or being without grasping;
to avoid all faults, the Noble Ones have no fixed teaching.
The ignorant outsiders fear annihilationism and eternalism.
Whether calculating the conditioned or the unconditioned, they are no different from me.
Some calculate them as one with the mind, while others consider them distinct from the mental faculty (*manas*);
if they are of a single nature, there is something to be grasped, and if they are of different natures, it is likewise so.
If this grasping is what determines [cognition], it is called mind and mental factors;
why then can this grasping not determine a single nature?
Where there is grasping and the performance of action, birth can be obtained and experienced.
Just as that which is produced by fire—its principles appearing both similar and dissimilar—and just as when fire suddenly burns, both the burner and the combustible are fully present;
so too is the false grasping of a self. How could there be nothing grasped?
Whether arising or non-arising, the nature of mind is eternally pure;
why then do you not take the "self" established by the non-Buddhists as an analogy?
Deluded within the dense forest of consciousness, they falsely conceptualize that which is apart from the true Dharma.
Because they delight in my own doctrine, they run hither and thither in pursuit.
That which is the domain of internally realized wisdom—the pure characteristic of the true self—is the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is not known by those outside the Way.
One discriminates among the aggregates as the grasper and the grasped;
if one can thoroughly understand these characteristics, then true wisdom arises.
These various non-Buddhists, regarding the locus of the ālayavijñāna—
If one’s thoughts are in accord with me, this is not what the Buddha has taught.
If one can discern and understand this, one will be liberated and see the True Reality;
by seeing and cultivating, all afflictions are severed and become utterly pure.
The intrinsically pure mind is that which sentient beings mistakenly grasp;
the stainless Tathāgatagarbha is free from the extremes of finitude and infinity.
The fundamental consciousness resides within the aggregates, like gold and silver within ore.
Once the smelting and refining are complete, the gold and silver both manifest.
The Buddha is neither a person nor the aggregates; he is simply untainted wisdom.
Fully knowing him to be eternally tranquil, I take refuge in him.
"The mind that is pure by nature, which follows after afflictions, the mental faculty (*manas*), and so forth,
and which is associated with a self— I pray that the Buddha will explain this for me.
"The mind that is pure by nature, wherein the mental faculty and others are regarded as other..."
The karma accumulated by that [mind] is twofold due to its defilements:
the afflictions such as the mental faculty and so forth defile the pure mind,
just as various stains soil a clean cloth.
Just as clothing is freed from dirt, and just as gold is extracted from ore;
as neither the clothing nor the gold is destroyed, so too is the mind freed from faults.
When the ignorant seek after it, they find it in instruments such as the *vīṇā*, the conch, and the drum.
Yet one seeks a wondrous sound; so too is the self within the aggregates.
Like a hidden treasure, or like water beneath the earth—though it exists, it cannot be seen; such is the true self within the aggregates.
The functions of mind and mental factors are gathered together in association with the aggregates;
lacking wisdom, one cannot perceive them, and the self within the aggregates is likewise so.
It is like a woman carrying a fetus in her womb: though it exists, it cannot be seen.
The true self within the aggregates, The ignorant cannot perceive.
Like the supreme potency within medicine, Or like fire within wood;
The true self within the aggregates, The ignorant cannot perceive.
The emptiness within all phenomena, as well as their impermanent nature;
the true self within the aggregates—those lacking wisdom cannot know these.
The masteries of the stages, the supernormal powers, and the supreme samādhi of empowerment;
If this true self did not exist, all these things would likewise be non-existent.
If someone were to speak with destructive intent, saying, "If it exists, show it to me," the wise person should reply: "Show me what you have conceptualized."
Those who preach that there is no true self slander the Dharma by clinging to existence and non-existence;
such bhikṣus should be subjected to *karmavācanā* and expelled, not to be spoken with.
To preach that a true self exists is as fiercely blazing as the fires at the end of an eon.
He has burned away the dense forest of selflessness and is free from the errors of all non-Buddhist paths.
Just as with butter, curd, honey, sesame oil, and the like—
though they all possess flavor, those who have not tasted them do not know it.
Within the body of the aggregates, one seeks the self in five ways;
the fool cannot comprehend this, yet through wisdom and vision, one is liberated.
Though the metaphors established by the wise have not yet become clear to the mind, [one must strive to understand them].
How could the meanings gathered therein be made clearly understood?
The distinct characteristics of all phenomena are not realized as being but the One Mind;
those who engage in conceptual calculation falsely cling to [the notions of] causelessness and non-arising.
“The one in meditative concentration observes the mind, yet the mind does not see the mind;
seeing arises from that which is seen—by what cause does that which is seen arise?”
“My surname is Kātyāyana; I have emerged from among the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
I preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, leading them into the city of Nirvāṇa.”
Based upon the primordially abiding dharma,
I and all Tathāgatas have extensively expounded the dharma of nirvāṇa within the three thousand sūtras.
Neither in the desire realm nor in the formless realm does one attain buddhahood therein.
In the ultimate heaven of the form realm, one attains awakening through the abandonment of desire.
The objective field is not the cause of bondage; rather, it is the mind that is bound by the field.
By practicing with the sword of sharp wisdom, one cuts through those afflictions.
If there is no self, how can there be existence? Are phenomena such as illusions existent or non-existent?
A fool should manifest true suchness; why then is there no true self?
Both that which has already been produced and that which has not yet been produced do not arise from causes.
All things are entirely without arising, yet the foolish cannot comprehend this.
That which acts does not arise, nor do the objects acted upon or their various conditions;
since both of these are without arising, how can one conceive of an "agent"?
Those who engage in false conceptualization claim that there exist causes— whether prior, subsequent,
or simultaneous— that manifest jars, disciples, and so forth, and they speak of the arising of all things.
The Buddha is not a conditioned phenomenon, yet he is endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence.
These are the merits of a wheel-turning monarch; this is not what is called a Tathāgata.
The Buddha takes wisdom as his characteristic and is far removed from all views;
that which he realizes within himself is the sphere of his practice, wherein all faults are severed.

Those who are deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired, as well as the elderly, children, and those harboring resentment—these particularly heavy [obstructions] all lack the potential for the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) being obscured leads to birth as a deva; the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) being obscured leads to becoming a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
These two are attached to negligence; only the Illustrious One has left the household life.
After my parinirvāṇa, Śākya, there shall appear Vyāsa, Kaṇāda, Śaiva, Kapila, and others.
One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be the treatises spoken by Vyāsa, such as the Mahābhārata; next will come the Khaśas.
Then there will be Kaurava and Rāma, followed by King Mleccha.
Nanda and Kṣemaka, followed by King Mleccha;
thereafter, weapons shall arise, and there will follow a time of extreme evil.
At that time, throughout all the worlds, the True Dharma will not be practiced.
After such a period has passed, the world revolves like a wheel;
the sun and fire unite together to incinerate the desire realm.
Once again, the various heavens are established, and the world is restored to completion.
When kings and the four castes, as well as the seers who bestow the teachings and transformations,
the Vedas, sacrifices, and offerings— when these dharmas arise;
when there are discourses, jesting, long prose, and commentaries.
Having heard such things as these, I am bewildered by the world;
regarding the various robes one receives, if they possess their original colors,
one must dye them with blue mud, cow dung, or the like to make them a discolored hue.
All garments worn shall cause one to leave behind the marks of non-Buddhists;
appearing as a practitioner, one displays the banner-signs of the Buddhas.
One should also fasten a waistband and filter water before drinking it.
Alms are sought in due order, never at improper places;
one is born in the sublime celestial realms, or among human beings.
Those endowed with the marks of excellence are born as gods or as kings of men.
The King ruled over the four continents, governing by the Dharma for a long time.
Having ascended to the celestial palaces, he lost it all through greed;
there were periods of pure goodness and three seasons, as well as two seasons of extreme evil.
Other Buddhas appear during good times, but Śākyamuni appears in an evil age;
after my parinirvāṇa, the Śākya Siddhārtha will appear.
Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and other non-Buddhist teachers will all emerge together.
"Thus have I heard," and so forth, was spoken by the Lion of the Śākyas;
his ancient tales and humorous sayings were spoken by the seer Vyāsa;
and after my parinirvāṇa, [they shall be spoken by] Viṣṇu and Maheśvara.
He spoke these words:
"I am able to create the world;
my name is Buddha Free from Dust (Vimala), and my clan is Kātyāyana."
My father’s name was Lokanātha, and my mother was known as Vasumatī;
I was born in the kingdom of Campā, the ancestral grandfather of my lineage.
Born from the Lunar Clan (Somavaṃśa), I am therefore called Candragarbha.
Having left the household life to practice austerities and expound upon a thousand dharma-gates,
he bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon Mahāmati, and only then entered parinirvāṇa.
Mahāmati entrusted [the teaching] to Dharma, who in turn entrusted it to Meghīya.
During the evil age of Mikhali, when the kalpa ends, the Dharma shall perish.
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and I,
who am free from dust and defilement— all have appeared during times of pure goodness.
When pure goodness gradually diminishes, there will be a teacher named Hui (Wisdom),
who achieves great valor and awakens to the five dharmas;
this shall not be during the second or third period, nor during a time of extreme evil.
In that age of pure goodness, he manifested the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment.
Although his robes were not cut from threads but pieced together from fragments like the eyes on a peacock’s tail, no one could ever seize them by force.
Whether two fingers or three fingers wide, pieced together in various patterns;
whatever is fashioned other than this, the foolish give rise to craving and attachment.
Wearing only the three robes, one constantly extinguishes the fire of greed and desire.
Wash yourself with the water of wisdom, practicing three times throughout the day and night;
like the momentum of a released arrow, one falls as another is launched,
and it is the same with the churning stick for curd— so it is with the wholesome and the unwholesome.
If one could produce many, there would be the characteristic of differentiation;
the giver would be like the field, and the receiver would be like the wind.
If one could produce many, everything would exist without cause.
The destruction of the causes of what has been produced is established through false conceptualization.
If that which is established by false conceptualization— like a lamp or a seed—
could produce many from one, it would only be similar [to its cause] and not manifold.
Sesame does not produce beans; rice is not the cause of coarse grain or wheat;
small beans are not the seeds of [other] grains—how then can one give rise to many?
Nāmasūtra composed the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, and Viśālākṣa created the *Rājaśāstra*.
The false doctrines of the Lokāyata will arise;
the Kātyāyanas will compose sutras, the Vālmīkas will preach sacrifices,
and the owl-like [Bārhaspatyas] will produce works on astrology— these shall appear in the age of degeneration.
The sentient beings of the world, through the power of their merit, have brought forth this king;
he governs all in accordance with the Dharma and protects the realm.
Even the blue ants and the red beans, the crooked paths and the horse tracks—[all are preserved].
These sages of great merit shall appear in future ages.
The son of the Śākyas, Siddhārtha; Bhūta and Pañcaśikha;
Vāgīśa and Medhāvin—these too shall appear in the future.
While I was dwelling in the forest, Brahmā came to bestow upon me a deer skin,
a triple-pronged staff, a shoulder strap, and a water jar;
this great practitioner shall surely become a venerable one free from defilement.
Having spoken of true liberation, the banner-sign of the Muni,
Brahmā and his host, the devas and their retinues,
presented me with deerskin robes and returned to their own sovereign palaces.
While I was among the forest trees, Śakra and the Four Great Kings offered me exquisite robes as well as alms bowls.
If one establishes the doctrine of non-arising, then this cause arises and arises again.
To establish non-arising in this manner is merely empty speech.
That which has been accumulated since beginningless time, with ignorance as the cause of the mind, continues through arising and ceasing;
it is the conceptual construction of false discrimination.
The Sāṃkhya treatise has two [positions]: primordial nature (prakṛti) and transformation (vikṛti).
If activity were to exist within primordial nature, then that which is produced would necessarily be self-existent;
yet primordial nature coexists with its objects, and the guṇas are said to be distinct.
The various things created and their makers, Their transformations cannot be found;
Like pure quicksilver, Which cannot be defiled by dust or grime,
So too is the purity of the ālayavijñāna, Upon which all sentient beings rely.
Just as with the scent of asafoetida and onions, the taste of salt, and the fetal womb, so it is with seeds: how could they not give rise [to sprouts]?
This applies equally to identity and difference, as well as to both together and neither.
It is not an existent that can be grasped, nor is it non-existent or a product of existence;
as the nature of a cow is absent within a horse, so too is a self absent within the aggregates.
Both the conditioned and the unconditioned that have been explained are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
To seek a self through reasoning, scripture, and so forth, is a false, defiled, and evil view.
Because one does not understand, one speaks of its existence; yet it is merely a vain grasping, leaving nothing behind.
Within the aggregates, a self—whether identical to or different from them—is in neither case established.
Those faults are manifest, yet the deluded do not perceive them;
just as various reflections appear in water, mirrors, and the eye,
so too is the self within the aggregates, free from being either identical to or different from them.
The practitioner cultivates meditative concentration, Perceiving both the Truths and the Path.
Diligently practicing these three kinds, One is liberated from all evil views;
Just as through a crack or opening, One sees a flash of lightning that vanishes in an instant.
The transformation of phenomena is likewise; one should not give rise to conceptual discrimination.
The minds of the foolish are deluded, grasping at the existence or non-existence of nirvāṇa.
If one attains the vision of the noble ones, one can understand it as it truly is.
One should know that the nature of transformation is far removed from arising and ceasing;
it is also free from existence and non-existence, as well as the characteristics of subject and object.
One should know that the nature of transformation is far removed from the doctrines of the heterodox paths.
Furthermore, it is free from names and signs, and the internal view of self is extinguished;
the gods experience pleasure touching their bodies, while those in hell are oppressed by physical suffering.
If that intermediate state (*antarābhava*) did not exist, the various consciousnesses could not arise.
One should know that within the various realms of existence, the diverse bodies of sentient beings—
whether born from a womb, an egg, or moisture— all arise following the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Apart from the correct reasoning of the Noble Teaching, those who wish to extinguish delusions only cause them to increase further.
These are the deluded words of non-Buddhists; the wise should not speak them.
First, one must definitively understand [the self] and distinguish the various forms of grasping;
yet, like the son of a barren woman, there is nothing to be definitively understood or distinguished.
I am free from the fleshly eye; with the divine eye and the wisdom-eye, I see the bodies of all sentient beings as being detached from all formations and aggregates.
Observing within these formations, I see both beautiful colors and ugly colors.
Liberation and non-liberation, those who dwell among the devas, and the bodies received in the various realms of existence—I alone am able to fully comprehend these.
They transcend what is known by the world; they are not within the sphere of conceptual speculation.
The mind arises despite the absence of a self; how, then, does this mind arise?
Is it not said that the arising of the mind is like a river, a lamp, or a seed?
If ignorance and the other [afflictions] were absent, the consciousness-mind would not arise.
Apart from ignorance, there is no consciousness; how, then, could a continuity arise?
This is what those who engage in false conceptualization say:
that it exists in the three times, or is non-temporal, or is the fifth, the inexpressible—this is what the Buddhas know.
The various formations (saṃskāra) are the basis upon which grasping (upādāna) rests;
these too serve as causes for wisdom (jñāna). One should not say that wisdom is itself called "formations.
Because of these causes and conditions, this phenomenon arises.
There is no separate agent; this is what I have taught.
Wind cannot produce fire, yet it causes fire to blaze up, and it is also by wind that fire is extinguished;
how, then, can it serve as an analogy for the self?
That which is spoken of as conditioned and unconditioned is entirely free from all grasping.
Why do the foolish discriminate, establishing a self by means of fire?
It is through the successive power of various conditions that fire is thus able to arise.
If discrimination is like fire, from whom is this "self" born?
Because the mind and other factors serve as its causes, the aggregates and sense-bases accumulate.
This merchant-leader that is without self always arises together with the mind.
These two are ever like the sun, transcending both agent and action.
They cannot be established by fire; those who engage in false conceptualization do not know this.
The nirvāṇa of the minds of sentient beings is their nature, which is eternally pure.
Defiled by habitual tendencies from beginningless transgression, it is no different from space;
like the "reclining elephant" and other non-Buddhist views, it is defiled by various dogmatic perspectives.
Covered by the mental consciousness, one reckons fire and such things to be pure.
If one attains suchness-as-it-is vision, one is then able to sever the afflictions.
Abandoning the thicket of false metaphors, one reaches the sphere traversed by the noble ones;
through the distinctions known by wisdom, each is analyzed according to its differences.
The ignorant do not know; they speak what should not be spoken.
Just as a fool might take various other woods and claim they are sandalwood or aloeswood, so too should one understand their false conceptualizations regarding true wisdom.
Having finished eating, one should take the bowl and return;
wash it until it is clean, and rinse the mouth to remove any lingering flavor—one should practice in this manner.
If one applies correct reflection to this Dharma-gate according to the principle, [one will attain liberation].
With pure faith free from conceptualization, you have accomplished the most supreme concentration;
detached from clinging, you abide in the ultimate meaning and have become the Dharma-lamp of Golden Light.
You have severed the webs of wrong views and the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence.
Having abandoned the three poisons and all else, one receives the empowerment from the hand of the Buddha.
Those who cling to a creator among the non-Buddhists, those who are confused about directions, those who hold to causelessness,
those who are terrified by dependent origination, and those who advocate annihilationism lack the nature of the noble ones.
The transformations that give rise to all karmic retributions are called the various consciousnesses and the manas;
the manas arises from the ālayavijñāna, while the consciousnesses arise depending on the manas.
The ālayavijñāna gives rise to all mental states, just as the ocean gives rise to waves.
With habitual tendencies as their cause, they arise in accordance with conditions.
Moment by moment, linked like a chain, they grasp the objects of one's own mind;
from these various forms and appearances, the consciousnesses of the mental faculty and the others are produced.
Due to beginningless evil habits, [consciousness] arises as if from external objects;
what is seen is only one's own mind, which is not understood by outsiders.
Because of that, it conditions that, and thus other cognitions arise.
Therefore, by giving rise to various views, one wanders through birth and death.
All phenomena are like illusions and dreams, like the moon in water, a mirage, or a city of the gandharvas;
know that all phenomena are nothing but one's own conceptual discrimination.
Right wisdom relies upon suchness, From which all samādhis arise;
Such as the illusion-like Śūraṅgama, And various other distinctions.
One attains entry into the stages, Mastery, and supernormal powers.
Having accomplished the wisdom that is like an illusion, all Buddhas bestow empowerment upon his crown.
Seeing the world as false and illusory, at that moment his mind undergoes transformation;
he attains the Stage of Joy, as well as all the other stages and the stage of Buddhahood.
Having already attained the transformation of the basis, like a mani jewel reflecting myriad colors,
one benefits all sentient beings, appearing according to their needs like the moon in water.
One abandons the views of existence and non-existence, as well as both [existence and non-existence] and neither.
Surpassing the practices of the two vehicles, And transcending even the seventh stage,
One internally realizes the Dharma for oneself, Cultivating and purifying stage by stage;
Far removed from all non-Buddhist paths— This should be called the Mahāyāna.
The teaching of the dharma-gate of liberation is like a rabbit’s horn or a mani-jewel;
it abandons conceptual discrimination and is free from death and transmigration.
The teaching is established by means of principle, and principle is revealed by means of the teaching.
One should rely upon this teaching and principle; do not engage in further conceptual discrimination.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
